[6] National Defense has demonstrated, in these years in which I have held the Presidency of the Republic, that it continues to be a fundamental institution for the development of the State of Chile

[7] Since the publication of the last Defense Book in 2010, during my previous administration, the country has been ravaged by catastrophes of increasing magnitude and frequency, causing human losses and significant material damage

[8] In all of them, the Ministry of National Defense and the Armed Forces have played a significant role in addressing these critical moments and overcoming emergencies during the reconstruction process

[9] Equipped with dual or multi-purpose capabilities

[10] The military institutions have thus fulfilled the obligation that the Constitution and the laws impose on them

[11] Chile has defense institutions that are professionally and materially prepared for this, as a result of the development of a stable and long-term defense policy

[12] The fundamental aspects of this policy have been captured in the successive National Defense books that democratic governments began publishing starting in

[13] Building broad agreements in the country regarding what its defense should be is not a simple task

[14] It requires political will, and there may be legitimate differences, but carrying out the effort must be the responsibility of every democratic government

[15] That is why, as President of the Republic, I am proud to present the fourth Book of National Defense, which summarizes the progress made to date in the evolution of Chile's Defense Policy

[16] These texts are among the most innovative initiatives in civil management in the defense sector, and in the public sector in general, in recent decades

[17] Together with the constitutional reforms of 2005 regarding this area of matters and the promulgation, in 2010, of Law No. 20,424, which established the new Organic Statute of the Ministry of National Defense, the publication of these successive books has constituted a step forward in the continuous improvement of the democratic governance of defense

[18] This has been reflected both in the normative dimension, materializing the constitutional and legal provisions according to which the conduct of defense must be exercised by the political authority, and in the practical dimension of political or civil control and leadership in the various processes linked to defense

[19] Specifically, the development of these books has made it possible to further develop the formulation of Defense Policy as a public policy and has provided greater transparency to the sector's activities at the national and international levels

[20] Along with creating conditions for the domestic and international public to have better judgment, the text reflects the work carried out by the Ministry of National Defense, particularly since late 2015, to achieve new standards of integrity and transparency throughout the sector

[21] To this end, and in addition to implementing the general integrity measures established by the laws enacted for this purpose, the role of the Internal Control Units was strengthened both in military institutions and within the Ministry itself, the Supplier Registry regulations were updated, and an annual audit plan was formulated

[22] Likewise, specific processes were established to standardize accountability and strengthen the prevention of conflicts of interest

[23] At the same time, in terms of international transparency commitments, practices for providing information to the United Nations and the Union of South American Nations were consolidated, while measures to build mutual trust with neighboring countries were increased

[24] This new book reaffirms the idea that Defense Policy, whose contents draw on contributions from various public and private sectors, is a matter that concerns society as a whole because it serves all those who live in our country

[25] Furthermore, presenting the Defense Policy to the international community is a clear way to renew Chile's commitment to safeguarding its external security in accordance with the principles of the United Nations Charter, the provisions of international law, and building trust through transparency and cooperation

[26] This text, the fourth since the Ministry of National Defense began publishing this type of document, establishes a line of continuity with the previous one, in force since

[27] This third book was prepared in conjunction with the legislative process that culminated in February of that same year with the approval of Law No. 20,424 and, consequently, was unable to reflect the contents and scope of this law

[28] The legal framework came into force, modernizing not only the organization of the Ministry of National Defense, but also the processes of defense leadership, planning, operation, and management

[29] The set of changes triggered by this legal regulation has been captured in this fourth version of the Book of Defense, a text that describes the institutional advances made, reports on new sectoral public policies, and anticipates their development prospects for the timeframe in which it is intended to come into force

[30] One such subject is defense planning methodology

[31] This period has demonstrated the importance of the regulation approved in 2010, which established the development of defense employment policy planning, also known as primary planning, among the functions of the civilian bodies responsible for defense, particularly the Undersecretariat of Defense, and organically linked it with military, or secondary, planning, located at the strategic level of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the institutional level of the Armed Forces

[32] However, this book goes further and anticipates the contents of the new capability-based planning methodology that the Ministry of National Defense has implemented

[33] The new methodology constitutes a paradigm shift in National Defense

[34] It was jointly prepared by the Ministry, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and the Armed Forces, bringing Chile closer to the highest international standards currently in use in both NATO countries and some Latin American countries, such as Argentina and Colombia

[35] These processes have been carried out in a fragmented manner

[36] Each branch of the Armed Forces has planned its long-term development, defining a time horizon and institutional objectives without having received the appropriate guidance from political authorities

[37] Until now, military institutions have relied on documents such as Defense books or on capacity employment planning, which has generally been medium-term

[38] With the new capability-based methodology, the Ministry of Defense will be tasked with defining, in conjunction with the relevant public sector agencies, the long-term international and national scenarios in which the use of defense resources is likely, the type of capability the State desires for its military institutions, and the level of effort required

[39] This planning will allow the Ministry of National Defense to formulate military policies accurately across the entire spectrum of needs for the development of required capabilities, including human and material resources

[40] National Defense will thus complete the transition from a bottom-up decision-making process to a top-down one, substantially strengthening its institutional capacities and, with it, the effectiveness of democratic political institutions' control over National Defense

[41] The new Defense Book reflects the evolution of the most recent public policies being developed in the sector

[42] For the first time in its history, the Ministry of Defense has begun preparing a policy that will allow it to contribute organically to national efforts to mitigate and adapt to the effects of global warming and climate change, an effort carried out in conjunction with the Ministry of the Environment

[43] Also for the first time, and within the framework of the National Cybersecurity Policy, which my government launched in 2017, the National Defense Ministry is implementing its first cyber defense policy, which will be integrated into capabilities-based planning for the development of cyber capabilities

[44] The Ministry of Defense has also prepared the first National Defense Human Rights Policy, providing a set of guidelines and guidance on the observance of fundamental rights that should guide all institutions in the sector

[45] Within this framework, the Book also reports on the progress made as a result of the launch, in 2014, of the Inclusion Roundtable of the Ministry of National Defense, both in relation to gender policies, as well as sexual diversity, people with disabilities, and indigenous peoples

[46] The same applies to joint institutionality

[47] This new version of the Defense Book includes a specific chapter on joint institutionality and another on the Joint Chiefs of Staff, reflecting the developments in this area since 2010, with the enactment of Law 20,424, which created this joint body, and putting it into perspective for its development

[48] This institution represents a milestone in both strategic management and planning at this level

[49] What has been achieved to date has allowed Chile to begin catching up with the joint development achieved not only by more advanced countries in defense, but also by some in our region

[50] What is needed is to strengthen joint institutionality, a task for which my government has prepared a bill

[51] The achievements made in the areas described over the seven years since the publication of the 2010 National Defense Book also respond to the need to support the international cooperation efforts outlined in the Defense Policy, contributing to Chile's Foreign Policy and its role in the international community

[52] After thirteen years of leading, alongside other countries in the region, the solidarity effort with Haiti, Chile concluded its military participation in the United Nations Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH) this year

[53] Together with the rest of the international community, our country was able to effectively contribute to the stabilization of that Caribbean nation, which has been confirmed by the growing stability of its political and electoral processes

[54] In this new phase of United Nations cooperation with Haiti, we will continue to collaborate through the support of the Carabineros and the Investigative Police to the Haitian National Police

[55] The book reports on other relevant policies underway at the international level, highlighting Chile's support for United Nations missions and, in particular, for the peace process in Colombia

[56] Our country has been one of the supporters of the Colombian peace process and one of the main contributors to the Political Mission approved by the UN Security Council in 2016, which concluded in 2017, and to the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia, approved in July 2017 and which is currently underway

[57] In the coming years, Chile will have to make significant efforts to maintain the prestige it has gained through its participation in MINUSTAH and in Colombia as a contributor to UN peacekeeping operations

[58] One of the important areas where Latin America and the international community are concentrating their efforts is Africa

[59] Chile has been one of the main global and regional promoters of UN Resolution 1325 “Women, Peace and Security.”

[60] It is the only country in the region that has implemented two action plans in this regard (2009 and 2014), and has decisively promoted its adoption in Latin America through an alliance with the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC) and several regional governments

[61] In the area of international cooperation carried out through defense, the Book reveals in great detail the significant progress that has been made, both with countries in other regions, multilateral institutions, and global forums, such as Europe and the Asia-Pacific, but with a special emphasis on our continent

[62] There are significant steps in which Chile has managed to contribute with clear leadership over time, whether within the Conference of Defense Ministers of the Americas or the South American Defense Council, promoting transparency, cooperation in the face of natural or man-made disasters, or gender equality in the region's armed forces

[63] Particularly rich is the agenda of bilateral relations that has been built with Argentina, Peru, and Brazil, among other countries

[64] In the case of Argentina, the Book reaffirms that both countries have ruled out any possibility of conflict

[65] With Peru, progress has been made toward a phase of greater cooperation, marked by the holding of the first Binational Cabinet meeting in 2017 and a Meeting of Foreign and Defense Ministers, which adopted the most ambitious work agenda achieved to date between the two countries

[66] Perhaps one of the most relevant aspects of this edition of the National Defense Book is the confirmation that the combination of the advances achieved in our region in recent decades has generated a Zone of Peace that contrasts with the growing global instability

[67] In this way, Latin America contributes to world peace both through the stability built by its democracies and through its growing contributions to peacekeeping operations

[68] I can say with satisfaction that we have a professional and increasingly institutionally robust Ministry of Defense, imbued with the firm commitment to contribute to political leadership based on civilian pre-eminence, as well as professional and effective Armed Forces in the performance of their duties

[69] The Defense sector can claim to operate in an environment of cooperation and inspired by the principles of democratic governance, which have evolved substantially since

[70] We are fully aware that, despite the progress made, there are still areas of weakness, and therefore significant challenges remain, both in the institutional development of the sector and in efforts to contribute through the Defense sector to a more stable and peaceful world and region

[71] This book helps citizens and the international community understand what National Defense does and intends to do, but it also encourages, perhaps like no previous version, reflection on a sector of the State that is dynamic and relevant to the country

[72] As President of the Republic, I invite you to learn more about this work

[73] We have been committed to promoting this project because we deeply believe we are providing a valuable tool, positioning defense as a modern, efficient area of public policy, and, above all, at the service of the Chilean people

[74] Finally, and as I expressed in the previous book, I would like to confirm that the Chilean State's central purpose in matters relating to defense is to ensure peace, offer peace, and work for peace

[75] INTRODUCTION JOSÉ ANTONIO GÓMEZ URRUTIA MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENSE Seven years after the publication of the third version of the National Defense Book, the Government of Chile makes the fourth version of this Book available to the national and international community

[76] Since the return of democracy, the National Defense Ministry has undergone a significant process of institutional reform and modernization, with Law No. 20,424, the "Organic Statute of the Ministry of National Defense," being one of the largest reforms in the history of this State portfolio

[77] National Defense books have been a reflection of the various modernization cycles the sector has undergone and the most complete expression of Defense Policy

[78] The 2017 version of the National Defense Book was born out of the need to update this policy to reflect the national and global changes impacting the defense agenda and, particularly, the transformations experienced by the sector

[79] This last aspect is particularly relevant considering that the Book in force since early 2010 failed to incorporate the rules and scope of Law No. 20,424, the Organic Statute of the Ministry of National Defense, also enacted in

[80] The Ministry of National Defense, in formulating the project for the development of a new Defense Book, determined that, as a new modernization cycle in the sector progressed with the implementation of the provisions of the aforementioned law, it was necessary to orient Defense Policy, Military Policy, and the main corresponding subsidiary policies from that perspective and with a medium-term time horizon

[81] Over the past 20 years, books have appeared, on average, one every five years, a period sufficient to verify the identification of challenges, the maturation of initiatives, the refinement of processes, and the incorporation of concepts associated with defense issues

[82] This is also the timeframe we have planned for the release of this new version of the National Defense Book

[83] The Ministry of Defense has promoted a broad sectoral agenda, which has included the update of the Defense Policy and the preparation of the 2017 Book

[84] This process, which began with an initial seminar in November 2015, culminates today with the publication of this new text for public awareness

[85] As has been the trend since the first version in 1997, the National Defense books have constituted a milestone in the formulation of Defense Policy, with the participation of both civilians and military personnel, and due to the range of defense topics that are the subject of open analysis and debate

[86] The first stage of the development of the 2017 National Defense Book took place through a widely attended program of seminars and workshops, with representatives from state agencies, the Armed Forces, the National Congress, academia, and civil society

[87] This program was developed during 2016 and included twelve seminars, one of which was held at the Southern Joint Command, located in the city of Punta Arenas

[88] These activities were intended to generate input for the content that would be incorporated into the new version of this important National Defense document

[89] The seminars covered a variety of topics of interest to Defense Policy, such as international security at its various levels, sector governance, Military Policy, the inclusion and non-discrimination agenda, and new challenges, especially focused on cyberspace and climate change

[90] All of these issues, among others, were addressed by panels of experts from both the defense sector and other public institutions and civil society

[91] A total of 37 exhibitors participated in the twelve meetings held

[92] Thirteen were officials from the Ministry of Defense and members of the Armed Forces, and eleven came from other public departments, including the Minister of Foreign Affairs

[93] Also presenting were a Representative of the Republic, the Mayor of Magallanes and Chilean Antarctica, and twelve panelists from the academic and scientific world

[94] The audience attending the workshops was made up of people from a wide range of institutions

[95] Representatives of the Senate of the Republic, the Chamber of Deputies, and former Ministers of Defense were invited to the meetings described above, as well as officials from other ministries and the National Congress, representatives of international organizations based in Chile and civil society, in addition to representatives of political parties with parliamentary representation and their respective think tanks, some twenty national and international research centers, and ten universities in the country

[96] Based on the recorded and transcribed discussions and specific documentary materials requested from institutions and experts, the second stage of the Book's development process was undertaken

[97] It consisted of systematizing the content and drafting it in advance. Five Working Groups were formed, comprised of staff from both ministerial undersecretariats, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and Armed Forces institutions, as well as guests from other state agencies

[98] This second phase of the process concluded with each Working Group submitting a compendium of materials addressed and processed, along with a preliminary draft

[99] In a third stage, a drafting committee was formed with members of the armed forces, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and the two undersecretariats of the Ministry of Defense

[100] The task of this panel was to review the Groups' materials, present observations, and propose a detailed treatment of the topics

[101] Finally, the systematized contents were made available to the team at the Undersecretariat of Defense, legally responsible for updating the Defense Policy, who assembled, corrected, and edited them to generate a first draft of the text

[102] This draft, subject to the comments of the relevant authorities, has become the new version of the National Defense Book

[103] The document that we make available to the national and international community is structured around eight parts: The State of Chile, The international political and strategic context, The National Defense Policy, The Military Policy, The financial resources of Defense, Integrity, transparency and control, The capabilities of National Defense, and Contributions of defense to development. The first two parts are general and have a background character

[104] The remaining six parts contain what National Defense does or contemplates within that framework

[105] The subjects of the parties are addressed in 27 chapters, ranging from the fundamental foundations of the State and Defense to the contribution of military organizations to the country's development and the work of the defense industry. This includes the challenges of international cooperation, the formulation of policies on new issues—such as climate change and cyberspace—a new defense planning methodology that considers the different mission areas of National Defense in which military institutions carry out assigned tasks, financial resource management mechanisms, and transparency and oversight initiatives, in addition to the respective chapters on the institutions of the Armed Forces

[106] Although some of these topics have been addressed in previous editions, particularly the 2010 version, they are reviewed and updated this time around in light of the changes that have altered our strategic environment, as well as the regulations that have strengthened the institutional structure of the sector, particularly the Ministry of Defense

[107] In this regard, the institutional advances that have shaped this Ministry through the creation of the Undersecretariat of Defense, the Undersecretariat for the Armed Forces, and the Joint Chiefs of Staff are noted

[108] Although there is still a long way to go, the Ministry of Defense has assumed an active role in the political leadership of defense and has taken charge of progress toward a civilian leadership capable of making the necessary decisions to respond to the challenges of 21st-century defense

[109] This involves making decisions on defense matters that have traditionally been a specialization of the military establishment, such as defense planning

[110] The current approach requires understanding planning as a single, integrated process that considers functions assumed by the political level responsible for National Defense and functions executed, under joint guidance, by the strategic and institutional levels, both in terms of employment and capacity development

[111] The development of joint institutionalism, another of the topics addressed in this version of the Defense Book, falls within this same framework

[112] The proposal for new initiatives for the development of the joint force will require refining and consolidating doctrinal content, the development of which gained significant momentum following the enactment of Law No. 20,424, which created the Joint Chiefs of Staff as a substitute body for the former National Defense Staff

[113] Regarding the modernization of the Armed Forces' institutions, this new version of the National Defense Book addresses areas related to capacity building and the development of the institutions that comprise Military Policy

[114] These areas include initiatives such as the promotion of human rights, inclusion and non-discrimination, and a gender perspective, all of which have been worked on jointly by ministerial bodies and branches of the Armed Forces

[115] The book also reflects the changes that have taken place in the international context, providing a backdrop that sheds light on the updating of the Defense Policy

[116] This diagnosis is a fairly developed aspect in this new version of the text, given the growing participation of National Defense in international activities

[117] In this regard, one of the emphases of Defense Policy has been on regional cooperation and, in particular, the active construction of a Zone of Peace in this part of the world, as well as its contribution to global security and peace within the framework of the United Nations

[118] Likewise, new topics that have become increasingly relevant in our times are being incorporated, such as the development of innovative sectoral policies that guide defense actions in the face of new challenges in the strategic environment, such as climate change, cyber defense, and technology and innovation

[119] The chapters relating to the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the institutional branches also include the mission areas of National Defense in which they carry out their tasks, thus providing a general account of the full spectrum of roles that the Armed Forces can perform for the benefit of the country

[120] The development of modern, versatile, and efficient forces is not a cost, but an investment, both for the execution of their military tasks and for the exercise of other roles

[121] This is a modern and integrative approach to serving the nation in times of peace and conflict, as required

[122] This is what has been called the versatility of our defense institutions

[123] Military capabilities are developed to ensure the country's external peace and security as its primary function

[124] However, Chile cannot refrain from employing these capabilities in a broader range of missions when the well-being of the population is at stake in catastrophic situations such as those experienced by our country, now exacerbated by the effects of global warming and climate change, which require a recurring response, or when responding to social needs such as health or the integration of national communities living in isolated or extreme areas

[125] Within the framework of the Constitution and the law, joint work in mission areas such as these has made it possible to launch coordinated operations with the direct participation of the Armed Forces, other state institutions, municipalities, private organizations, non-governmental organizations, and organized society, bringing relief to the community

[126] The processes and changes described, institutional strengthening in general, and modern defense require increasing levels of transparency

[127] For several decades now, the defense sector has ceased to be a remnant of other state institutions

[128] On the contrary, despite the strategic nature of defense for national interests, efficiency, transparency, and integrity appear in today's world as important elements for ensuring the security and stability of countries

[129] We hope that this new edition of the Defense Book will make a contribution in this regard

[159] From this framework, state action in the area of external security is guided, while also considering the international context and the obligations that arise from it

[160] This first part establishes the fundamental features of Defense in the Chilean State, for which it succinctly describes the constitutional bases of Defense, such as the purposes of the State related to security and defense, and the constitutional duties related to Defense

[161] The links between the State, society, and the individual are also addressed, and a section is included that refers to the Chilean population, one of the constituent elements of the State relevant to National Defense

[162] This section also describes the national territory from a defense perspective, considering land, sea, and airspace, as well as Chile's presence in Antarctica and outer space

[163] CHAPTER I. THE STATE AND NATIONAL DEFENSE The principles of the republican and democratic institutional order of Chile and the objectives set by the Nation play a crucial role within the elements on which National Defense is based

[164] These are the foundation for the State's action in pursuit of the country's external security, an area in which the convergence and collaboration between Defense Policy and Foreign Policy are essential, with the former acting in support of the latter

[165] This chapter describes the institutional order, the constitutional foundations of Defense and the conceptual aspects of the links between the State, society and the human person

[166] Institutional Order: Democracy and the Rule of Law Chile is a democratic republic where the rule of law prevails, along with the principles of constitutional supremacy, legality, judicial protection, and oversight of state administration actions

[167] In this context, the State guarantees the right of people to participate with equal opportunities in national life and the full exercise of individual freedoms and essential human rights

[168] According to the Political Constitution of the Republic, sovereignty resides essentially in the Nation and is exercised by the people, either directly (elections and plebiscites) or through the authorities that represent them, recognizing as limits to their actions the essential rights that emanate from human nature

[169] The State of Chile is unitary and is administratively organized into regions, provinces, and communes

[170] In its foreign relations, it conducts itself based on the principles and norms of international law, to which it has sovereignly and voluntarily adhered

[171] It exercises its sovereignty in the air and maritime spaces that belong to it and extends its jurisdiction over those in which it has sovereign rights and jurisdiction in accordance with international law

[172] At the same time, it has responsibilities and rights in outer space, founded on international treaties, and recognizes the principle of non-sovereignty and the principle of the common good of humanity that apply to outer space

[173] Chile has sovereign rights over its Antarctic territory based on historical, geographical, and legal grounds, which it exercises in a manner consistent with its membership in the 1959 Antarctic Treaty and other instruments of the Antarctic System

[174] Constitutional Basis of Defense The Political Constitution of the Republic contains purposes of the State related to Defense that are explicitly mentioned, such as the defense of the homeland and the protection of the population. Article 1 (paragraph 5): It is the duty of the State to safeguard national security, provide protection to the population and the family, tend to strengthen it, promote the harmonious integration of all sectors of the Nation and ensure the right of people to participate with equal opportunities in national life

[175] Article 5 (paragraph 2): The exercise of sovereignty recognizes as a limitation the respect for essential rights that emanate from human nature

[176] It is the duty of State bodies to respect and promote these rights, guaranteed by this Constitution, as well as by the international treaties ratified by Chile and currently in force

[177] Article 101: The Armed Forces dependent on the Ministry in charge of National Defense are constituted solely and exclusively by the Army, the Navy and the Air Force

[178] They exist for the defense of the homeland and are essential for national security

[179] The Public Order and Security Forces are composed only of Carabineros and Investigations

[180] They constitute the public force and exist to enforce the law, guarantee public order and internal security, in the manner determined by their respective organic laws

[181] They depend on the Ministry in charge of Public Security

[182] The Armed Forces and Carabineros, as armed bodies, are essentially obedient and non-deliberative

[183] The forces under the ministries responsible for National Defense and Public Security are also professional, hierarchical, and disciplined

[184] Aside from the aforementioned constitutional foundations, Chile, like any state, has aspirations that are part of its general political interests or that are part of the historical purposes that inspire some of its public institutions. These include maintaining international relations aligned with national development, the needs for cooperation, and the country's international projection, but also promoting and maintaining the values contained in the United Nations Charter or achieving interests common to all humanity

[185] Likewise, certain aspirations are found in the political and cultural heritage of the Chilean people

[186] This category includes peaceful and supportive civic coexistence; the preservation and enhancement of national identity and cultural heritage; and the achievement of sustained and sustainable economic development, with equal opportunities for all

[187] State, society and human person The State is the political organization that society provides to promote the common good, through the creation of social conditions that allow each and every member of the national community to achieve their greatest possible spiritual and material fulfillment

[188] To this end, the democratic state guarantees the essential rights of individuals, also known as fundamental rights or human rights, and strives to ensure that they are reflected as broadly as possible in the Constitution and laws

[189] The State has the obligation to create conditions of security to fulfill its purposes, both to promote the common good and to protect the population and to serve the human person, fully realizing their essential rights

[190] These concepts have international endorsement in the human rights system of the United Nations (UN) and the Organization of American States (OAS

[191] CONSTITUTIONAL DUTIES RELATED TO DEFENSE (CPR) Article 22: • Every inhabitant of the Republic must respect Chile and its national emblems

[192] • Chileans have a fundamental duty to honor their country, defend its sovereignty, and contribute to preserving national security and the essential values of Chilean tradition

[193] Military service and other personal obligations imposed by law are mandatory under the terms and forms determined by law

[194] • Chileans who are able to carry weapons must be registered in the Military Registries, unless they are legally exempt

[195] Every State carries out purposes such as those mentioned above within a defined territory and with political independence

[196] That is why the UN Charter, embodying principles of international law, identifies in Article 2, No. 4, territorial integrity and political independence as the most important assets for guaranteeing the validity of the collective security system that the UN represents

[197] The population of Chile, which is one of the constituent elements of the State, enshrined in the Political Constitution of the Republic, with the features and particularities that characterize it, is a priority object of National Defense, because one of its duties is to protect the population of the country and support the national community in certain circumstances and scenarios

[198] Based on population growth, distribution, and density, it is possible to infer the priorities of the Defense sector, and particularly of the Armed Forces institutions, in relation to support for the national community, with emphasis on those regions, cities, and towns located in remote or more isolated areas of the country, or those that comparatively present greater deficiencies

[199] To this end, the military institutions of National Defense utilize their respective capabilities to contribute to its development in two main areas: military operations other than war (in the face of natural or man-made disasters) and institutional social responsibility through various inherent actions

[200] The elements of the population's identity have been shaped by various social factors that constitute a particular historical and cultural legacy

[201] Also contributing to this heritage are the influences and contributions from the growing migratory flows that have chosen our country—for the diverse opportunities it offers—to settle there, progress, develop, and fulfill themselves personally or as a family

[202] For National Defense, the protection of the territory and its population represents a priority interest

[203] For this reason, the specific characteristics of the national territory and the new dimensions that this area has acquired constitute fundamental references to consider in the formulation of the National Defense Policy

[204] The territorial approach: the geographical, the multidimensional and the integration into the region and the world Territorial sovereignty implies the capacity of the political authority to make the exclusive jurisdiction of the State prevail over the territory, in accordance with international law and within the framework of national legislation and the country's Foreign Policy

[205] It assumes that the State exercises a presence through its various agencies, including defense institutions, in those areas where it is determined and under the stipulated conditions, and public policies that, as a whole, aim to maintain the country's territorial integrity and integration

[206] This concept is complemented by an approach that, without overlooking the geographical aspect, includes a multidimensional view of the territory and integration with the region and the world

[207] From this perspective, it is necessary to incorporate new dimensions into the analysis of the areas in which the State extends its jurisdiction: Firstly, today it is necessary to consider outer space and its relationship with the dimension of cyberspace, where multiple forms of activity are generated, some of them illegitimate and illegal

[208] The need to connect cyberspace with outer space lies in the integration that occurs between the physical infrastructure serving cyberspace and that located in outer space

[209] Secondly, border areas and isolated and extreme zones are particularly relevant to the work of the Defense

[210] In these areas, military forces contribute to local or regional development and the maintenance of state sovereignty, while protecting the population

[211] At the same time, defense institutions contribute to relations with our neighbors in the area of cross-border cooperation, for example, by implementing confidence- and security-building measures, as well as by developing broader cooperation processes

[212] Border areas, whether isolated or extreme, can also be points of communication between Chile and its neighboring, regional, and global environment

[213] • Thirdly, the importance of the Pacific Ocean and the southern seas for our development and global stability makes it necessary to integrate our responsibilities as a State in the protection and security of a vast maritime territory, a commitment already made to the international community

[214] The multidimensional nature of the approach to national territory, which corresponds to an integrated vision of territorial space, is important because it is aligned with the predominance of the joint conception of the employment and development of military force

[215] This represents a transition from a relatively disaggregated view, based on the territorial dimension most characteristic of each institution's use, to an integrated vision of the territory, seeking to balance the policies generated by national and central institutions with the vision articulated by regional institutions, as the country's democratic institutions evolve

[216] This approach also constitutes one of the fundamental references for National Defense planning

[217] In short, Defense Policy responds to the challenges posed by the multidimensional approach to national territory and international law

[218] This will impact the conduct of joint military operations, or specifically land, sea, air, and cyber operations

[227] General description of the national territory The territory is one of the basic conditions for the existence of the national State

[228] It constitutes the space where the state legal system is applied and geographically individualizes the Chilean population

[229] It also establishes the scope of state action materialized in public policies, one of which corresponds to Defense Policy

[230] The characteristics of the territory and its fundamental elements entail needs that the State must address, and which impose the duty to act responsibly in its protection and defense

[231] It is located in the western and southern parts of South America, and includes the Chilean Antarctic Territory and Easter Island in the western Pacific

[232] Considering its South American continental and insular parts, it has an area of 756,096 km2, which, when adding the area of the Chilean Antarctic Territory, rises to 2,006,096 km

[233] Of its total land border of 6,418 km, it shares 168 km with Peru, 850 km with Bolivia, and 5,400 km with Argentina

[234] THE NATIONAL TERRITORY AND AREAS OF JURISDICTION Book of the National Defense of Chile 2017 II CHAPTER Chart No. 1 MAP OF CHILE Source: National Directorate of Borders and Limits of the State II CHAPTER 38 THE NATIONAL TERRITORY AND AREAS OF JURISDICTION Book of the National Defense of Chile 2017 2.3 The continental land space The continental territory, without considering the oceanic insular territory, has an area of approximately 755,776 km

[235] This vast land area—or continental Chile—has diverse geographic characteristics and a wide range of natural resources

[236] It therefore constitutes one of the essential factors in defining defense objectives

[237] From this perspective, three areas of strategic importance are identified: a) The northern zone, with large, sparsely populated areas and predominantly desert-like climatic conditions, concentrates large- and small-scale mining, contributing a high percentage to the country's Gross Domestic Product

[238] This area also has a port and transportation infrastructure whose importance lies in its ability to meet our country's international commitments

[239] More than 85% of the population lives in the central and southern areas

[240] It represents the administrative, agricultural and industrial heart of the country

[241] c) The southern zone is characterized by its geographical fragmentation, although attenuated by the maritime and air connectivity provided by the Chilean Navy and Air Force, respectively

[242] In recent decades, progress has been made in land connectivity implemented by the State, through the ongoing actions of the Army through the Military Labor Corps

[243] Its potential is linked to one of the largest freshwater reserves in South America located in Campos de Hielo, to aquaculture, to its tourist interest, its privileged location close to the interoceanic passages and its projection to the Antarctic continent

[244] In addition to the continental part, Chile's territory also includes oceanic islands and the Chilean Antarctic Territory, with their respective maritime and airspace

[245] Territorial sea and maritime spaces In accordance with the legal regime of the oceans, Chile's maritime spaces comprise the oceanic waters that extend from the baselines on the continental coast to the limit of the Exclusive Economic Zone and the continental shelf

[246] In these spaces the following territorial and legal concepts apply: 39 THE NATIONAL TERRITORY AND AREAS OF JURISDICTION Book of the National Defense of Chile 2017 II CHAPTER • Territorial Sea of 12 nautical miles (NM) in length (22 km), measured from the baselines

[247] • Contiguous Zone of 12 NM (22 km), extending from the outer limit of the territorial sea to 24 NM, counted from the baselines

[248] • Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), understood as the maritime area that extends up to 200 NM (370 km), measured from the baselines

[249] These concepts are included in the Chilean Civil Code, which, in its article 593, states: "The adjacent sea, up to a distance of twelve nautical miles measured from the respective baselines, is territorial sea and national domain

[250] However, for purposes concerning the prevention and sanction of violations of its customs, tax, immigration or health laws and regulations, the State exercises jurisdiction over a maritime space called the Contiguous Zone, which extends to a distance of twenty-four nautical miles, measured in the same manner.”

[251] He adds that "The waters located within the baselines of the territorial sea form part of the internal waters of the State

[252] Similarly, Article 596 of the Code states that "The adjacent sea extending up to two hundred nautical miles from the baselines from which the breadth of the territorial sea is measured, and beyond the latter, is called the exclusive economic zone

[253] In it, the State exercises sovereign rights to explore, exploit, conserve and manage the living and non-living natural resources of the waters overlying the seabed, the seabed and the subsoil of the sea, and to develop any other activities with a view to the exploration and economic exploitation of that area

[254] It adds that "The State exercises exclusive sovereignty rights over the continental shelf for the purposes of conservation, exploration, and exploitation of its natural resources

[255] Finally, it establishes that, "In addition, the State is entitled to all other jurisdiction and rights provided for in international law with respect to the exclusive economic zone and the continental shelf

[256] Chile's territorial sea extends from the maritime boundary with Peru in the north to the shores of the Antarctic continent in the south, excluding the high seas formed by the Drake Passage south of Cape Horn and the Shetland Islands in Antarctica

[257] Chile has a coastline of more than 4,300 km in length

[258] If, in a transversal sense, its extension is considered up to 200 nautical miles from the coast, without including the maritime projection of the Chilean Antarctic Territory or the respective continental shelf, it reaches an area of 3,468,273 km

[259] The total area of the territorial sea and maritime spaces where Chile exercises sovereign rights and jurisdiction is 4.5 times the continental land area

[260] If you add the Maritime Search and Rescue Area of Responsibility, which extends to the 131° west longitude meridian, located 3,200 nautical miles from the continent (5,926 km), it is 35 times larger

[261] The insular part of the national territory has an area of approximately 320 km2 and includes several islands in the Pacific Ocean

[262] The closest are the Juan Fernández Archipelago, 360 nautical miles (667 km) from the continent, and the San Félix and San Ambrosio islands, 500 nautical miles (926 km

[263] The furthest are Salas y Gómez Island, 1,870 nautical miles (3,463 km) from the continent, and Easter Island, 2,000 nautical miles (3,700 km

[265] EASTER ISLAND (Rapa Nui or Te Pito Te Henua) Since 1888, Easter Island became part of Chilean sovereignty in an act that was agreed upon by the native population and their representatives

[266] In 1995, UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization) declared Easter Island a World Heritage Site, in accordance with the Convention on the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage

[267] In 2007, the State of Chile approved the declaration in the Political Constitution of the Republic that Easter Island and the Juan Fernández Archipelago are "special territories," that is, they are parts of Chilean territory governed by a "special statute"2, with decentralized administration, in order to strengthen their integration with the continent and promote development with respect for their traditions and culture

[268] In May 2016, the Chilean government submitted a bill to parliament to regulate the rights to reside, remain, and travel to and from the special territory of Easter Island

[273] At the same time, in the maritime spaces surrounding the Chilean Antarctic Territory, between the meridians 53° W and 90° W, Chile exercises its rights in accordance with the regime of the Antarctic Treaty and the rules of the Antarctic System

[274] In accordance with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and international custom, Chile has a large area of inland waters in the southern and southern sectors

[275] These inland waters are those found within the straight baselines, being fjords, bays, channels and other features or indentations typical of the territory

[276] The continental waters that make up navigable lakes and rivers are part of the land area they border, although, for the purposes of national legislation, they are considered part of the administration of inland waters

[277] In these bodies of water, the State exercises full sovereignty in accordance with the general rules of international law

[288] Airspace Airspace results from the projection of imaginary lines into the atmosphere from maritime and land territories under sovereignty, national jurisdiction or national responsibility in its different degrees

[289] On the one hand, the State of Chile exercises sovereignty or jurisdiction over the areas overlying its South American continental territory, its oceanic islands, its territorial sea, and its exclusive economic zone; this airspace extends from the northern border to the South Pole, extending beyond the mainland, the territorial sea, and the areas under national jurisdiction

[290] Furthermore, and in accordance with international regulations, our country has been assigned airspace under its control, where it is in charge of search and rescue activities5 and flight information6, from the international political boundary in the east to the 131° 00' meridian in the west

[328] Through Supreme Decree No. 1,747, Chile specified the boundaries of Chilean Antarctica or the Chilean Antarctic Territory in “the part that extends toward the polar quadrant called 'American Antarctica'.”

[329] This Decree establishes that "the Chilean Antarctic or Chilean Antarctic Territory is made up of all the lands, islands, islets, reefs, glaciers and other known or unknown, the respective territorial sea, existing within the limits of the ice cap formed by the meridians 53° and 90° longitude West of Greenwich", with a land area of 1,250,257.6 km

[330] The Chilean Antarctic Territory is a border zone for all legal purposes

[331] Chile is a country with a vocation for Antarctica due to its history and geographical proximity. The year 1906 was especially significant when the first Chilean Antarctic Commission was created, which was responsible for planning the first Chilean Antarctic Expedition, which could not be carried out due to the earthquake that affected the city of Valparaíso

[332] Chile's Antarctic rights are based on geographical, historical, and legal foundations, consolidated and communicated to the international community, with Chile's effective presence on the Antarctic continent since

[333] Based on this background, Chile participated in the negotiation of the Antarctic Treaty in 1959, along with eleven other States

[334] Before the Antarctic Treaty came into force in 1961, seven countries had claimed sovereign rights in Antarctica, two of which overlapped

[335] In relation to territorial sovereignty rights, the Antarctic Treaty, in its Article IV, establishes that: "Nothing in this Treaty shall be construed: (a) as a waiver by either Contracting Party of its rights to territorial sovereignty or territorial claims in Antarctica previously asserted; (b) as a waiver or impairment by either Contracting Party of any basis for claiming territorial sovereignty in Antarctica which it may have, whether as a result of its activities or those of its nationals in Antarctica, or for any other reason

[336] CHILEAN TERRITORY

[337] ANTARCTIC CHILE

[338] Since the beginning of the 20th century, this interest has gained greater prominence in national politics

[339] This has translated into a physical presence, making it one of the countries with a population center today, which has allowed for the gradual development of various activities and greater penetration into the frozen continent

[340] Chile was an original signatory to the Antarctic Treaty signed in Washington and, therefore, a consultative member of this international regime that regulates the relations between countries and their activities in Antarctica

[341] CHILEAN TERRITORY

[342] ANTARCTIC National Defense Book of Chile 2017 III CHAPTER (c) as prejudicial to the position of any of the Contracting Parties, with regard to its recognition or non-recognition of the right of territorial sovereignty, of a claim or of a basis for a claim of territorial sovereignty of any other State in Antarctica

[343] In paragraph 2 of the same article IV it is added that “No act or activity carried out while this Treaty is in force shall constitute a basis for asserting, supporting or denying a claim of territorial sovereignty in Antarctica, nor for creating sovereign rights in this region

[344] No new claims to territorial sovereignty in Antarctica shall be made, nor shall any previous claims be extended, while this Treaty is in force.”

[345] Furthermore, the Antarctic Treaty prohibited new claims of territorial sovereignty during its term and established an international regime that respects the positions of the Parties on issues pertaining to sovereignty over the continent

[346] In this way, Chile irrevocably maintains its rights to territorial sovereignty in Antarctica and, under the recognition established in Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty, protects the legal status of the Chilean Antarctic Territory

[347] It should be noted that the Chilean Antarctic Territory is a relevant element in the definition of the National Antarctic Policy for

[348] The National Antarctic Policy The evolution of the Antarctic Treaty System demands current policies that are in line with national interests in Antarctic matters, which is why Chile updated its National Antarctic Policy (PAN) in January

[349] a) Objectives of the National Antarctic Policy

[350] The PAN aims to achieve the following goals, among others: Protect Chile's sovereign rights over the Chilean Antarctic Territory

[351] Safeguard and promote national interests in the Antarctic Continent

[352] III CHAPTER 48 CHILEAN ANTARCTIC TERRITORY Book of the National Defense of Chile 2017 Antarctic Treaty, also promoting the development of an effective regime, ensuring the maintenance of that territory free of international conflicts

[353] • Protect and promote the care of the Antarctic environment, including the marine environment and its dependent and associated ecosystems

[354] • Develop research in the natural and social sciences based on excellence, focusing on global issues of political interest and those of national economic interest, through a robust Chilean Antarctic Institute, the hub of Chile's international scientific collaboration in Antarctica

[355] Develop and promote the Magallanes and Chilean Antarctic Region as a center for national and international Antarctic activity, including its consolidation as a hub for scientific and logistical development in Antarctica

[356] Strengthen connectivity between this region and the Antarctic continent

[357] • Facilitate the development of economic activities permitted by the Antarctic Treaty System, including sustainable and responsible fishing, as well as controlled and sustainable tourism

[358] • Strengthen national Antarctic awareness and identity, and protect and disseminate Chile's Antarctic historical and cultural heritage

[359] • Improve national Antarctic institutions and legislation

[360] with a view to facilitating the implementation of this National Antarctic Policy

[361] The institutions of the Armed Forces must contribute to achieving the objectives defined in the National Antarctic Policy, making use of their operational and logistical capabilities, especially in those areas where, due to their specific roles, they are irreplaceable

[362] A gateway to Antarctica Chile makes an effort every day of the year to be present in Antarctica through the activities carried out by Antarctic operators: the Chilean Antarctic Institute (INACH) and the institutions of the Armed Forces

[363] For this effort, the Magallanes and Chilean Antarctic Region, especially the cities of Punta Arenas and Puerto Williams, is the national logistics platform that provides the infrastructure for maritime and air connectivity

[364] In addition, four independent digital connectivity projects are being worked on

[365] Of these, one corresponds to the Southern Submarine Trunk Project, starting in Puerto Williams and ending in Punta Arenas, Porvenir, Puerto Natales, Caleta Tortel, and finally, Puerto Montt; the other three correspond to Land Trunk Projects, in the Magallanes Region and Chilean Antarctica

[366] At the same time, the Region is a scientific platform, as it is home to INACH and academic institutions dedicated to Antarctic studies, organizations that cooperate with scientific institutions in other countries

[367] To this end, the creation of an International Antarctic Center in the city of Punta Arenas is being promoted as a hub for scientific development, and a sub-Antarctic center in Puerto Williams for science, higher education, and outreach

[368] Within the Armed Forces, the Chilean Army transferred its Antarctic Department to report directly to the VI Division, based in Punta Arenas, the city where the Institution's Antarctic Studies Center was founded. This has allowed for the consolidation of management in support of the effective presence of the Chilean State at O'Higgins Base, support for scientific activity and search and rescue activities, and optimized compliance with international agreements

[369] In turn, the Chilean Navy, together with its presence in Antarctic bases and maritime stations, and the development of the Third Naval Zone of the Antarctic campaign carried out annually, hopes to complete the construction of an icebreaker to replace the current one at the ASMAR shipyard by 2022, thereby increasing its capacity as an Antarctic operator

[370] Finally, the Air Force, in addition to operating bases, uses its aircraft to cover transit between the American continent and the Antarctic sector

[371] For these purposes, it maintains the Teniente Marsh airstrip at Frei Base and supports the only population center in the Chilean Antarctic Territory: Villa Las Estrellas

[372] In 2014, Chile projected its presence toward the South Pole with the installation of the “Unión Glacier” Joint Scientific Polar Station, located within the Antarctic Circle

[373] The operational and logistical aspects are the responsibility of the three branches of the Armed Forces, with INACH responsible for developing the scientific program carried out each season at the polar station

[374] This station is occupied annually between the months of November and January

[375] The defense sector in Antarctic affairs The Ministry of National Defense and its dependent institutions are linked with the Antarctic Directorate of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the body responsible for conducting the National Antarctic Policy, for the purposes of their participation in Antarctic affairs

[376] The Antarctic Treaty prohibits all military measures on the continent, such as the establishment of military bases and fortifications, the conduct of military maneuvers, and the testing of any type of weapons

[377] The foregoing is without prejudice to the use of military personnel or resources in support of scientific research or other peaceful activities, which is expressly authorized

[378] Within this framework, the Armed Forces carry out an effective presence and provide logistical and operational support for national activities in the Chilean Antarctic Territory

[379] For the purposes of their activities in Antarctica, they act in accordance with the National Antarctic Policy and the special guidelines issued by the Antarctic Policy Council

[380] Among the activities carried out, the following stand out: • Help achieve the objectives of the National Antarctic Policy

[381] Maintain an effective presence in Antarctic territory, implementing national legal regulations for nationals who are in or visiting Antarctica

[382] • Carry out human life protection tasks through land search and rescue and maritime and air SAR, in accordance with current international obligations. • Through INACH, support national and international scientific activities. • Oversee matters related to the Convention for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources

[383] • Maintain permanent maritime and air connectivity between the South American continent and Antarctica, as well as land, sea, and air projection on the continent

[384] • Operate and provide protection for human life in general and all activities undertaken in Antarctica

[385] • Maintain maritime signage in the Chilean Antarctic Territory

[386] • Protect the Antarctic environment by developing the capacity to respond to an environmental emergency

[387] • Contribute to international cooperation by supporting other countries' Antarctic programs

[388] • Carry out land exploration, maritime navigation and aerial exploration in the Antarctic territory in general and its projection to the South Pole

[389] • Carry out combined actions with international Antarctic programs, such as the Combined Antarctic Relief and Rescue Patrol (PARASAR) and the Combined Antarctic Naval Patrol (PAN), both activities carried out with Argentina

[390] • Development of official Antarctic land, sea, and air cartography by the State of Chile, which is available to the national and international community

[391] In another development, on January 1, 2017, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) adopted the international code for ships operating in polar waters, known as the "Polar Code

[392] This instrument aims to improve the safety of operations in polar waters, in the areas of marine environmental preservation, operational safety, and the protection of human life

[393] Chile's Antarctic facilities The implementation of Chile's presence in Antarctica has generated the need to establish different bases, stations and shelters on the Antarctic continent, which is combined with both compliance with the provisions of the Antarctic Treaty and with the interests that our country has in that continent, thus implementing the National Antarctic Policy

[394] To date, Chile has a significant number of Antarctic facilities that allow it to maintain an effective presence, support the scientific activities carried out by INACH, safeguard human life in Antarctica, and monitor environmental measures that protect the continent

[395] This has also meant the possibility of having a logistics, operational, and scientific support chain for the national and international scientific community, within the scope of international cooperation provided for by the Antarctic Treaty
