[444] The Antarctic Treaty System The Antarctic Treaty not only represents an interest of the twelve original signatory states, but has become a growing interest of a large part of the international community

[445] Through this instrument, the international community seeks to ensure that Antarctica continues to be used exclusively for peaceful purposes, preventing it from becoming a stage or object of international discord

[446] This was the original spirit of the Treaty in 1959, which continues to this day

[447] In October 1991, Chile signed the Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty (commonly referred to as the Madrid Protocol), with the aim of strengthening the protection of the Antarctic environment and dependent and associated ecosystems, recognizing the importance of safeguarding the ecosystem integrity of the seas surrounding Antarctica

[448] Chile had already signed the Convention on the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources in September 1980 in Canberra, Australia

[449] Its provisions include: Antarctica will be used exclusively for peaceful purposes

[450] Freedom of scientific research in Antarctica and cooperation toward that end […] will continue

[451] • The Contracting Parties agree to proceed […] to the exchange of observations and scientific results on Antarctica, which will be freely available

[452] • Among the signatories of the Treaty are seven countries (Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, Norway, New Zealand and the United Kingdom) with territorial claims, which in some cases partially overlap

[453] Other countries do not recognize any claims, while others, such as the United States and Russia, consider that they have “grounds to claim”

[454] In addition to the Antarctic Treaty

[455] The International Antarctic System is made up of the following instruments: Convention for the Conservation of Antarctic Seals (CCFA, London, 1972; entered into force on 11 March

[456] Applies to the sea from 60° south latitude); and • Convention for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR, Canberra, 1980; in force since 7 April

[457] It applies south of an artificial Antarctic Convergence line or Antarctic polar frontal zone that surrounds Antarctica

[458] Protocol to the Antarctic Treaty on Environmental Protection (Madrid, 1991; in force since January

[459] The Antarctic Treaty maintains the status quo regarding the sovereignty claims of all original signatory states

[460] At the same time, the implementation of the Antarctic Treaty has evolved through the creation of mechanisms and instruments that involve a high degree of self-regulation, as is the case with scientific research, fishing, mining activities, and tourism

[461] ANTARCTIC TREATY On 1 December 1959, the twelve member countries (Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Chile, France, Japan, New Zealand, Norway, South Africa, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States) that carried out scientific activities in Antarctica and adjacent regions signed the Antarctic Treaty in Washington, D. C., which entered into force in

[462] All these countries had actively participated in the International Geophysical Year (IGY) of

[463] There are currently 53 signatories: the original twelve have been joined by another 17 with consultative status, meaning they participate in the Consultative Meetings of the Antarctic Treaty System with the right to speak and vote, in addition to having an active presence and carrying out scientific activities

[464] On the other hand, there are 24 countries that are non-consultative

[465] The latter have the right to participate in the consultative meetings of the Treaty, but only with the right to speak

[466] COUNTRIES WITH CLAIMS IN ANTARCTICA Claimant country | Claim boundaries | Territory ---|---|--- Argentina | 74° W - 25° W/South Pole - 60° S | Department of the Province of Tierra del Fuego, Antarctica and the South Atlantic Islands (South Orkney Islands) Australia | 45° E - 136° E and 142° E - 160° E South Pole - 60° S | Australian Antarctic Territory Chile | 53° W - 90° W South Pole - northern limit undefined | Chilean Antarctic Territory France | 136° E - 142° E South Pole - 60° S

[467] Adélie Land (District of the French Southern and Antarctic Lands) Norway | 20° W - 45° E Coast, southern limit unspecified | Queen Maud Land New Zealand | 160° E – 150° W South Pole – 60° S | Ross Dependency United Kingdom | 20° W - 80° W South Pole - 60° S | British Antarctic Territory Since its entry into force, the Treaty has produced an international regime that countries have tended to maintain and respect

[468] In this context, Chile has carried out measurements of the Extended Continental Shelf in Antarctica, although, according to its Regulations, the United Nations Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf does not rule on any territorial claim on that continent, a situation that is known and accepted by the countries claiming Antarctic sovereignty

[469] The Antarctic Treaty, built on the principles of the United Nations Charter, contributes to international peace and security, fosters cooperation in scientific research and knowledge, and enables the increasingly urgent need for environmental protection against the effects of climate change and human activity on the continent

[470] In 2016, the Consultative Parties, on the occasion of the XXXIX Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meeting held in Santiago, Chile, reiterated their firm and unconditional commitment to the objectives and purposes of the Antarctic Treaty and its Environmental Protocol, recognizing with concern the effects of climate change on the Antarctic environment and its dependent and associated ecosystems, through the so-called “Santiago Declaration.”

[471] TERRITORIAL ORDER POLICIES

[472] The concept of sovereignty assumes the existence of a territory as a physical space, circumscribed by boundaries whose scope is also geospatial, as well as the ability to assert the exclusive jurisdiction of the State over it in accordance with international law

[473] The defense sector plays a contributing role in policies aimed at developing those areas of the country that, due to their characteristics and location, require state support

[474] Contribution of National Defense to State policies related to territorial affairs In accordance with its legal structure, the Defense sector agencies participate in various committees and working groups with other State agencies that have jurisdiction in these matters, which allows for the strengthening of sectoral technical capacities in matters of territorial management

[475] Within the framework of the definitions adopted in these bodies, the institutions of the Defense sector implement various territorial policies, programs, and actions, according to the powers granted to them by law and in collaboration with other State administration agencies at their various levels

[476] Specifically, the contribution of National Defense to territorial order policies is materialized in: Generation of basic geographic information Presence and support in border areas Contribution to the development of isolated and extreme areas Control of jurisdictional spaces BASIC GEOGRAPHIC INFORMATION The Defense sector includes the official and technical agencies of the State that are in charge of everything related to cartographic, hydrographic and aerospace matters of the national territory

[477] Based on the above, the Military Geographic Institute (IGM), the Oceanographic and Hydrographic Service of the Navy (SHOA), and the Aerophotogrammetric Service of the Air Force (SAF) are responsible for maintaining and developing tools and methodologies for adequate knowledge of the country's geography

[478] The Space Operations Group (GOE), a Chilean Air Force agency responsible for the operation of the FASat-Charlie satellite (and future Chilean spacecraft), as well as all matters related to the use of space and the development of space capabilities, also contributes to this task

[479] These institutions cooperate with other state agencies in developing national policy on territorial and geospatial information

[480] The development of border areas, isolated zones, and extreme zones results from the concern to minimize the various types of vulnerabilities that manifest in the population settlements located there

[481] Hence, the State is considering the need to adopt specific measures to improve living conditions, preserve environmental and cultural heritage, and facilitate national and cross-border integration

[482] The institutions of National Defense contribute in various ways to these purposes

[483] The presence of Armed Forces units in border areas aims not only to protect the country, but also supports its development, the provision of certain social services, and preparation for and response to potential disasters

[484] The same thing happens in isolated areas far from vital centers, where the presence of military units can also create a magnet for human life

[485] Likewise, the various military institutions have cooperated in the development and flexibility of our country's road system, in territorial consolidation, and in connecting continental, island, and Antarctic territories

[486] Support for the development of border areas Chile has defined its border area considering special characteristics, generally linked to adjacency to international boundaries and to the dominant characteristics of isolation or, in certain cases, where international treaties with permanent effects apply

[487] Special decision-making mechanisms operate in this area and guide State action regarding fiscal real estate, water resources, natural resources, scientific and mountaineering expeditions, and the application of legal provisions for extreme zones

[488] Furthermore, with neighboring countries, the Integration and Border Committees have been one of the tools created to establish channels that give vitality to border areas, facilitate the cross-border flow of people and goods, and foster normal, active, and impactful relations with citizens

[489] Through them, the development of national communities located in these geographical areas can be energized

[490] Additionally, the concept of "Integration and Development Axes" implies a comprehensive approach to improving access, achieving connectivity, and developing productive and service potential in the aforementioned geographic areas

[491] Chile shares this vision, which aims to achieve greater levels of integration, alongside all South American states, by valuing the relationship that exists between border areas under different sovereignties and populated by communities that, in turn, generate economic activities of mutual influence and benefit

[492] States participate in integration processes in these areas, accepting their respective national identities and mutually recognizing their territories

[493] They also ensure that the development of border communities is integrated into national metropolitan centers

[494] Policy for the development of isolated areas The National Policy for the Development of Isolated Localities was formalized by Supreme Decree No. 608 of the Ministry of the Interior, published in the Official Gazette on November 27, 2010, and is in line with the spirit of modernization of the State and decentralization of the regional administrative organization

[495] An isolated territory is "one with a low level of accessibility, a low population and high dispersion of this, low presence and coverage of basic and public services, and which, as a result of these factors, is in a situation of disadvantage and social inequality with respect to the development of the country

[496] In these aspects, this national policy is inspired by the principles of social equity, subsidiarity, exceptionality, and sovereignty. Policy for Extreme Zones Starting in 2010, the Undersecretary of Regional Development of the Ministry of the Interior and Public Security decided to provide specific and differentiated treatment to territories defined as "extreme zones

[497] This special treatment is based on and responds to the Executive's desire to implement the principle of territorial equity, meaning equal public services across all regions of the country

[498] In 2014, the government issued new public policy guidelines for extreme zones aimed at "overcoming the unfavorable living conditions of residents who require preferential attention from the State," considering that regions located at the geographic extremes or with difficult connectivity require special public policies to facilitate their development

[499] The policy for the country's extreme zones has been materialized through the implementation of territorial development plans for all regions and provinces classified as such

[500] These plans have been designed and implemented in coordination with the respective regional governments

[501] Thus, the development plans for extreme zones in the regions of Arica-Parinacota, Aysén, Magallanes, the province of Palena, and the commune of Cochamó, in the Los Lagos Region, were developed with the active participation of citizens and social organizations in the territories involved

[502] As part of the effective recognition of the territorial specificities of extreme regions, it was established that for public investment initiatives included in the plans, a technicaleconomic analysis would be carried out using the Minimum Cost methodology. This allows projects to obtain favorable technical recommendations with greater flexibility, something that was previously difficult due to the small population and its geographical dispersion

[503] National Territorial Planning Policy The National Territorial Planning Policy (PNOT) has the capacity to lead and coordinate initiatives with territorial impact, to advance more efficiently and effectively towards overcoming inequality gaps, multiplying the opportunities of inhabitants and improving their quality of life, in order to privilege the common good

[504] It also seeks to build a harmonious, integrated, safe, and inclusive territory across its diverse and vast geography, expressing its potential and fostering the revitalization of its economic, environmental, social, and cultural resources. Ultimately, the PNOT promotes a process of sustainable development with a territorial identity

[505] All of this is achieved through public policies designed through strategic and synergistic governance, within the framework of decentralization, and with an empowered citizenry involved in the future of the territory

[506] Territory is considered the geographic space that constitutes the support and basic resource of a country's common vision, the sphere of life and deployment of social, environmental, economic, and cultural practices, the landscape and identity in personal and collective memory

[507] Territory is also the social construction resulting from the dynamic and systemic interrelationship between communities, economic activities and natural resources, and from the various transformations resulting from human interventions

[508] It combines functional, identity, administration and management aspects

[509] It is the geographic space that the State is responsible for managing and administering the well-being of individuals and society as a whole, ensuring harmonious and equitable management

[510] Maritime Territory Policy Throughout the national maritime territory and other maritime areas of national responsibility, it is the responsibility of the Chilean Navy, in conjunction with other State agencies, to monitor, guard, secure and support maritime users

[511] The Navy is the State institution that oversees maritime authority, contributing to ensuring safer, more sustainable, healthier, and better-known seas

[512] In the national maritime jurisdiction, this Authority guides its work under the concept of "surveillance, control, alert, and response

[513] This concept is embodied in a comprehensive system that allows for effective and timely knowledge of all activities carried out in the maritime, river, and lake areas of responsibility that may affect national security and Chile's maritime interests

[514] The execution of the traditional defense functions carried out by the Navy and those developed by the Maritime Authority, under a single superior command, contribute to the generation of the conditions that allow the development of the country's maritime interests. As a public service, the Maritime Authority, together with other State bodies, acts primarily to ensure the security, preservation and safe development of activities in the maritime, river and lake scenarios

[515] To this end, it oversees, promotes, and safeguards the activities carried out there, thereby facilitating the actions of the stakeholders who interact there and placing special emphasis on protecting the person carrying out the activity and the aquatic environment that makes it possible

[516] This Authority primarily performs maritime police and security duties, protecting human life at sea, preserving the aquatic environment, combating pollution, and promoting maritime interests

[517] The twelve original signatories are: Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Chile, France, Japan, New Zealand, Norway, South Africa, Russia (former USSR), Great Britain and the United States

[518] Undersecretariat of Regional Development, Decree No. 608 on “A national policy for the development of isolated localities”, of June

[519] The functions of the Space Operations Group are detailed in Chapter XXVI. The National Territorial Planning Policy was approved by the Interministerial Commission for City, Housing and Territory in September

[520] PREPARATION OF THE NATIONAL OCEAN POLICY As part of the promotion of Chile's maritime interests, the Government promotes the formulation of a National Ocean Policy, coordinated by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, with the active participation of the Ministry of National Defense and its dependent institutions

[521] This challenge seeks to provide the country with a comprehensive, multisectoral vision that will enable us to coordinate and address ocean challenges from a long-term perspective, achieving a balance between the economic, social, security, environmental, and sustainable development dimensions, and advancing toward consolidating our commitment to international ocean governance

[522] Among others, the National Ocean Policy aims at the following objectives: • Conservation of the ocean and its resources

[523] • Provide security to the national oceanic territory, maritime interests, and ocean routes vital to the country

[524] Within the framework of international cooperation, interact with other countries regarding extra-jurisdictional areas (the High Seas and the Seabed and Ocean Floor Zone) to monitor activities carried out in these common spaces and thus conserve the resources found there. Ensure the rational and sustainable use of the ocean and its resources

[525] • Strengthen national port logistics institutions and governance, ensuring public policies that facilitate coordination between ministries and public services, national and regional public-private dialogue bodies, as well as with the port logistics communities of each port and its logistics corridors

[526] National Space Policy Chile has participated in space development issues since 1967, the year in which it joined the International Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space

[527] This instrument constitutes the regulatory framework that enshrines the benefits of space development for civil society, future generations, and the life and activities of states. It also extends to the need to maintain outer space as a peaceful environment, in order to guarantee the security of missions and the de-escalation of conflict through cooperation

[528] In 1995, Chile launched the FASat program, thus providing itself with autonomous satellite capacity for Earth observation

[529] This capacity was consolidated in 2011 with the FASat-Charlie satellite or SSOT (Satellite System IV CHAPTER 66 Chilean National Defense Book 2017 TERRITORIAL ORDER POLICIES of Terrestrial Observation), an initiative that incorporates civil society with national spatial development and the identity of Defense with the active spatial role of the country

[530] In 2014, the National Space Policy (PNE) was enacted with a 2020 perspective to achieve the stated goals

[531] This is a political instrument that considers “access to space” as a public issue, given the difficulty that Chile faces in accessing space technologies that impact the daily activities of civil society

[532] In this sense, the National Space Policy (PNE) is an instrument of limited scope and does not involve full space development

[533] Rather, it sought to stimulate State action regarding the use of outer space as an area of relevance to the country's development

[534] Specifically, the PNE proposed: "To establish institutional changes, promote the efficient coordination of state resources, generate the necessary support and incentives, and promote the constant progress of science, technology and innovation in the space field, with a view to strengthening the country's human and productive capital

[535] a) Strategic axes and lines of action The PNE establishes three strategic axes, in each of which various lines of action were defined: Strategic Axes: • Space institutionality • Promotion and access to information • Space infrastructure and applications

[536] LINES OF ACTION: Innovation and entrepreneurship, Research and development, Space industry, Geographical position and climatic and environmental characteristics

[537] Human Capital • Specialized Advanced Human Capital Training

[538] • User training • Science and Research NATIONAL SPACE POLICY A detailed explanation of the satellite project intended to replace FASat-Charlie is contained in Chapter XXVII

[539] For example, those related to access to information, satellite communications (voice and data), or weather forecasting for planting and land use processes

[540] TERRITORIAL POLICIES b) Objectives of the PNE The objectives of National Defense in terms of contributing to State policies related to outer space are: • Generate space capabilities that give Chile autonomy in Earth observation, directing their benefits to different fields of application, including those of interest to civil society and its multiple areas of development. • Develop autonomous and sovereign state management of geospatial data by linking Defense agencies such as the Military Geographic Institute (IGM), the Hydrographic and Oceanographic Service of the Navy (SHOA), and the Aerophotogrammetric Service of the Air Force (SAF)13. • Contribute to international cooperation in this field, including the consolidation of a regional Zone of Peace. • Contribute to the development of the country through intersectoral cooperation activities in the territorial, agricultural, fisheries, and scientific fields

[541] The presence of a State in outer space constitutes a task for the defense sector that, due to both its physical characteristics and current international and national regulations, requires understanding said space as a new environment for peaceful purposes and requires specific legal regulation

[542] c) Current spatial situation The current spatial institutionality of Chile is based on the provisions contained in Decree No. 181 of the Ministry of Transport and Telecommunications, promulgated in February 2016, by which the Presidential Advisory Commission called "Council of Ministers for Spatial Development" was created, of which the Ministry of National Defense is a part

[543] Its purpose is to advise the President of the Republic on the development of public policies, plans, programs, and specific actions aimed at contributing to the promotion and development of space activities, as well as on the use of space technologies and applications

[544] This Council set itself the task of reviewing the current National Space Policy (2014-2020) and developing the foundations for a Space Policy projected to 2030, which should represent a general vision with the most relevant topics that would need to be considered to promote space development in the next decade

[545] In this sense, this work should serve A more detailed explanation of the activities of these agencies can be found in the respective chapters on the Army, Navy and Air Force, as well as in Chapter XXVI

[546] TERRITORIAL ORDER POLICIES as a set of recommendations and guidelines not only for the Government, but also for other sectors of the country that demand the benefits generated by spatial development

[547] The inclusion of space issues in the security agendas of many countries demonstrates that this new scenario, which is not subject to sovereignty claims and is governed by public international law, can impact the international security situation

[548] However, states have tended to generate measures of mutual trust and reduce the environment of insecurity

[549] The role of National Defense in outer space is inspired by the promotion of peace through international cooperation and the advancement of state interests

[550] The contribution of the Armed Forces in space matters is based on collaboration between military institutions, given the unique nature of outer space

[551] The international action of Defense takes place in a global strategic context of uncertainty and complexity, denoted by the reconfiguration of international power, by the existence of risks and threats of diverse nature and by the difficulty of the institutions of the international system to face the present challenges

[552] Under these conditions, states possess a series of common elements—such as principles, norms, and cooperative practices—that are essential to addressing current strategic challenges

[553] In this environment, Chile's Defense Policy has increasingly incorporated international aspects and developed actions aimed at increasing the State's contribution to global and regional security

[554] The end of the Cold War, regional changes, and the restoration of democracy in Chile in 1990 created conditions for advancing international cooperation

[555] This was expressed in the decision to explicitly state policies in this regard, manifested in the Foreign Policy and the Defense Policy, particularly through the successive National Defense Books

[556] In this regard, Chile is working hard to strengthen ties and interactions between the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of National Defense

[557] In a global context where international security is marked by uncertainty and complexity, coordination between both institutions is essential to fostering the country's external integration

[558] The content of this chapter aims to account for some features of the evolution that the international environment has experienced, with the purpose of explaining and updating the objectives and actions that Chile carries out to promote international peace and security

[559] Evolution of the international environment The prolonged process of transformation of the international scene since the end of the 20th century and the changes that have occurred since the beginning of the 2000s have resulted in the incorporation of new risks and threats to the international security agenda

[560] These transformations have broadened this agenda, characterized by the emergence of non-state actors and the more complex configuration of conflicts, a situation that has exposed the vulnerability of the civilian population, especially women and children

[561] In this changing landscape, various international actors have developed different responses, including, in a significant part of the international community, the search for cooperative solutions

[562] In addition to traditional regimes of international cooperation in security matters—disarmament and non-proliferation—there has been growing global action through United Nations peacekeeping operations, which seek to create the conditions for maintaining peace in countries affected by conflict

[563] Additionally, there is a multiplicity of regional regimes that seek to promote and consolidate cooperation in security and defense

[564] Chile has focused its international defense policy on working within cooperation regimes with the goal of contributing to global peace and security

[565] Likewise, it has focused on strengthening cooperation institutions at the subregional, regional, and inter-American levels to consolidate Latin America as a zone of peace

[566] The Ministry of Defense supports Chile's foreign policy, which seeks to preserve an international legal order based on law, the promotion of peace, security, and the peaceful resolution of disputes

[567] V CHAPTER THE INTERNATIONAL CONTEXT OF DEFENSE Book of National Defense of Chile 2017 5.2 Global changes The world is increasingly interconnected and interdependent, a situation that means that Chile's security depends on factors that appear in distant scenarios

[568] Uncertainty is a characteristic of increasing impact as a component of the conditions in which the world evolves and of contemporary conflict in its various manifestations

[569] Changes in the international power structure and the emergence of new powers are also noted

[570] CONTEMPORARY CONFLICT Nowadays, conflicts have multiple dimensions

[571] Some of them are in the traditional dimension, which involves conflict between states

[572] While these types of conflicts have declined in recent decades, the current redistribution of power and international uncertainty have led to the resurgence of historical tensions between states, as well as the emergence of new sources of conflict between different countries

[573] In several cases, this conflict has taken on a regional dimension due to the interests at stake, the diversity of actors involved, and the interdependence between them

[574] Moreover, most contemporary conflicts do not occur exclusively within the interstate sphere, which is different from traditional conflicts. This has led to significant debate about their nature and the generation of new conceptualizations and categorizations

[575] Concepts such as irregular warfare and asymmetric conflict have been coined; more recently, "hybrid warfare" or "nonlinear warfare

[576] The latter incorporates several of the characteristics of contemporary conflict, including the fact that threats can come from both the State and non-State actors, and that the use of tactics and forms of confrontation can be conventional or irregular, with the non-combatant civilian population being the primary victim

[577] Additionally, the main characteristics of the current conflict include: **Origin:** It is mainly taking place within the state, but has consequences - a product of phenomena such as globalization and interdependence - for other states and international actors

[578] According to the United Nations, since the 1990s more than 90 percent of conflicts have occurred within states rather than between states (UN

[579] The origin of these conflicts stems from diverse sources within the state, which may include political, economic, social, ethnic, and religious disputes, and not necessarily the struggle for international power that characterized traditional conflict

[580] Target of attacks:** Currently, attacks deliberately focus on the civilian population, especially women and children, unlike traditional conflicts that focused on military targets

[581] Forms of confrontation:** Traditional conflict focused on direct confrontation between opposing military forces

[582] Currently, there is a trend toward the use of technologies that allow attacks to be carried out from remote distances, through the use of weapons and robotic systems, and through outer space and cyberspace

[583] Also in numerous asymmetric conflicts, the use of unconventional means against both military and civilian targets has become widespread

[584] International Response: The various international actors, mainly organized within the United Nations system and other regional organizations recognized by all states, have had to modify their ways of dealing with contemporary conflict, generating cooperative, preventive, peacekeeping and enforcement instruments, in addition to the traditional coercive and deterrent threat through the use of military instruments

[585] To this traditional agenda in transformation, a non-traditional agenda is added, which includes risks and threats of an economic, social, political or environmental nature and which, although they may have an intra-state origin, have international implications, as is the case of cyberattacks or climate change

[586] Changes in global power relations have impacted the traditional security agenda, manifesting, for example, in the shift of global interest from the Atlantic to the Pacific, the rise of China and its progressive consolidation as a global power, the growing repositioning of Russia, and, more recently, the international position that the United States is beginning to assume in this context

[587] All these changes in the power structure raise questions about the emergence of new alliances, commitments, tensions, demands, and threats

[588] These changes also pose a series of impacts at the economic, political, social, and cultural levels. Combined with the process of globalization and rapid technological development, these impacts are strategic, both in terms of patterns of cooperation and conflict

[589] Added to this situation are phenomena such as the expansion and access to technology, which can be used by state and non-state actors in ways that negatively impact international security

[590] This growing agenda of security threats and risks has altered the global strategic environment, with varying degrees of emphasis on different regions of the world

[591] The rise of terrorism in the United States, Europe, Russia, the Middle East, and Africa is an example of this situation

[592] Furthermore, emerging phenomena linked to technological development and the illicit use of cyberspace, organized crime, and drug trafficking, among other phenomena, complicate the strategic landscape

[593] We are also seeing an increase in natural disasters associated with climate change, increasing security risks

[594] Natural resources have acquired greater relevance in recent decades

[595] Their depletion and environmental degradation are factors that impact international security by increasing potential competition and sources of conflict

[596] The efforts of various states and international organizations are still insufficient to address the current strategic agenda

[597] The weakening of global governance-characterized by a more diffuse distribution of power, the weakening of multilateral institutions, and the changing nature of conflicts—makes it difficult to maintain an adequate level of security

[598] CHAPTER THE INTERNATIONAL CONTEXT OF DEFENSE Book of National Defense of Chile 2017 Faced with this scenario, strengthening international cooperation requires the improvement of current international institutions or the creation of new bodies that are capable of strengthening international security and responding to new challenges

[599] These challenges include, in addition to the new and traditional strategic agenda, concepts that rethink the fundamental foundations of the international system and affect the actions of their countries

[600] These are concepts such as the Responsibility to Protect, according to which - according to the UN - sovereignty no longer means exclusively the protection of states against external interference, but rather constitutes a burden of responsibility that generates the obligation to protect when there is a significant threat to the physical survival of large communities

[601] THE RESPONSIBILITY TO PROTECT In 2001, as an experience derived from the civil wars in Rwanda and Burundi (1993 and 1994), the expression “responsibility to protect” appeared in the report submitted by the International Commission on Intervention and State Sovereignty (ICISS)15 to the UN General Assembly, which sets out the essential principles of the responsibility to protect and the principles for military intervention

[602] When a country manifestly fails to protect its own population, the international community has a responsibility to protect them and may take collective action in a timely manner or even use force as a last resort

[603] It is a principle aimed at protecting the most vulnerable populations from cases of genocide, ethnic cleansing, civil wars, or incitement to them

[604] If a State cannot guarantee the security of its people, whether due to a lack of capacity or will, the international community assumes this responsibility

[605] How is it implemented

[606] States have the primary responsibility for investigating and prosecuting such crimes

[607] The responsibility to protect is assumed by the international community through a United Nations Security Council Resolution on the use of force

[608] Its implementation is carried out in phases: Call on the State in question to protect its population

[609] • Imposition of sanctions by the United Nations

[610] • If there are no changes, the Security Council approves the use of force to end the violence in that country

[611] Who protects

[612] Source: Prepared by the authors based on documentation from the United Nations Office on Genocide Prevention and the Responsibility to Protect

[613] Office of the Special Adviser on the Prevention of Genocide

[614] http://www.un.org/es/preventgenocide/adviser/responsibility Independent body that supported the UN during the Millennium Assembly in

[615] Its purpose was to complement the efforts that had been made on issues of intervention and sovereignty in other contexts

[616] THE INTERNATIONAL CONTEXT OF DEFENSE Chilean National Defense Book 2017 All of the above is relevant for the updating and adaptation of the policies of the Defense sector, in which international cooperation takes precedence to face the uncertainty of a complex strategic context, with direct implications for the security of people

[617] New Global Challenges for Security and Defense Many of the numerous existing challenges for security and defense require responses from a cooperative perspective

[618] Based on the initiatives being carried out by the defense sector in Chile, climate change, science and technology, cyberspace, and the presence in outer space have been considered here

[619] a) Climate change Environmental protection and, in particular, the risks posed by climate change have been at the center of debate in recent years

[620] While these issues were not part of the traditional security and defense agenda, they have increasingly been included as challenges that should be addressed

[621] CLIMATE CHANGE, INTERNATIONAL SECURITY AND DEFENSE The effects of climate change pose risks to international peace and security by amplifying existing vulnerabilities, due to resource scarcity, the spread of diseases, or forced population displacement

[622] On the other hand, military forces can be directly affected by climate change

[623] Rising sea levels, extreme weather events and temperatures, among other phenomena, can affect military installations, requirements, and operations

[624] THE INTERNATIONAL CONTEXT OF DEFENSE CLIMATE CHANGE IN THE INTERNATIONAL SPHERE For the UN, “climate change is a complex problem that, despite being environmental in nature, has consequences in all areas of existence on our planet.”

[625] According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), warming of the climate system is unequivocal, and many of the changes observed since the 1950s have been unprecedented

[626] As a result, there is an increase in average atmospheric temperature, changes in precipitation patterns, the shrinking of glaciers, rising sea levels, and the frequency of extreme weather events, among other phenomena that affect different regions of the world in different ways

[627] As the culmination of the IPCC's reporting process, the organization's member governments endorse it

[628] The approval process is based on a dialogue between governments, who are the users of the report, and scientists, who are the authors

[629] In this dynamic, the governments' approval confirms that the report is an assessment on which there is global consensus

[630] Considering the IPCC's diagnoses and recommendations, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the leading international body on the subject, has considered mitigation and adaptation as its main strategic axes of action to address the challenges of climate change

[631] At the various conferences held by the Panel, the member countries agreed at the 21st Conference of the Parties (COP 21), held in Paris in 2016, to set targets for reducing global greenhouse gas emissions, ensuring that global warming does not exceed 2 degrees Celsius by the end of the century

[632] Among the initiatives aimed at this goal, the need to use new or alternative, efficient, and clean technologies in various sectors of activity stands out

[633] Source: Prepared by the authors based on UN and IPCC documentation. Climate change has gained increasing relevance as a strategic issue

[634] Although there is no evidence that climate change increases the likelihood of interstate conflict, there is certainty that the various consequences of global warming pose risks to national security

[635] The IPCC reports indicate that climate change could have a greater impact on the most vulnerable countries, reduce available resources, affect territorial and maritime borders, and damage existing infrastructure, both public and private, including military installations

[636] These and other effects of climate change can directly affect defense, which is why several countries have begun to implement sectoral policies on the matter

[637] Additionally, the Armed Forces are significant users of fossil fuels, so there is a challenge in establishing mitigation measures to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions

[638] In the area of adaptation, the use of new technologies and clean energy will be the main alternative to help contain global warming

[639] All of this can be addressed cooperatively, as it constitutes, on the one hand, common risks and challenges, and, on the other, represents an opportunity to change energy resource use patterns and modernize technologies, including defense technologies

[640] Science, Technology and Innovation Historically, science, technology and innovation have played a central role in the military sphere and international security

[641] These dimensions remain relevant today, but others have been added that need to be taken into consideration

[642] On the one hand, we have witnessed a process of rapid advances—nanotechnology, information and communications, artificial intelligence, etc.—that are altering social, political, economic, and cultural spheres

[643] On the other hand, access to these advances is not only available to states, but in many cases also to individuals, groups, corporations, and, in general, various non-state actors

[644] This impacts the conflict and the forms of confrontation, in addition to generating various challenges for the international standards that regulate it

[645] States not only seek to incorporate and adapt to ongoing changes, but also generate internal and external actions that have consequences for the international system as a whole

[646] At the same time, the availability of technological resources for non-state actors poses challenges both from a positive perspective (science and technology development, innovation, public-private cooperation, etc.) and from a negative perspective (use of these resources for purposes that jeopardize international and national security

[647] At the same time, international organizations and states must review and reformulate the regulations on this matter to adapt to the new realities created by technology

[648] This has led states to try to respond to the associated challenges

[649] On the one hand, some have made efforts to promote their own technological initiatives, which can encourage research, innovation, and technological development, but can also mean a heavy tax on public resources

[650] On the other hand, if they are unable to develop their own technology, states choose to acquire it abroad, which leads to technological dependence, with its corresponding military, economic, and political impact

[651] The varying levels of technological development among states can encourage the use of strategic options that avoid conventional forms of conflict in which the possession of advanced technologies represents a decisive advantage, giving rise to so-called asymmetric conflicts

[652] Global trends in science and technology applied to defense are primarily evident in the areas of information technology, robotics, and cyberspace control

[653] THE INTERNATIONAL REGIME ON SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY The impact of technological development in the strategic sphere, particularly of “military technological revolutions,” has been a historical concern of the international community

[654] In the contemporary period, the speed of changes in science and technology has outpaced the adaptation of international standards in this area

[655] This creates a series of challenges and greater uncertainty for the international community

[656] Some milestones in international security, science, and technology include: • A draft resolution, sponsored by India in 1988, during the First Committee of the General Assembly, which recalled that increasing resources were being devoted to the development of new weapons systems, which was causing uncertainty and insecurity. • Resolution 43/77 of May

[657] By this Resolution, the UN Secretary-General was urged to monitor future scientific and technological developments, especially in the areas of nuclear technology, space technology, materials technology, information technology and biotechnology, and to assess their impact on international security. • Sendai Conference (Japan, 1990) where scientists, strategy analysts, arms control and disarmament experts, politicians and diplomats from more than 20 countries addressed the five issues mentioned above and their impact on the international security agenda

[658] Resolution 61/65, adopted by the General Assembly on 6 December 2006, reaffirms that scientific and technological advances should be used for the benefit of all humanity to promote the sustainable economic and social development of all States and safeguard international security

[659] In this regard, international cooperation in the use of science and technology should be promoted through the transfer and exchange of technical knowledge for peaceful purposes

[660] Although the issue remains on the United Nations agenda, the latest resolution on the matter was issued in

[661] This highlights the gap between rapid technological change, with its strategic impact, and the international response

[662] These new trends impact defense in both its internal and external dimensions

[663] In their internal dimension, they influence organizational aspects, decision-making, and capacity development options

[664] On the external level, while the acquisition of new technologies can be understood as an element that increases the strategic capabilities of actors, to the extent that information is transparent, technological exchange is encouraged and an international regulatory framework is established, it is possible that scientific and technological developments contribute to increasing interstate confidence, reducing uncertainty and cooperatively confronting threats from non-state actors

[665] Cyberspace is the set of physical and logical infrastructures and the interactions that occur there

[666] Today, cyberspace is composed of both open networks—the Internet being the most well-known—as well as closed networks, such as intranets or closed communications systems

[667] One of the fundamental characteristics of cyberspace is its massiveness and ubiquity

[668] This massiveness generates dependence and, therefore, a growing vulnerability of our society to the services and activities carried out in cyberspace

[669] In terms of defense, this potential vulnerability could be critical for the country's external security and sovereignty

[670] This requires considering, from a security perspective, the protection of both the networks of interactions that occur in cyberspace and the infrastructure that makes them possible

[671] International conflicts in cyberspace can manifest themselves in many ways

[672] This creates new challenges for the international community, such as the number and diversity of cyberattacks, the difficulty in determining their origin or attributing responsibility, and the ubiquity with which they occur given the exponential growth of devices connected to the Internet

[673] These challenges require the development of strategies to guarantee the country's essential services, including defense functions

[674] Efforts such as the Tallinn Manual 2.0 on rules of international law applicable to operations in cyberspace, prepared by a group of experts invited by NATO's Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence, contribute to the interpretation of key concepts of international law, such as sovereignty and jurisdiction, to make them applicable to cyberspace and to guide the actions of States in protecting this new dimension

[675] The international system and cyberspace The international community's concern about information security has been addressed by the United Nations since 1998, when the General Assembly approved the resolution on advances in computerization and telecommunications in the context of international security (A/RES/53/70), which has been systematically updated and approved over the last two decades by that international body

[676] THE INTERNATIONAL REGIME ON SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY The impact of technological development in the strategic sphere, particularly of “military technological revolutions,” has been a historical concern of the international community

[677] In the contemporary period, the speed of changes in science and technology has outpaced the adaptation of international standards in this area

[678] This creates a series of challenges and greater uncertainty for the international community

[679] Some milestones in international security, science, and technology include: • A draft resolution, sponsored by India in 1988, during the First Committee of the General Assembly, which recalled that increasing resources were being devoted to the development of new weapons systems, which was causing uncertainty and insecurity. • Resolution 43/77 of May

[680] By this Resolution, the UN Secretary-General was urged to monitor future scientific and technological developments, especially in the areas of nuclear technology, space technology, materials technology, information technology and biotechnology, and to assess their impact on international security. • Sendai Conference (Japan, 1990) where scientists, strategy analysts, arms control and disarmament experts, politicians and diplomats from more than 20 countries addressed the five issues mentioned above and their impact on the international security agenda

[681] • Resolution 61/65, adopted by the General Assembly on 6 December 2006, reaffirms that scientific and technological advances should be used for the benefit of all humanity to promote the sustainable economic and social development of all States and safeguard international security

[682] In this regard, international cooperation in the use of science and technology should be promoted through the transfer and exchange of technical knowledge for peaceful purposes

[683] Although the issue remains on the United Nations agenda, the latest resolution on the matter was issued in

[684] This highlights the gap between rapid technological change, with its strategic impact, and the international response

[685] In 2004, pursuant to resolution A/RES/58/32, the United Nations Secretary-General established the first Group of Governmental Experts (GEG) on developments in information and telecommunications in the context of international security. This group was comprised of specialists from fifteen countries and tasked with preparing a study on the most relevant concepts for strengthening the security of information systems

[686] The Group of Governmental Experts has had its mandate renewed three times, issuing compelling reports (A/60/202, A/65/201, A/68/98 and A/70/174) that have guided the development of cybersecurity policies and strategies around the world, by identifying the risks to international peace and security that cyberspace can pose and the measures that States must adopt to adequately manage these risks

[687] In parallel, since 2011, four versions of the Global Conference on Cyberspace have been held. This informal multi-stakeholder discussion space brings together representatives from government, the private sector, civil society, and academia to discuss and promote practical cooperation and cyber capacity building, as well as debate standards for responsible behavior in cyberspace

[688] This area has also become a priority concern for organizations such as NATO, where cyber defense is part of the collective defense agreement, as reflected in the final report of the 2014 Wales Summit and the Cyber Defense Pledge emanating from the 2016 Warsaw Summit

[689] For its part, the European Union adopted the Cybersecurity Strategy of the European Union: An Open, Safe and Secure Cyberspace in February 2014, and the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) plays an important role in strengthening cybersecurity and information and communications technologies, particularly by reducing the risks of conflicts between states arising from their use

[690] At the regional level

[691] the Organization of American States, pursuant to resolution AG/RES

[692] of the year 2003, of the General Assembly, instructed the preparation of the Cyber Security Strategy (AG/RES

[693] which seeks to increase the security of information networks and systems and develop a culture of cybersecurity in the Americas, based on a strategy with a comprehensive, international and multidisciplinary approach

[694] In its implementation, the Cybersecurity Program was created—under the coordination of the Inter-American Committee against Terrorism—which promotes cooperation in the development of national strategies, the strengthening of technical capabilities, and the promotion of public-private collaboration in cybersecurity

[695] Recently, Chile and Colombia's proposal for the creation of the Working Group on Cooperation and Confidence-Building Measures in Cyberspace was approved. It will begin its sessions in December

[696] At the subregional level, the Union of South American Nations, through its South American Defense Council, agreed to include the Cyber Defense Action Plan and the formation of a working group to study the feasibility of establishing regional policies and mechanisms to address cyber threats in the defense field

[697] At the national level, several countries have developed national cybersecurity strategies and policies, and cyber defense policy documents are expected to be adopted in the medium term

[698] d) Outer Space Outer space is a dimension susceptible to conflict, even though international law has regulated the peaceful use of space, the legal equality of States in it and the use of space benefits for the good of humanity, regardless of the origin, language, culture, religion or economic capabilities of the State

[699] This set of international regulations, which make up the Corpus Juris Spatialis, is under the auspices of the Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA), an ad hoc United Nations body that includes the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) and the Legal Committee

[700] Over the past decade, the risk of the peaceful uses of outer space being undermined by the actions of new actors who do not subscribe to the international treaties of the Corpus Juris Spatialis, or to complementary international conventions, such as the International Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, has increased

[701] This, combined with technological advancements, could affect the exercise of defense in its strategic component

[702] Current challenges in this area guide defense institutions toward understanding the complex outer space and the constant search for integrating factors that contribute to this mission, especially those related to science, technology, information, and cyberspace

[703] Maintaining the peaceful use of outer space requires signatory states to include the space dimension in their defense sector, in order to understand the nature of the challenges and contribute to international peace and security beyond the biosphere

[704] The National Space Policy, related to this matter, is developed in Chapter IV

[705] Regional dynamics Despite global problems and challenges, there is a growing importance of the various regions of the world in understanding the dynamics of international security and defense

[706] In Chile's case, while efforts are focused on the American continent, the country is also a coastal nation and an important player in the Pacific Rim, and has historical ties to Europe

[707] It is also necessary to consider the Middle East, with which Chile maintains important ties, as well as Africa

[708] a) Pacific Basin The world's focus of attention has progressively shifted from the Atlantic to the Pacific, mainly encouraged by the economic dynamism of the countries that make up the Basin

[709] In parallel, its political and strategic relevance has increased

[710] Four continents converge in this vast space, and together, the macro-region generates more than half of the world's GDP

[711] Within the Pacific Rim, the Asia-Pacific region holds central importance in politics, economics, security, and international relations

[712] However, phenomena such as climate change and its impact on countries and nations that are part of the Pacific community, or its effects on the Arctic and Antarctic, require a view of the Basin as an integrated whole

[713] The main trends regarding international security converge in this region of the world, among which those linked to the new strategic agenda stand out—such as technological development, cybersecurity, the increase in natural hazards, and the impact of climate change—which coexist with a traditional strategic agenda linked to interstate conflict and nuclear proliferation

[714] In this regard, it is noteworthy that the Pacific is home to major powers with nuclear capabilities, and that numerous interstate tensions persist, as well as historical disputes that challenge international peace and development prospects

[715] To respond to this environment, the macro-region is also showing significant and growing development in areas of international cooperation

[716] Cooperation has developed in both the economic and security spheres, and is a necessary condition for ensuring the stability of the Basin: its challenges and risks concern the international community as a whole

[717] However, there is no single institutional framework encompassing the entire Basin; rather, an evolving architecture exists at different levels, at a multilateral, subregional, and bilateral level

[718] The aforementioned elements demonstrate the strategic importance of the Pacific Rim, where a dense institutional framework is evident, incorporating organizations, agreements, and strategic dialogues, encompassing a multitude of issues relevant to security and defense

[719] Europe, specifically the European Union (EU), has been a global benchmark in terms of regional integration and a common security model17, and has also been a major contributor to the search for cooperation with other regions

[720] However, it has had to face, especially recently, various threats to its security, with traditional and non-traditional threats coexisting

[721] Interstate tensions persist, as well as a wide range of interests that include strategic aspects such as regional stability and energy security, among others

[722] Regarding non-traditional threats, Europe faces a complex scenario, linked to a significant increase in terrorist activity on its territory

[723] Mass migration is also a significant consequence of extraregional conflicts with direct repercussions in Europe

[724] Regarding security and defense organizations, both the European Union and NATO, of which 22 of its members are currently EU-18 countries, face the challenge of responding to the complexity of the current strategic landscape under new modes of action

[725] Africa The continent has been expanding its strategic importance in recent years

[726] African countries have managed to increase their growth rates, while various private and state actors have increased their investments in this part of the world

[727] This promising trend has not been enough to overcome the problems that have plagued the continent for decades, which are primarily related to extreme poverty, instability, and intrastate conflicts with far-reaching interstate consequences

[728] The international community, primarily through the United Nations, in collaboration with African agencies and non-governmental organizations, has made efforts to help improve the living conditions and security of the continent's population

[729] Despite the importance of this effort, security challenges remain high in the region

[730] The Union's competence in matters of the common foreign and security policy shall cover all areas of foreign policy and all questions relating to the security of the Union, including the progressive definition of a common defence policy which may lead to a common defence" (Treaty on European Union, Art

[731] The United Kingdom approved its withdrawal from the EU in a referendum held in June 2016, but the process had not yet materialized at the time of writing

[732] Risks associated with power vacuums have been a source of problems; there are areas devoid of any state control and subject, instead, to the activity of international mafias

[733] There are also geographical areas occupied by terrorist groups, which contribute to reviving old border disputes between neighboring countries

[734] Factors such as these have diminished the ability to combat piracy, biological diseases, and drought, among other phenomena

[735] The above highlights the need to continue seeking new options for international cooperation

[736] Middle East The Middle East is a region of particular importance for global political and economic stability

[737] It has been the scene of many wars over the past fifty years and continues to concentrate the main factors of international conflict, with a high capacity to spread its effects on a global scale

[738] In geostrategic terms, it possesses considerable sources and reserves of fossil fuels and some of the most important maritime transport routes on the planet

[739] Wars and armed conflicts in the region have not resulted in far-reaching political agreements that would generate a degree of political and strategic stability

[740] Political and security volatility in the Middle East has been exacerbated by massive civilian displacement, the rise of corruption, and rising sectarianism, all of which add to traditional regional threats

[741] The American continent and the creation of a Zone of Peace in Latin America America is a vast and diverse continent

[742] Analysis of the evolution of security must distinguish between the continental sphere comprising all the countries from Alaska to Cape Horn—the Latin American and Caribbean region, and the Latin American subregions of Mesoamerica, Central America, the Caribbean, and South America

[743] As a continent, the Americas face a multidimensional set of risks and threats, and a plurality of state and non-state actors are present

[744] The most significant and widespread security problems are largely related to non-traditional security issues, which are transnational in nature, such as organized crime related to drug trafficking, human trafficking, and arms trafficking, although the intensity and treatment varies from subregion to subregion and from state to state

[745] CONFERENCE OF DEFENSE MINISTERS OF THE AMERICAS (CMDA) The CMDA is a multilateral political meeting of an international nature initiated in 1995 and constituted by the Ministries of Defense of the hemisphere

[746] Its purpose is to promote mutual understanding, analysis, debate, and exchange of ideas and experiences in the field of defense and security, or any other interaction mechanism that allows for this

[747] The Conference cycles last two years, during which a member country assumes the Presidency

[748] The function of maintaining institutional memory has been assigned to the Inter-American Defense Board, an entity of the Organization of American States

[749] Member countries: Antigua and Barbuda, Argentina, Bahamas, Barbados, Belize, Bolivia, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominica, El Salvador, Ecuador, United States of America, Grenada, Guatemala, Guyana, Haiti, Honduras, Jamaica, Mexico, Nicaragua, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Dominican Republic, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago, Uruguay, Venezuela

[750] The continent is also experiencing increased risks associated with globalization, such as the increased spread of pandemics and climate change

[751] In the latter case, the increasing frequency of extreme weather events, the impact on polar regions, the melting of glaciers, and rising sea levels have introduced new types of risk that are placing a growing demand on state capabilities, including those of national defense institutions

[752] From an institutional perspective, the continent has gradually developed a complex, multi-level architecture of cooperation regimes in the various geographic areas of security and defense

[753] At the continental level, Chile participates in the security and defense institutions of the Inter-American System

[754] This is organized around the Organization of American States (OAS), the Inter-American Treaty of Reciprocal Assistance (TIAR) and the Conference of Defense Ministers of the Americas' (CMDA), which has been framed, since its inception in 1995, within the Summits of the Americas Process

[755] In the specific area of continental defense, the Conference of Defense Ministers of the Americas has gradually developed into the most important political forum in the defense sector of the inter-American system, with a cooperative nature and the participation of the largest number of defense ministries on the continent

[756] The Inter-American Treaty of Reciprocal Assistance includes two institutions that remain active: the Inter-American Defense Board (IADB) and the Inter-American Defense College (IADC), both of which are currently part of the OAS

[757] A second level of security practice on the continent corresponds to the Latin American and Caribbean region, which has gradually been equipped with institutions and whose general situation contrasts positively with the global context of growing uncertainty and instability summarized in the previous sections

[758] Latin America and the Caribbean is a region where, despite existing difficulties and shortcomings, democracy has prevailed as a political regime for several decades

[759] The practice of Latin American regionalism has also taken important steps in recent years, with the creation of the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States (CELAC), the Union of South American Nations (UNASUR) and its South American Defense Council (CDS), and, more recently, the Pacific Alliance

[760] The CDS-UNASUR was created in 2008 by decision of the Heads of State of the member countries of the Union of South American Nations (UNASUR

[761] The organization is defined as the entity responsible for implementing defense policies in the areas of military cooperation, humanitarian actions and peacekeeping operations, defense industry, and training and capacity building

[762] Among the objectives proposed are consolidating a South American Zone of Peace and a common vision on defense, in the spirit of articulating regional positions in various multilateral forums, among other cooperation activities within the region

[763] Member countries: The member countries are Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Guyana, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay and Venezuela

[764] In this context, the region has made and is making very significant global contributions to the maintenance of peace and international security

[765] Considered as a region, Latin America and the Caribbean, and especially South America

[766] It is one of the areas in the world that has had the fewest international conflicts since the end of the 19th century until today

[767] The region has also since then displayed a strong tradition of promoting and respecting the principle of sovereign equality of states and the peaceful resolution of disputes, a tradition that has endured throughout the 20th century to the present, with very few exceptions

[768] In promoting these principles and values, Latin America has contributed to the construction of the main contemporary international regimes that have institutionalized the principles of Public International Law, in particular the Charter of the United Nations

[769] Regionally, Latin America's commitment to peace and international law has been reflected in the creation of numerous regional and bilateral regimes, the most significant of which is the 1948 Bogotá Pact

[770] These advances were greatly boosted by the regional democratization process that began in the mid-1980s and continues to this day, consolidating the regional tradition of peaceful dispute resolution

[771] During that effort, Central America carried out a successful peace process, and in South America, countries resolved, through bilateral channels, most of the then controversial territorial issues. Particularly relevant were the agreements between Argentina and Chile from 1984 and 1991, between Argentina and Brazil from 1985, which led to the creation of the Southern Common Market (MERCOSUR), and between Ecuador and Peru in

[773] The second Conference on CSBMs was held in El Salvador in 1998, and numerous expert meetings and specialized forums on the subject have subsequently been held, including the Miami Conference in

[775] In addition to the continental framework, Chile has established CSBMs with its neighboring countries, particularly Argentina and Peru

[776] These processes have allowed for everything from symbolic gestures, such as invitations to celebrate anniversaries, to combined military exercises and the institutionalization of cooperation mechanisms

[777] As a trust-building measure, Chile shares information on various defense matters at multiple levels: globally, through the UN; continentally, through the OAS; and subregionally, within the framework of UNASUR-CDS

[778] Additionally, it sends information to non-governmental organizations

[796] CSBMs, understood as concrete bilateral or multilateral actions that seek to prevent the occurrence of conflicts between states, have made it possible to operationalize the will to cooperate

[803] The persistence and combination of the aforementioned achievements have allowed Latin America and the Caribbean to become a region that is increasingly conceptualized or defined as a Zone of Peace

[804] The construction of the Zone of Peace is a historic achievement and a regional attribute in a global context that must be politically recognized and strengthened

[805] Therefore, the fundamental political objective of the Ministry of National Defense's international policy is to contribute to consolidating and strengthening the Zone of Peace in Latin America and the Caribbean, supporting its institutions and promoting its expansion, deepening, and enrichment

[806] As summarized in the previous sections, this does not mean that all the internal conflicts that have characterized the region throughout its history have disappeared, that the region has not had or does not have security problems, or that disagreements and even international controversies do not persist

[807] During the 20th century, there were international armed conflicts, such as the Chaco War and the two conflicts between Ecuador and Peru, in addition to numerous internal conflicts

[808] But the long-term trend that has prevailed is to maintain democratic regimes as the general rule, to make progress in resolving internal conflicts—as in the Republic of Colombia, which began its peace process in 2016—and to maintain the tradition of peaceful resolution of international disputes

[809] The use of the concept of Zone of Peace in the region has begun to become broader, although there is still no single definition that reflects a regional political consensus

[810] In general, the use of the concept of Zone of Peace tends to reflect the regional stability achieved, which has allowed for a significant increase in the regional contribution to the efforts of the international community, and in particular the United Nations, to maintain international peace
