[832] SPECIFIC POLICIES IN PROCESS National Defense is the set of material, human and moral means that a nation can oppose to the threats of an adversary against its interests, mainly its sovereignty and territorial integrity

[833] Its purpose is to achieve a condition of external security such that the country can achieve its objectives, free from external interference

[834] Defense is a non-transferable function of the State, guided by clear state principles and led by a set of institutional authorities, who make up a system whose central figure is the President of the Republic

[835] In terms of public policy, this is reflected in defense policy, which considers the basic guidelines for the entire sector

[836] In addition to the conceptualization of National Defense, this section of the book addresses Defense Policy and its implementation through the defense system, defense planning, and the management, development, and use of its resources and capabilities

[837] It also explains the contribution of defense to international security at its various levels, which includes cooperation at the global level, with various regions, and, in particular, with Latin America and its neighboring countries

[838] Finally, specific policies currently under development are addressed: climate change, cyber defense, and scientific and technological development

[839] CONCEPTUALIZATION OF NATIONAL DEFENSE This chapter describes the principles of National Defense, the defensive and deterrent orientation of its policy

[840] The conceptual aspects that link defense with security and development, respectively, are also described, with special emphasis on the human security approach

[841] Finally, citizen participation in some of its processes and areas of management is highlighted

[842] General concept Fundamentally, the concept of defense relates to the action of the State to maintain the political independence of the country and its territorial integrity, as well as to protect its population from the use of force or the threat of the use of force by international actors

[843] It considers the set of material, human and moral means that a nation can oppose to an adversary's threats against such assets and interests

[844] Its purpose is to contribute to achieving a condition of external security such that the country can achieve its objectives free from external interference

[845] Given the long-term nature of defense matters, it will be easier to achieve citizen commitment to the country's defense and security the greater the awareness and consensus regarding the goals to be achieved

[846] The long-term stability of decisions made by political authorities, essential to ensuring the success of defense sector processes, will depend largely on their ability to provide their policies with a broad and in-depth consensus on their purposes and objectives, supported by informed participation and the checks and balances exercised by citizens, the media, and public institutions

[847] The following are principles of the Defense Policy: The State of Chile has the will and the duty to protect its population, defend its national interests, safeguard its political independence, its national sovereignty and its territorial integrity

[848] In accordance with the Charter of the United Nations, the State of Chile shall settle its international disputes by peaceful means and shall refrain from resorting to the threat of use of force or the use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of other States, in any manner incompatible with the provisions of Article 51 of the Charter

[849] The State of Chile does not harbor aggressive intentions against any nation in the world, nor does it have territorial claims in its neighboring areas

[850] The State of Chile has the inherent right and responsibility to employ all national capabilities, and in particular its war potential, if necessary, for the defense of the country and the protection of national interests against external threats

[851] Chile will exercise this inherent right to self-defense in accordance with the provisions of the Charter of the United Nations and the norms of international humanitarian law

[852] The State of Chile has the responsibility to maintain sufficient military capacity to facilitate the achievement of the country's interests and objectives, within a framework of resource allocation to the sector in harmony and balance with the priorities and needs of the State as a whole

[853] The Chilean State must foster citizen commitment to National Defense, considering, among other objectives, the necessary provisions for the provision of Compulsory Military Service, the satisfaction of national mobilization needs, and those arising from maintaining the capacities and skills of the reserves

[854] • For the State of Chile – as for all States in general – its relative geographical location remains an important reference in the formulation of Defense Policy

[855] • The State of Chile places its defense policy fully within the institutional legal framework in force in the country, and recognizes and respects the international treaties and agreements incorporated into said framework, such that its Defense Policy possesses the legitimacy inherent to any State policy and is representative of the political commitment that binds the State to its national citizens, on the one hand, and to the international community, on the other

[856] For the State of Chile, the close link and coordination between its defense policy and its foreign policy is of particular interest and convenience, complementing and strengthening each other, although the former acts in support of the latter

[857] The security of the Chilean nation must be understood as a condition that varies according to the actions that the State carries out to advance the country towards the intended objectives and safeguard national interests with the least interference from risks, threats, problems or other important obstacles

[858] However, the pursuit of national security must be achieved through institutions with distinct and specific responsibilities, which the State employs in conjunction with other complementary state functions for this purpose

[859] Defense institutions and responsibilities are primarily combined with diplomatic institutions and responsibilities to achieve external security; public order institutions and responsibilities are implemented in conjunction with the administration of justice for internal security purposes; and disaster safety is achieved through civil protection and environmental protection functions

[860] The institution of defense exists to provide external security to the country, a public good that extends to all members of the national community, because once it is provided, no one obtains it at the expense of others. To guarantee this effect, the following conditions must be met: • The monopoly of legitimate force must belong to the State

[861] That the State organize it, provide it with resources and assign it objectives with a national sense

[862] • That the State carry out this task continuously over time, whether in peace, crisis or war

[863] • That the exercise of the function encompasses the sum of activities of the State institutions necessary for defense, since its scope exceeds the limits of the strictly military

[864] The Defense institution, like other state institutions, requires an organizational structure capable of planning and executing its objectives, management control mechanisms, supporting legislation, financing, and guiding policies

[865] A public policy, known as Defense Policy, includes its main aspects

[866] In its purpose of providing external security to the country, Defense Policy complements Foreign Policy

[867] Similarly, in terms of internal security, it contributes to the Public Order and Internal Security Policy; the direct participation of Armed Forces resources in internal order tasks is regulated in Article 39 et seq. of the Political Constitution of the Republic by virtue of certain States of Constitutional Exception

[868] Finally, in terms of disaster safety, the Defense Policy supports the specific policies in which it is embodied

[869] Source: Prepared by the authors based on “Human Security at the United Nations”, New York

[870] OBJECTIVES OF NATIONAL DEFENSE Preserve the country's independence and sovereignty

[871] • Maintain the integrity of the national territory

[872] • Contribute to the creation of fundamental external security conditions to achieve the common good of the nation

[873] • Support Chile’s Foreign Policy

[874] • Contribute to the maintenance and promotion of international peace and security, in accordance with national interests

[875] • Contribute to national development and cooperate in achieving other State capabilities

[876] • Contribute to the preservation of Chile's institutional framework as a democratic Republic and the rule of law

[877] • Contribute to the maintenance of Chile's historical and cultural legacy

[878] • Contribute to the activities that the State carries out with the purpose of strengthening citizen commitment to Defense

[879] • Participate in the civil protection system, contributing to the timely response to emergency and disaster situations, particularly in actions to protect at-risk populations

[880] • Contribute, through the presence of the Armed Forces in the national territory, to the physical integration of border, isolated, and special areas, and to the social and economic development of local communities in these areas

[881] Political leadership and coordination between different public policies is the responsibility of the Head of State and Government, and in Chilean institutions, it is organized around the President of the Republic and his or her Cabinet, as well as around the intersectoral institutions permitted by the current regulatory framework

[882] Defense and citizen participation Citizen participation constitutes an axis of public policies with regard to the construction of co-responsibility between the State and civil society, and constitutes a fundamental part of the modernization of the State

[883] With the approval of Law No. 20,500 in 2011, on Associations and Citizen Participation in Public Management, the right of citizens to influence state policies, plans, actions, and programs was established

[884] The mandatory mechanisms for citizen participation include access to relevant information, citizen consultations, participatory public accounts, and civil society councils in state administrative bodies

[885] Civil society councils, in particular, have an advisory nature and should be composed of diverse, representative, and pluralistic members based on non-profit associations relevant to the respective body's jurisdiction

[886] This regulatory framework led to the formation, in 2015, of the Civil Society Council of the Ministry of National Defense (COSOC-MINDEF

[887] The Council defined the following as its medium-term priorities: Strengthen and promote the human security paradigm in National Defense Policy

[888] • Contribute to an adequate adaptation of National Defense to the new human security challenges arising from the Sustainable Development Goals

[889] • Encourage the participation of National Defense in disaster situations, both nationally and internationally, in collaboration with relevant civilian organizations

[890] • Gather information from the Ministry of Defense to make recommendations in specific areas that will improve the performance of this State portfolio in these areas of its work

[891] In 2015, the United Nations agenda known as the "Millennium Development Goals" concluded, and in 2016, the Sustainable Development Goals agenda was officially launched

[892] These are 17 global goals that aim to eradicate poverty and protect the planet

[893] Each goal considers targets to be achieved by 2030, engaging governments, the private sector, civil society, and individuals

[894] VI CHAPTER NATIONAL DEFENSE POLICY Chilean National Defense Book 2017 Source: Prepared by the author based on “Human Security at the United Nations”, New York

[895] HUMAN SECURITY APPROACH The concept of “human security” was incorporated by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in its 1994 Human Development Report to refocus the attention of States and the international community on the survival, livelihoods and dignity of individuals as the basis for achieving peace, development and human progress

[896] Human security is the first approach that brings together the three pillars of the United Nations system: peace and security, development, and human rights

[897] Its main objective is to protect people from multidimensional threats, basing its processes on human strength and aspirations for a more dignified life

[898] According to the definition adopted by the United Nations, this concept considers threats from an integrated, multidimensional, and broad perspective

[899] Not only does it help mitigate the impact of such threats, but it also reduces the risk of them escalating into larger, more intractable crises. By contextualizing the causes and their effects on people, the concept of human security highlights the real needs, vulnerabilities, and capabilities of those affected and contributes to the search for solutions geared toward specific priorities and objectives

[900] Along these lines, states and governments are encouraged to promote integrated public policies to address insecurities that pose serious risks to their populations and, therefore, affect vital aspects of their countries

[901] One of its values is addressing the root causes of various threats, which helps promote precautionary systems that prevent their occurrence or mitigate their impact

[902] Chile subscribes to the human security approach

[903] For our country, this approach's primary function is to enable an existence that provides conditions for the sustainable development of the human person, free from vulnerabilities

[904] This approach requires the incorporation of new actors into security management, coordinating their actions with the growing challenges that the 21st century presents to states and the international system

[905] Defense, security and development The political definition coined in the mid-1990s oriented the work of the Armed Forces in general terms towards the external, with an increasingly clear emphasis on the tasks of classic defense and cooperation in international security, but always preserving an important role for those functions in matters of security or development

[906] That perspective, which was an important aspect of Chile's international profile in defense matters, remains in force

[907] However, given the country's experiences with disasters in recent years, along with changes in the security agenda at the global and regional levels, new emphasis has been placed on the role of defense sector organizations and institutions in areas such as disasters and cyberspace, which require providing protection to the population

[908] a) Security Security consists of a condition that is desired to be achieved in order to achieve the purposes of the State and the Nation, particularly those of social, economic and sustainable development, and is consequently the result of the set of activities that the State carries out to advance towards the achievement of its objectives and safeguard national interests in relation to risks, threats or interference

[909] Although defense and security are closely related, defense is a more specific concept than security, referring to the development and use of military capabilities for the tasks defined by the Constitution and laws

[910] Defense alone does not produce the desired security condition, but it is undoubtedly one of the essential factors for achieving it

[911] Traditionally, this trait has been manifested, in particular, in the external aspects or areas of security

[912] Currently, as a result of changes in the strategic context affecting the country, which give security issues a transnational, crossborder, and societal connotation, the State has been strengthening its institutional framework regarding the role of defense against these issues, as well as issues arising from new phenomena such as climate change or the challenges posed by cybersecurity and cyberdefense

[913] Contribution of Defense to development National Defense contributes, through various policies, to the development of the country, constantly updating and adapting to national and global transformations

[914] The Defense Ministry contributes in situations such as emergencies or disasters, and contributes to the unity of the national territory through the support provided in isolated and extreme areas

[915] It carries out ongoing work to protect the environment and seeks to adapt to changing climatic conditions and their effects

[916] Likewise, Defense contributes to the country's scientific and technological development

[917] It is also an important source of human capital development, an area that has also been able to incorporate topics such as gender perspective

[918] The final part of this Book, with chapters 26 and 27, records the activities and initiatives carried out by the National Defense institutions as a contribution to the development of the country, according to the guidelines of the various sectoral policies that aim at this general purpose

[919] Through its international action, the Defense contributes to the country's development by providing the public good "international security," either through cooperation or through the coercive use of its resources in accordance with International Public Law, International Humanitarian Law, and International Human Rights Law

[920] THE NATIONAL DEFENSE SYSTEM The defense system is a generic name to designate the set of organizations that participate in both decision-making and the execution of the actions that materialize Defense

[921] They are part of the State and receive inputs such as data and information from other state institutions and authorities to incorporate them into their processes

[922] Similarly, they generate products or effects intended for other public sectors as well as for society itself

[923] The political and military organization of Defense Due to the nature and repercussions of decisions related to National Defense, its management requires a specific system and order

[924] This system is made up of decision-making authorities at different levels—primarily the political, joint strategic, and institutional levels—advisory bodies, executive bodies, and those entities that produce goods for Defense

[925] In this system, political and military authorities interact in a regulatory environment and are involved in the execution of various processes relevant to the decisions and actions that materialize Defense

[926] Furthermore, the defense system is intertwined, in its organization and operation, with other systems with their own institutional framework and in which defense sector agencies participate and perform specific functions

[927] The most notable, from the perspective of the role the Armed Forces play in them, are the State Intelligence System, established by Law No. 19,974 of 2004, and the future Civil Protection and Risk and Emergency Management System, a function currently handled by the National Emergency Office of the Ministry of the Interior and Public Security (ONEMI), which is currently under review by a bill currently being processed in the National Congress

[928] THE NATIONAL SECURITY COUNCIL (COSENA) Strictly speaking, COSENA is not part of the political organization of defense, since the scope of matters that can be submitted to its consideration is related to the security of the country in general

[929] Its function exceeds, although it includes, defense matters

[930] It was created by the Political Constitution of the Republic in 1980 and reformed in

[931] Its mission is to advise the President of the Republic on matters related to national security and to exercise other functions entrusted to it by the Constitution

[932] Under the presidency of the Head of State, it is comprised of the Presidents of the Senate, the Chamber of Deputies, and the Supreme Court of Justice, as well as the Comptroller General of the Republic, the Commanders-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, and the Director General of the Carabineros

[933] According to the President of the Republic's determination, some Ministers may be included, including the Minister of National Defense

[934] The Council meets at the call of the President of the Republic and requires a quorum of an absolute majority of its members

[935] a) Main institutions and authorities of the system In the presidential government regime of Chile, the main superior institution of defense corresponds to the President of the Republic

[936] Other bodies, which perform various functions according to the current constitutional and legal order of our country, are the National Congress, the Ministry of National Defense and the institutions of the Armed Forces

[937] Article 24 of the Political Constitution of Chile, when referring to the President of the Republic, indicates that he is responsible for the government and administration of the State and that his authority extends to everything that has the objective of preserving public order within the country and the external security of the Republic, in accordance with the Constitution and the laws

[938] In relation to the defense function, the special powers of the President of the Republic are: The description of the Ministry of National Defense is found in Chapter IX

[939] In turn, the description of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the branches of the Armed Forces are found in Chapters XXII, XXIII, XXIV and XXV, respectively

[940] To arrange, organize and distribute the air, sea and land forces - To assume, in case of war, the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces - To declare war, with prior authorization by law, and must record having heard the National Security Council - To declare, with the concurrence of other organs of the State, the States of Constitutional Exception of Assembly and Siege

[941] National Congress The National Congress is made up of the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies

[942] Each legislative branch has a Defense Committee, which is responsible for analyzing and reporting to the respective plenary session on all bills relating to National Defense, in general, and the Armed Forces, in particular

[943] Regarding the defense sector, the National Congress, in addition to analyzing and approving the Public Sector Budget Law, which includes financial resources for Defense, collaborates with the Executive Branch in approving sectoral legislation

[944] Likewise, Congress has the power to decide on the state of the Assembly in the event of a foreign war

[945] Furthermore, it is the exclusive power of the Senate to authorize or deny the entry of foreign troops into the territory of the Republic, as well as the departure of national troops abroad

[946] In turn, the Chamber of Deputies is responsible for overseeing and monitoring the actions of the State administration

[947] b) Main defense decision-making processes The main processes carried out by the institutions of the political and military defense organization are planning, management - at its different levels -, capacity development and the use of force, subjects that are explored in depth in the following chapters

[948] Every organization of a defense system is fundamentally concerned with resolving issues related to the proper development and use of military force by the Executive, within the framework established by the Constitution and the laws

[949] The concept of military force used here refers to military means – air, naval and land – organized and trained in accordance with a specific doctrine

[950] DEFENSE PLANNING Based on studies conducted by the Ministry of Defense between 2012 and 2017, the implementation of a new capability-based defense planning model is contemplated

[951] According to the planned design, the process begins at the political level to guide both the use of force and the development of capabilities through the development of the respective guiding documents

[952] The strategic level planning process begins based on the definitions contained therein

[953] The output of the strategic planning phase will be the "Force Employment" plans and the "Strategic Capability Development Plan," documents whose preparation will be under the responsibility of the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff

[954] The planning system: Regulatory basis The enactment of Law No. 20,424 introduced several regulations relating to National Defense planning into the sector's legislation

[955] These rules gave rise to a planning system with a greater number of participating actors, both civilian and military, and with more precise links between the different levels of responsibility within the system in decision-making

[956] In general, the law identifies the actors who must intervene in the system and establishes their corresponding functions

[957] In particular, it expanded the participation of actors at the political level of responsibility by establishing the dimension of so-called "primary planning" or policy at this level

[958] Similarly, it redefined the role of the Joint Chiefs of Staff by giving this collegiate body an advisory role, establishing that the Minister of National Defense must seek its opinion on various matters, including both primary and secondary planning, as well as the acquisition of war materiel

[959] Because of its advisory nature, the opinion of the Joint Chiefs of Staff is not binding on the Minister, but the timing of the stipulated consultations must be considered in the planning process

[960] However, Law No. 20,424 does not specify how the functions that are the responsibility of each actor in the system should be carried out

[961] Some rules, particularly those relating to planning the employment of force, were subsequently developed by Supreme Decree No. 113, published in

[962] This Decree repealed Supreme Decree No. 37 of 1950, which until 2010 was largely the basis of National Defense planning

[963] The new Decree provided some relevant definitions, such as clarifying that the National Defense planning process is a single process, comprised of a primary and a secondary segment, and describing the documentation that makes up primary and secondary Defense planning, although with an emphasis on the dimension of the use of force

[964] He also pointed out that primary documentation refers to sectoral documentation—and not national documentation, as established by Supreme Decree No. 37 of 1950—and is of a political nature, while secondary documentation is of a military nature and corresponds to that produced by the joint strategic level in the general and unique planning process

[965] Development of a new planning methodology Within the normative and conceptual framework of the Defense planning system, the Ministry of Defense has made progress in developing a methodology that, along with materializing the functions assigned by law to the different actors in the system, replaces a planning modality that, with regard to capacity development, still follows the "threat-based" planning model, which prevailed universally during the 20th century, also in Chile

[966] In this model, capability building is conceived as the satisfaction of “requirements” in the face of that specific threat

[967] However, there are several reasons why a different planning model is needed

[968] Among these reasons, the following can be mentioned: • Greater international uncertainty: The foundations of the strategic environment prevailing during the 20th century have been altered, both at the global level (areas of influence, types of actors involved, etc

[969] as regional (new policies, new spaces for cooperation, new actors with transnational capacity

[970] • The possible scenarios are diverse and the factors that influence their configuration are more difficult to anticipate

[971] • Military technology, which is part of the Defense capabilities, is expensive, and the economic context in which decisions are made regarding the allocation of financial resources requires complex and transparent financial choices

[972] At the more limited level of National Defense, there are also changes and challenges to be taken into account: • At the ministerial level, there has been a lack of long-term planning

[973] • Planning has focused on a single area of National Defense activity (the defense of the country), without considering mission areas where sectoral capabilities are also employed

[974] • Regarding the employment of force, planning is the responsibility of ministerial bodies at the political and strategic levels and is top-down; in turn, current capacity development planning is the responsibility of each branch of the Armed Forces

[975] For reasons such as those indicated, the Ministry of Defense began a transition process from a threat-based approach to a capability-based approach

[976] This is a new planning methodology that avoids the fragmentation of capability development planning into partial and independent processes; adequately links the mission areas of National Defense, the capabilities to operate within them, and the financial resources necessary to generate and sustain those capabilities; integrates financial planning from the outset of capability generation; allows for a coherent catalog or portfolio of capabilities and makes optimal use of the financial resources allocated to the sector; considers non-material solutions (that save resources) as the first option when facing operational challenges; and provides control mechanisms at various procedural stages for decisions that may involve the investment of financial resources

[977] Some initial steps toward modernizing and integrating defense planning, especially with regard to capability development, were taken in 2004, with the ministerial decision to adopt international standards on the subject, and in 2006 with the adoption of the joint operational planning methodology used by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO

[978] Beginning in 2012, work began on developing a new long-term plan for capacity development

[979] This effort was primarily exploratory and culminated in some conceptual advances

[980] Among other results, it enabled the development of a comprehensive categorization of the life-cycle costs of military materials and equipment (including weapons systems), which was ultimately reflected in a "Conceptual Primer on Life-Cycle Cost Elements," formalized in

[981] In 2014, the decision was made to redesign the entire National Defense planning process

[982] The task of generating the preliminary design of a new planning process began in 2015, and continued in 2016 with the scheduling of various presentation and debate sessions aimed at perfecting and validating the design

[983] The methodological option adopted is planning based on the standard capacity-based planning model, but adapted to the conditions and realities of the national environment

[984] In the conceptualization of this model, the fundamental elements are the following: The notion of planning under conditions of uncertainty

[985] • The idea of developing capabilities to effectively address a series of potential challenges and circumstances, and • An economic framework with growing demands where increasingly conditional choices must be made

[986] According to this model, the procedural approach to capability-based defense planning (employment and development) is intended to follow a top-down approach, so that decisions and guidelines adopted at the political level are reflected in secondary or strategic planning documents, under the responsibility of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, from which, in turn, projects are derived through which the EMCO itself and the military institutions will materialize the military needs identified in strategic planning into capabilities

[987] The rationale behind this design is to unify the capability development process under the centralized guidance of the political level and the strategic conceptualization of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, with all the advantages this entails in terms of streamlining the investment project portfolio

[988] From a procedural perspective, the idea is to view defense planning as a single, connected process that integrates everything from top-level policy guidelines for both short-term employment and long-term capability development to the development of the corresponding strategic plans, the evaluation of investment projects arising from capability development, and the allocation of financial resources to implement these projects, if approved

[989] The diagram represents only the first layer of the new planning process; therefore, the subprocesses into which each element is broken down, as well as the actors involved, are not shown

[990] Planning at the political level of National Defense Conceptually, the new methodology designed uses a series of basic concepts from the standard capability-based planning model, although adapted to the National Defense environment

[991] The main concepts are the following: a) Capacity The new planning methodology is based on the guiding concept of “capacity”

[992] Capability is one of the defining elements of any planning process, but in the standard capability-based planning model, it is not conceived as a requirement for war material in response to a previously designated or defined threat

[993] Rather, it is understood as a "skill" that allows assigned missions to be accomplished, and this skill depends on the combination of different intervening factors

[994] Comparative experience shows that the combination of factors that produce a "capacity" does not have a unique syntax among countries that employ this type of planning methodology; however, some of the factors involved are standard, as they are found in all syntaxes of the concept

[995] These factors are the following: Material, Infrastructure, Human Resources, Training and Organization

[996] The formal structure of the concept of capability is unique and includes both standard, universally accepted factors and specific factors defined by each country

[997] In Chile's case, capacity has been defined as the "ability derived from the interdependence and balancing of capacity factors to fulfill the missions assigned to National Defense

[998] Similarly, the factors considered in the configuration of a capability are those indicated below, in a purely syntactical and non-priority order: Material, Training, Human Resources, Organization, Doctrine, Infrastructure, Sustainability and Information (MERDIOSI

[999] Areas and Sub-Areas of the National Defense Mission The mission areas correspond to groups of general and interrelated missions, assigned to the National Defense institutions by different legal or regulatory bodies of the country

[1000] Comparative experience indicates that Mission Areas should be defined that are stable over time and in a limited quantity to avoid complicating subsequent analyses

[1001] Among other advantages, the Mission Areas provide an overview of the work of National Defense and provide a common framework for planning the development of capabilities and defining the duties or tasks that Defense must consider for their fulfillment at all levels of leadership

[1002] The five National Defense Mission Areas that have been defined are: Defense, International Cooperation, National Emergency and Civil Protection, Contribution to National Development and State Action, Security and Territorial Interests: • Defense Groups the missions aimed at preventing and deterring the use of military force against the country or rejecting aggressions and hostile acts against the population, sovereignty, territorial integrity, national resources and assets and national interests

[1003] Regarding the population, it also considers the protection, rescue, and evacuation of nationals facing dangerous situations abroad, in accordance with Article 15 of Law No. 20,297, which amends Law No. 19,067 on the entry of foreign troops into national territory and the departure of national troops abroad

[1004] • International Cooperation Groups the missions to be carried out in the international sphere, by virtue of international security commitments assumed by the country in accordance with national interest

[1005] It covers a broad spectrum of missions, including those contributing to the preservation of world peace and international security, as well as humanitarian demining and humanitarian aid; it also considers cooperation in the face of disasters in other countries, measures to build mutual confidence, and other contributions to foreign policy

[1006] National Emergency and Civil Protection Includes missions carried out as a contribution to other State bodies to address natural or man-made disasters, minimize or neutralize their immediate effects, cooperate in solving the problems that arise, and support the recovery of affected infrastructure and services

[1007] • Contribution to National Development and State Action It brings together the missions related to the use of the Armed Forces in support of the community and other State agencies to address social needs, requirements derived from public policies and the country's development initiatives

[1008] It also includes related missions to support the integration of border and island areas and environmental preservation

[1009] It includes tasks that the Armed Forces carry out in the scientific and technological field to develop their own capabilities, and which can simultaneously contribute to the creation of knowledge in areas of specific national interest, in addition to the development of national cartographic elements

[1010] • Security and Territorial Interests Concentrates the missions that the institutions of the Armed Forces execute to, according to current legal norms, control maritime and air traffic, air and maritime activities, in addition to preventing and controlling illicit activities in the national maritime territory and airspace

[1011] It also includes the responsibility to safeguard human life at sea and in the event of air accidents, including search and rescue actions in territorial areas under Chilean control by international agreements

[1012] It also includes missions to maintain and consolidate the national presence in Antarctica, and to maintain public order, which national legislation assigns to the Armed Forces during states of constitutional exception—particularly states of catastrophe—or during elections

[1013] Since Mission Areas are general and abstract categories that cover the entire spectrum of missions assigned to National Defense, they must be broken down into more concrete and manageable subsidiary categories, called "Sub-Mission Areas," to facilitate the determination of the tasks or activities to be executed in each area

[1014] The Mission Areas and Sub-Areas scheme is a political resolution and its terminology must be differentiated from military language, which is specific to the strategic planning level

[1015] Furthermore, this framework facilitates the integration of the planning process into the allocation of direct and indirect financial resources, both in the areas of force employment and capability development

[1016] The General Areas of Capability encompass a set of generic and related skills

[1017] The way in which the General Areas of Capability are stated may vary from one country to another

[1018] However, some of them are inherent to the functions of any military force and are therefore considered standard: for example, Integrated Command and Control, Intelligence, Mobility and Strategic Projection, Sustainability

[1019] The definition of the General Areas of Capacity is a political resolution

[1020] Hence, to the standard-type areas, the political authority must add those it deems relevant to the national case, so that the definition determines specific areas of capacity that it aspires to have or even those it decides to renounce

[1021] In order to make the analysis of the capabilities to be developed more manageable, it is necessary to break down the General Capability Areas into more specific areas

[1022] Based on comparative experience, it is common for the level of analysis that immediately derives from the General Capability Areas to be called "Military Capabilities" (or Military Capability Areas), a term already assimilated into National Defense planning

[1023] The definition of these military capabilities, based on the General Areas of Capability, is a responsibility that falls to the military establishment (strategic level

[1024] Level of Ambition It is a concept from the capacity development aspect of the general planning process

[1025] It corresponds to what the political leadership of Defense expects military institutions to be capable of doing in the long term and is a fundamentally qualitative expression of the capabilities it hopes to achieve within that time frame

[1026] The “Level of Ambition” is the final result of a series of subprocesses carried out within the framework of Defense policy planning

[1027] It is communicated to the strategic planning level (secondary planning) through a directive document that initiates the planning phase of military capability development at this level

[1028] Similarly, for the planning aspect of the use of force, a series of subprocesses are executed within the dimension of political planning of Defense, culminating in the determination of a desired final state or desired political effects

[1029] That is, what the political leadership of defense wants as a result of the use of current capabilities (in inventory) of National Defense, in a short and medium-term time horizon

[1030] It is communicated at the strategic planning level through a directive document that initiates the planning phase for the employment of force at this level

[1031] AREAS OF INTEREST From the perspective of National Defense, it is relevant to identify the areas of interest because they affect the analysis of the present and future strategic environment on which defense planning is based, since it is reasonable to focus this analysis on the established areas of interest and not on areas of the world or matters that have not been considered

[1032] They correspond to geographical areas of the world that are important to the country or to a certain order of matters that are considered to be of national interest, according to definitions at the political decision-making level

[1033] They are substantially included in the guidelines of the Defense Policy and Foreign Policy

[1034] The geographical areas of interest are those mentioned in chapters IX and X of this Book

[1035] In turn, the following can be considered thematic or functional areas of interest to National Defense, among others: - The promotion of global peace - Participation in international security regimes - Climate change - Cyberspace - Presence in outer space - Technological development and innovation

[1036] Planning at the strategic level of National Defense a) Planning the use of force It is the planning process that derives from the decisions adopted in the planning done at the political level (primary) and that is carried out at the strategic level

[1037] This process envisions the use of joint forces for various anticipated short-term scenarios, based on the new Defense planning methodology

[1038] The above is directly related to the development of the capabilities that the State requires to achieve the objectives in the different Mission Areas of National Defense

[1039] For this definition, different short-term scenarios must be analyzed, prioritized by the political level in primary planning

[1040] Force employment plans The generation of plans at the strategic level will be done in accordance with the Mission Areas and scenarios determined by political decision

[1041] It will consider the joint use of force, and the types of plans contemplated will be based on those established in the Joint Doctrine of the Armed Forces Operational Planning Manual

[1042] This document serves as a reference for defining the type of force employment plans that are expected to be implemented in the new general capability-based defense planning process

[1043] b) Capacity development planning It is the planning process that derives from the decisions adopted in the planning done at the political level (primary) and that is carried out at the strategic level with the purpose of developing the National Defense capabilities that the State requires to face different possible scenarios, within a determined time horizon, long term, in a context of greater uncertainty and an economy in which complex options must be made

[1044] Planning at this level will conceive the technical response that, as defined in the corresponding directive issued by the political level, translates into the generation of military capabilities to coherently structure a force with flexible and versatile characteristics

[1045] This directive will specify the "Level of Ambition," a fundamental input for the initiation of strategic planning for capacity development

[1046] While this is a qualitative concept regarding what the State requires from its military instrument in the future, its formulation must contain some quantitative factors that allow for better guidance for the strategic level process

[1047] This is a process that must be carried out under a joint and integrative vision, and the technical responses may consist of material or non-material solutions, the latter being the ones that should be considered first

[1048] To this end, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, in coordination with the military institutions, translates the Level of Ambition into a Level of Effort Required of the Force

[1049] The concept expresses what the joint force must execute, given a given scenario, in a defined time and with conditions for its materialization (Source: Joint Chiefs of Staff

[1050] For this purpose, the most demanding scenarios are considered within the framework of the Level of Ambition

[1051] At the strategic level, this means considering the uncertainty surrounding the country's potential challenges as a key factor at this stage of planning, along with the relevant financial baseline estimates

[1052] The planning process at the strategic level considers the same concept of "capability" already defined and takes into account both existing capabilities within the operational structure of the Armed Forces and those that are entirely new

[1053] In both cases, each MERODISI factor (see) must be analyzed and related to the others

[1054] In the case of existing capabilities, if one of these factors is degraded, there will be a gap that will need to be filled

[1055] Capacity gaps will give rise to different solutions—material or non-material—that must be tested through an analysis of alternatives

[1056] The outcome of this analysis is the recommended solution to be incorporated into a joint capability development plan, developed with input from all three branches of the Armed Forces at the joint strategic level

[1057] The ultimate purpose of joint capability development planning, and its expression in the plan, is to provide a coherent vision of the capabilities that need to be developed or acquired and to guide the Armed Forces institutions regarding the timelines, priorities, and impacts to be achieved

[1058] Planning at the level of the institutions of the Armed Forces essentially resides in the units of the operational structure of each of them

[1059] These plans must also contain provisions to guide capacity development based on the requirements and obligations imposed by national legislation, particularly those established by special laws

[1060] In a later phase, such plans will be formulated in terms of investment projects

[1061] Planning and Policy Decision The overall capability-based planning process is organized according to the standard integrated planning and control scheme called the “Planning, Programming and Budgeting System” (PPP), as shown in Figure

[1062] Considering the PPP scheme, the Planning stage itself will conclude, at the political level, with the presidential directives that give way to the preparation of the investment drafts derived from the Strategic Plan for Capacity Development and the institutional plans that are subsidiary to it

[1063] Subsequently, a programming stage will be entered with the preparation of the investment plans derived from the master plan and the previous subsidiary plans

[1064] At this stage, these preliminary projects will be subject to an analysis process, where, in addition to strategic aspects, political criteria and financial factors (for example, historical costs, committed resources, and new resources) will be considered

[1065] The purpose of this analysis is to determine which of the preliminary projects could become definitive investment projects

[1066] Responsibility for this analytical body will fall to the Undersecretariat of Defense, by virtue of the authority granted by law to this body to propose guidelines to the Minister for Armed Forces acquisitions, including those for weapons systems and other equipment

[1067] In addition to relevant personnel from the Undersecretariat of Defense, the analysis that materializes will include personnel from the Undersecretariat for the Armed Forces, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and the three branches of the Armed Forces

[1068] The analysis of the preliminary projects will be presented to the Minister of National Defense, who will then submit it to the President of the Republic for a final decision on the investments to be made by the sector for capacity development. These investments will become part of the National Defense Acquisition Program over a specific period

[1069] Implementation program of the new planning methodology The transition to a Defense planning methodology such as the one described is a complex process that has effects on various aspects of the sectoral organizations involved

[1070] Therefore, it has been deemed necessary for the design and validation phases to continue with a gradual implementation program for the new methodology, which could even consider regulatory modifications

[1071] Hence, implementation should include a sufficiently extensive trial phase to correct those aspects that hinder the operational efficiency of the entire Defense System

[1072] Given that the regulatory framework of Law 20.424 has allowed for the definition of a planning cycle with a limited time horizon, coinciding with the term of each government, a trial phase of the implementation program could cover the period between 2018 and

[1073] Once the appropriate adjustments have been made to ensure that the processes considered at the different levels and organizations, as well as the interfaces between them, operate smoothly, the new capability-based defense planning methodology could finally be implemented

[1074] Implementation program of the planning methodology Phases of the process: Study and design: 2014-2015 White March: 2018-2022 Regime: 2022–> Validation and verification: 2016-2018 CONDUCT, DEVELOPMENT AND USE OF DEFENSE MEANS The conduct of Defense is the result of a process through which decisions are made to direct the country's defense

[1075] This process flows through a regulated and systematized structure, from the highest decision-making level of the State, which corresponds to the President of the Republic in his capacity as political leader, to the strategic level

[1076] At this level, strictly military, leadership is embodied in the exercise of command for the use of force and is the responsibility of the strategic leader

[1077] “Force” refers to the means developed, organized and trained to achieve defense objectives

[1078] The leadership process is carried out on two levels: the political leadership of Defense and military leadership, which is reflected in strategic, operational, and tactical leadership

[1079] The function of the Ministry of National Defense (MINDEF) is to materialize the process of leadership of Defense, a responsibility that the Constitution and the law attribute to the President of the Republic

[1080] With the entry into force of Law No. 20,424 in 2010, the Ministry transitioned from an organization primarily focused on the administration of the sector and its dependent agencies and institutions to one essentially dedicated to the management of Defense

[1081] The political leadership of Defense is essentially carried out within the Ministry of National Defense through the actions of its principal agencies: the Minister, as a direct collaborator of the President of the Republic, with the support of the Undersecretariat of Defense and the Undersecretariat for the Armed Forces, as well as with the advice of the Joint Chiefs of Staff on matters within its jurisdiction

[1082] Additionally, the Minister has a military advisory body, the Joint Chiefs of Staff

[1083] Chart No. 7 ORGANIC STRUCTURE OF THE MINISTRY OF NATIONAL DEFENSE

[1084] The organizational structure of the Joint Chiefs of Staff is illustrated and described in Chapter XXII

[1085] The chart of the organizational structure of the Ministry of National Defense does not include agencies or institutions dependent on the Ministry or related to the State through any of the Ministry's bodies: Army Factory and Workshops, Navy Shipyards and Workshops, National Aeronautics Company, General Directorate of National Mobilization, and National Academy of Political and Strategic Studies

[1086] Contents of Chart No. 7: - MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENSE - UNDERSECRETARY OF DEFENSE - JOINT GENERAL STAFF - CABINET - DIVISION OF PLANS AND POLICIES - DIVISION OF INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS - DIVISION OF TECHNOLOGICAL DEVELOPMENT AND INDUSTRY - DIVISION OF PROJECT EVALUATION - MILITARY AID - UNDERSECRETARY FOR THE ARMED FORCES - DIVISION OF INSTITUTIONAL AFFAIRS - ADMINISTRATIVE DIVISION - DIVISION OF BUDGET AND FINANCE - LEGAL DIVISION - AUDIT DIVISION Source: Prepared by the authors b) The leading functions of the Minister of National Defense The Minister of National Defense (MDN) is the political authority in charge of leading the sector in accordance with the instructions given by the President of the Republic

[1087] For these purposes, the law grants him responsibilities such as the following: - Proposing to the President of the Republic the National Defense Policy, the Military Policy, other sectoral policies and the primary planning of National Defense

[1088] Approve, in accordance with the instructions issued by the President of the Republic for this purpose, the secondary planning of National Defense

[1089] Collaborate with the President of the Republic in the conduct of National Defense in the event of an external war or international crisis that affects the external security of the Republic

[1090] Collaborate with the President of the Republic in the exercise of supreme command of the Armed Forces and in the other special powers in matters of defense and external security established in Article 32 of the Political Constitution of the Republic

[1091] Propose, for the President of the Republic's resolution, the strategic objectives specific to the function of the Armed Forces and their priorities

[1092] Assume, when the President of the Republic so decides, the coordination of the work of the various ministries in matters necessary for National Defense

[1093] Approve the joint doctrine and regulations proposed by the Joint Chiefs of Staff

[1094] To preside over and convene the Joint Chiefs of Staff

[1095] THE JOINT CHIEFS OF COMMANDERS IN CHIEF (LAW No. 20,424) Article 10.- The Joint Chiefs of Staff shall be the advisory body of the Minister of National Defense on common matters of the Armed Forces relating to the development and use of military means

[1096] The Minister of National Defense shall request the opinion of the Joint Chiefs of Staff on the following matters: a) On primary and secondary planning of national defense and on joint doctrine and regulations

[1097] On the creation or activation of commands, forces or other maneuvering bodies, divisions or units of a joint nature

[1098] On the allocation of land, naval, air, or joint resources to operations carried out in situations of external war or international crisis affecting external security, as well as on the allocation of resources to peacekeeping missions

[1099] On institutional, common and joint acquisitions of war material

[1100] e) On other matters of a common or joint nature that the Minister deems appropriate to submit for consideration

[1101] Article 11.- The Joint Chiefs of Staff shall be convened by the Minister of National Defense, who shall preside over it, and shall be composed of the Commander-in-Chief of the Army, the Navy, the Air Force, and the Chief of the Joint Chiefs of Staff

[1102] The Deputy Chief of the Joint Chiefs of Staff will act as its secretary

[1103] The Undersecretariat of Defense (SSD) is the collaborating body of the Minister of National Defense, fundamentally dedicated to the formulation of policies, plans and doctrines of a general nature and applicable to all agencies in the sector

[1104] This Undersecretariat is also responsible for proposing to the Minister policies and guidelines for the Ministry's international cooperation activities in matters of security and defense, in coordination with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs

[1105] It is also responsible for evaluating acquisition and investment projects submitted by defense sector agencies and proposing and coordinating sectoral policies for the scientific, technological, and industrial development of National Defense

[1106] The Undersecretariat for the Armed Forces (SSFFAA) The Undersecretariat for the Armed Forces is the body of collaboration of the Minister of National Defense in those matters that relate to the formulation of policies and the management of administrative affairs and processes that the Ministry of National Defense and the Armed Forces require for the development of the force and the fulfillment of its functions

[1107] To this end, it carries out a range of activities related to personnel, finance and budget matters, and management control of the sector

[1108] Among others, the following: Perform the corresponding administrative functions in relation to matters of a territorial, environmental, social responsibility or development collaboration nature that are the responsibility of the Ministry or its dependent agencies

[1109] Study the financing of acquisition and investment projects for the Armed Forces

[1110] Propose to the Minister and coordinate sectoral policies for National Defense personnel in matters within their jurisdiction

[1111] Propose recruitment policy to the Minister

[1112] Military Leadership a. The Joint Chiefs of Staff (EMCO) Law No. 20,424 transformed the National Defense Chiefs of Staff into the Joint Chiefs of Staff and defined it as the permanent working and advisory body of the Minister of National Defense on matters related to the preparation and joint employment of the Armed Forces

[1113] The definition of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the description of its functions are found in Chapter XXII

[1114] Advances in joint institutions Law No. 20,424 entailed a redesign of the organization of the defense system in which the Joint Chiefs of Staff develops the strategic planning for the employment of force and its Chief assumes command of the forces assigned to operations, in the event of an international crisis that affects the external security of the Republic or a foreign war

[1115] Under this law, any other form of non-joint employment remains implicitly under the respective institutional control

[1116] The Commanders-in-Chief of each military institution carry out force development planning and exercise command of their own branch's resources in a separate and distinctive manner, under the general direction of the Ministry

[1117] The above represents the general rule, with some exceptions where other tasks fall under the command of the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, such as his role as the National Military Authority for Peacekeeping Operations or the command of joint organizations in peacetime (Northern Joint Command and Southern Joint Command

[1118] The establishment of the Joint Chiefs of Staff made it possible to address highly complex current military problems, such as force preparation and its use under a joint leadership model

[1119] The Joint Chiefs of Staff has made substantial progress in its institutional development

[1120] Notwithstanding this, a perfected defense system requires strengthening the position of the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, so as not to limit his command exclusively to the use of force in situations of crisis or foreign war, but rather to extend it to joint action in other situations in times of peace

[1121] In addition, the current legal status governing the Joint Chiefs of Staff must be strengthened to provide it with greater powers and capabilities that facilitate its operations

[1122] This implies a review and deepening of the organizational and operational design agreed upon in

[1123] To advance in this direction, the Ministry of Defense's policy objective in the area of joint action was defined as the establishment of a sectoral agenda to promote the development and implementation of joint action, with the aim of moving toward a force modality designed to act jointly, at all levels, and in any situation or time

[1124] The Ministry of National Defense has prepared a bill for the development of joint institutions

[1125] Development of capabilities and employment of defense resources The development of capabilities and employment of defense resources are the other two major processes of the defense system, and they materialize the planning in these areas

[1126] a) Capacity development This process aims to generate the military capabilities necessary to carry out the tasks or activities contemplated in the different Mission Areas of National Defense

[1127] Currently, most of this process is carried out within each of the Armed Forces' institutions, which generate the acquisition and investment projects for weapons systems

[1128] These projects are evaluated and rated by the Ministry of National Defense for the President of the Republic's consideration, and if approved, the corresponding financial resources are allocated

[1129] In the future, and based on the new planning methodology to be implemented, force development is expected to be modified to incorporate planning processes in this area, which will be handled by political-level bodies within the Ministry of National Defense and by the strategic-level bodies through the joint institutional framework of the National Defense

[1130] b) Use of defense means

[1131] This is a process that Law No. 20,424 substantially established in the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the body that develops strategic plans for National Defense in situations of international crisis and armed conflict, and whose Chief, in his capacity as strategic leader, has the power to exercise command of the forces assigned to the operations, coming from the operational structure of the Armed Forces

[1132] The new Defense planning methodology incorporates new analytical processes and integrates a scenario-building stage to be carried out at the political level of the Ministry of National Defense, maintaining strategic employment planning in the manner established by Law No. 20,424 through the powers assigned to the Joint Chiefs of Staff, an agency that also plans the employment of resources in the event of catastrophes or national emergencies and for the participation of Chilean forces in peacekeeping operations

[1133] The differentiation between institutional and operational lines of command The sectoral modernization implemented since 2010 follows the provisions of the Political Constitution of the Republic and Law No. 18,948, Constitutional Organic Law of the Armed Forces

[1134] The Commanders-in-Chief who exercise supreme command of each armed institution are responsible for the design, development, preparation, and maintenance of their respective institution's operational resources, in accordance with the guidelines issued by the Ministry of National Defense. They are also responsible for commanding their own institution's resources when special laws so provide

[1135] In turn, the military authority responsible for strategic leadership exercises command over the resources assigned to operations, whether in situations of international crisis or armed conflict

[1136] This authority is exercised by the figure created by law under the name of Chief of the Joint Chiefs of Staff

[1137] It is responsible for achieving the strategic objectives planned and established by the political authority, which are materialized in secondary or strategic planning, the development of which is also its responsibility

[1138] This allows for the creation of a joint organization for the use of resources in situations affecting external security, and which operates in peacetime on development tasks necessary for the use of force

[1139] Chile is a country that prioritizes the law over the use of force and, consequently, respects the international legal system that governs the use of the latter

[1140] For this reason, Chile has decided to have a military power capable of satisfactorily fulfilling the definitions established for its use in the National Defense Policy: legitimate defense, deterrence, and international cooperation

[1141] Legitimate defense The Chilean State recognizes as situations of legitimate use of military force those established within the framework of the Charter of the United Nations

[1142] In Article 51, the Charter recognizes every State's inherent right to self-defense, individually or collectively, in the event of an armed attack against it

[1143] The Charter defines it in the following terms: “Nothing in this Charter shall impair the inherent right of individual or collective self-defense in the event of an armed attack against a Member of the United Nations, until the Security Council has taken the necessary measures to maintain international peace and security

[1144] Measures taken by Members in the exercise of the right of self-defense shall be immediately communicated to the Security Council and shall not in any way affect the authority and responsibility of the Council under the present Charter to take at any time such action as it deems necessary to maintain or restore international peace and security

[1145] Pursuant to the Charter of the United Nations and other treaties signed and ratified by our country, Chile reaffirms its commitment to peace and its determination to abide by international law and apply the principles of international dispute settlement

[1146] In exercising its inherent right to self-defense, Chile will always act in accordance with international humanitarian law and the general rules of national law applicable in these circumstances

[1147] This framework constitutes the context in which the National Defense Policy and the strategic attitude in the use of force are oriented

[1148] modalities OF USE OF THE MEANS OF DEFENSE In 2010, at the Review Conference of the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, held in Kampala (Uganda), the States Parties to the Statute, including Chile, approved an amendment that describes the crime of aggression, establishes its penalty and sets out the conditions under which the International Criminal Court would exercise jurisdiction over such crime

[1149] Following the conclusions of the Conference, a bill was submitted to the National Congress in May 2016, initiated by a parliamentary motion, amending Law No. 20,357 on crimes against humanity, genocide, and war crimes and offenses to incorporate the crime of aggression and extend war crimes to include noninternational conflicts

[1150] Article 1 of Law No. 20,424, Organic Statute of the Ministry of National Defense, introduced the concept of crisis into our legal system, stating that in the event of an international crisis that affects the country's external security, the President of the Republic will order the activation of the respective national defense plans and will order the use of military forces, handing over the strategic management of the assigned means to the Chief of the Joint Chiefs of Staff

[1151] It should be kept in mind that, in a crisis situation, the use of force is occasional and may take the form of deterrence or effective but limited and restricted use, in accordance with the political objective of avoiding the escalation of the conflict in the context of a foreign policy based on the principle of the peaceful resolution of disputes

[1152] Deterrence The concept of deterrence encompasses both an effect and the action that causes it

[1153] It is an effect insofar as it corresponds to a psychological or subjective dimension that occurs in a potential adversary

[1154] Deterrence is not intended to paralyze all actions contrary to the national interest, but rather to instill in potential adversaries the conviction that the cost of coercive interference against their own vital interests will be higher than the benefits to be obtained

[1155] It is an action that can be understood as a form of force used to inhibit a potential adversary from acting coercively against one's own vital interests and to influence the adversary to adopt non-coercive courses of action

[1156] Deterrence as a form of force must be clearly distinguished from the threat of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of a State, or any other form of force contrary to the purposes of the United Nations, an issue expressly prohibited by the Charter

[1157] Deterrence is a legitimate form of force, which does not involve coercion or military coercion

[1158] The threat, on the contrary, is an illegitimate act, prohibited by the jurisdiction issued by the United Nations regarding relations between states

[1159] PRINCIPLE OF ABSTENTION FROM THE THREAT AND USE OF FORCE By Resolution No. 2625, approved at the XXV Session of the General Assembly, dated October

[1160] The United Nations issued its “Declaration on Principles of International Law concerning Friendly Relations and Cooperation among States in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations.”

[1161] In the "Recitals" of this Resolution, the United Nations states that it is "the duty of States to refrain, in their international relations, from exercising military, political, economic or any other form of coercion against the political independence or territorial integrity of any State

[1162] The operative part of the document establishes the principles on which relations between States must be based and formulates the principle of abstention from the threat or use of force in the following terms: "Every State has the duty to refrain from resorting to the threat or use of force to violate the existing international boundaries of another State or as a means of settling international disputes, including territorial disputes and problems concerning the boundaries of States

[1163] The incorporation of the use of cyberspace in contemporary conflict has generated reflections on deterrence that need to be considered: Some of the elements that typically make up a deterrence strategy in the physical world are very difficult to interpret and apply in the digital world

[1164] For example, attribution (assigning responsibility for an attack) is done with certainty and with little difficulty in the physical world, but in the digital realm it is very difficult to confidently attribute an attack to a state or a group under the control of a state

[1165] • There is uncertainty regarding the magnitude of the effects caused by a cyberattack: unlike an armed attack, where there is always a clear idea of the magnitude of the damage inflicted, a cyberattack may not produce any obvious effects, or it may produce a massive catastrophe (including the entire range of intermediate damage

[1166] This makes determining the proportionality of a legitimate response very complex. • Although several countries have declared that cyberwarfare must be limited in accordance with international law on armed conflict and enshrined in documents that stipulate rules on cyber engagement operations, such as the Tallinn Manual 2.0, there is still no specific, internationally validated legal instrument on the use of force in cyberspace, beyond the current norms of Public International Law, International Humanitarian Law, International Human Rights Law, and International Law against cybercrime, contained in the criminal activity criminalized in the “Budapest Convention on Cybercrime,” promulgated in November 2001 (also known as the Budapest Convention

[1167] International cooperation Chile considers the modalities of use of force in a context of international cooperation under the generic name of “International Cooperation Operations”

[1168] They correspond to the use of National Defense resources to address situations of breaches of the peace and threats to international stability, or to respond to catastrophic situations in other countries

[1169] Conceptually, the international cooperation carried out by Chile's National Defense contributes to promoting international peace and stability, thereby generating the external security necessary for the country's development

[1170] Every international cooperation operation must be limited to a framework of legitimacy and legality reflected in the resolutions of the United Nations Security Council, under the provisions of Chapters VI, VII and VIII of the United Nations Charter

[1171] At the same time, they can also respond to agreements and commitments that Chile, as a sovereign nation, has established with other states and international organizations

[1172] Decisions regarding the deployment of military assets in an international cooperation operation are governed by the rules contained in Law No. 19,067, which establishes the procedures for the withdrawal of national troops from the territory of the Republic, and its amendment by Law No. 20,297, of December 13, 2008, which included a chapter on peacekeeping operations

[1173] In the case of operations authorized within the framework of humanitarian cooperation and disaster risk management, the National Defense adheres to the principles expressed by the international community through the Oslo Guidelines, the Hyogo and Sendai Framework for Action, as well as by the relevant United Nations agencies (OCHA and UNISDR

[1174] Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) and United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNISDR) a) Peace Operations Over the last three decades, Chile has gone from being a contributing country with observers to being an actor that provides troop contingents and military equipment to the international effort to maintain peace under the mandate of the United Nations

[1175] • Legal framework for peace operations Chile's participation policy is defined in Supreme Decree SSG

[1176] No. 68, of October 14, 1999, “Chilean National Policy for Peacekeeping Operations.”

[1177] Within this framework, Chile understands a peace operation to be any international deployment of civilian or military resources and public order and security measures that, under the command and control of the United Nations or a State or command expressly designated and authorized by it, has the direct objective of contributing to the consolidation of a cessation of hostilities

[1178] Both peacekeeping and peace enforcement operations are included

[1179] The decisions are made by the President of the Republic in accordance with the provisions of the Political Constitution of the Republic and the relevant laws: Law No. 19,067 of July 1991, and Law No. 20,297 of May 2008, which modifies the former and establishes standards for the participation of Chilean troops in peacekeeping operations

[1180] The decision must take into consideration the joint report submitted by the Ministers of Defense and Foreign Affairs, as established in Supreme Decree No. 75, Creating the Interministerial Commission on Peacekeeping Operations, dated September

[1181] Among others, the general criteria for Chile's participation in peace operations are contained in both the policy and the aforementioned laws: • Operations involving Chilean forces must satisfy the national interest, must obey a mandate from the United Nations Security Council, and no contingents will be formed or made available to the United Nations or any particular State for it to autonomously determine their deployment

[1182] The Public Sector Budget Law will contain an annual provision to cover the costs of preparing and participating in Chilean forces or personnel in peacekeeping operations, the distribution of which will be carried out by the Ministry of Defense

[1183] In accordance with Article 9 of the law on the departure of national troops abroad

[1184] The President of the Republic must request the Senate's approval for the deployment of troops to certain International Cooperation Operations through a reasoned document signed by the Ministers of Foreign Affairs and National Defense

[1185] • Command of national military and police troops and resources participating in peacekeeping missions will be the responsibility of the Chief of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, who will be the National Military Authority for such purposes

[1186] • Once the national forces have been deployed, operational command of the Chilean military and police contingents is assumed by the National Military Authority in the person of the Chief of the Joint Chiefs of Staff

[1187] The peacekeeping force commander or police commissioner designated by the UN in the mission area, as appropriate, is given operational control of the Chilean contingent

[1188] Nothing stated above may be construed as a waiver or limitation of the right of the State of Chile to comply with obligations that may arise from other bilateral international agreements

[1189] CHILE'S PARTICIPATION IN PEACEFUL OPERATIONS The first precedent of Chile's participation in this type of mission occurred on the occasion of the deployment of Chilean observers in 1935-1936 in the Neutral Military Commission for the Chaco-Boreal, prior to the creation of the United Nations Organization (UN

[1190] The trajectory since then includes the presence of Chilean troops in operations carried out by the United Nations, as well as by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, the European Union, and the Organization of American States
