[1192] The UN's approach to peacekeeping has evolved as a result of the need to provide a relevant response to the new characteristics of armed conflict, such as the asymmetry of means and tactics, the presence of unconventional threats (organized crime, international terrorism, etc.), and the existence of state crises that pose threats to international security

[1193] By virtue of this change, since the early 1990s Chile has deployed contingents in Cambodia (1992-1993), Iraq (1991-1992/1996-1998/2000-2003) and East Timor (2000-2003); in Cyprus, together with the Argentine Task Force (2001 to the present); in Bosnia-Herzegovina (1997-2002/2004 to the present), first as part of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) Force and then with the European Union; in the UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH) (2004-2017); in the Congo (MONUC), through a medical unit; and, more recently, in the UN Multidimensional Integrated Mission for the Stabilization of the Central African Republic (MINUSCA) and the United Nations Political Mission and Verification Mission in Colombia (since

[1259] Resolution 1325 on "Women, Peace, and Security," adopted by the United Nations Security Council on October 31, 2000, calls upon Member States and the Secretary-General to undertake a series of actions aimed primarily at incorporating a gender perspective into peacekeeping operations; increasing women's participation at all levels of decision-making in institutions and mechanisms for conflict prevention, management, and resolution; considering the special needs of women and girls in the negotiation and implementation of peace agreements; protecting women and girls from gender-based violence in situations of armed conflict; and supporting local women's peace initiatives

[1260] This resolution constitutes a historic milestone in the recognition and promotion of women's participation in situations of armed conflict, also highlighting their significant contribution to peace processes

[1261] Indeed, Resolution 1325 addresses the situation of women from the different roles they can play in armed conflicts: • As decision-makers at the international and national levels; 144 X CHAPTER MODALITIES OF USE OF DEFENSE MEANS National Defense Book of Chile 2017 • As members of forces deployed in conflict zones; • As women victims of conflicts and gender-based violence; and • As women who, nevertheless, can be victims simply by living in a conflict zone, are empowered to negotiate and resolve the conflict, rebuild their societies, and work for peace

[1262] This Resolution has been followed by seven resolutions that have deepened certain aspects, reaffirming the need for its application

[1263] Chile promotes the incorporation of a gender perspective and greater participation of women in defense, specifically a greater role in conflict prevention, management, and resolution within the framework of United Nations peacekeeping operations

[1264] CHILE AND UN SECURITY COUNCIL RESOLUTION 1325 Chile was the first country in Latin America to generate an action plan to implement UN Security Council Resolution 1325 in 2009, and in 2015 the Second National Action Plan was presented, which includes compliance indicators in accordance with United Nations guidelines, and assumes, among others, the commitment to include this issue in the regional defense agenda, promote and disseminate the Women, Peace and Security agenda and work on the development of training and capacity building programs that contribute to the institutionalization of the gender perspective in the defense sector based on the improvement of human capital

[1265] The implementation of this Second Action Plan was entrusted to an Interministerial Working Group, coordinated by the Ministry of National Defense and comprised of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Women and Gender Equality, with active participation from the Ministry of the Interior and Public Security

[1266] In this context, training and consulting sessions are held annually at the global, regional, and bilateral levels

[1267] Of particular note is the partnership with the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC), which, since 2014, has implemented the Regional Workshop on the Implementation of Resolution 1325, bringing together representatives from the Ministries of Defense, Foreign Affairs, and Women's Affairs from Latin American and Caribbean countries

[1268] Chile also co-chairs the Group of Friends of the global study on Resolution 1325, along with Canada, Ireland, Japan, and Namibia, and is also part of the Network of Focal Points on Women, Peace, and Security, along with Spain, Canada, the United Arab Emirates, Japan, and Namibia

[1269] Chile's participation in this area is recognized for promoting the "Women, Peace, and Security" agenda in high-level dialogues and meetings at the United Nations, the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States (CELAC), the Central American Integration System (SICA), the Union of South American Nations (UNASUR), the Conference of Defense Ministers of the Americas (CMDA), and the bilateral agenda with neighboring countries, as well as for its contribution to dissemination and training in executive bodies of governments in Latin America and the Caribbean

[1318] The work carried out by the Demining Units has cleared 153 mined areas (with 150,402 mines destroyed) out of a total of 194 areas, representing a progress level of 78.87%

[1319] The challenges assumed by Chile, managed by the National Demining Commission (CNAD), are the following: Regarding demining operations, the aim is to declare the national territory free of antipersonnel mines during

[1322] Compliance with the Oslo Convention Chile shares the global concern generated by the use of cluster munitions, as these weapons cause civilian casualties during and after conflicts

[1323] That is why our country actively participated in the "Oslo Process," which began in 2003 and culminated in the Oslo Convention in

[1324] The Oslo Convention on Cluster Munitions is the multilateral instrument addressing the problem of indiscriminate conventional weapons

[1325] The Convention prohibits the comprehensive use, production, and transfer of cluster munitions and sets strict deadlines for the destruction of stockpiles and the clearance of contaminated land

[1326] It also requires States to provide comprehensive assistance to survivors and affected communities

[1327] Cluster munitions are a type of conventional weapon that claim civilian casualties, both during and after a conflict

[1328] About 30% of the submunitions contained in cluster bombs do not explode after being launched from aircraft, helicopters, missiles, or artillery shells

[1329] On August 2, 2011, Chile published Decree No. 59, which promulgates the Convention on Cluster Munitions

[1330] Prior to this date, cluster munitions were used in Chile by the Army and Air Force only for instruction and training purposes, within military ranges, access to which is prohibited to civilians

[1331] For this reason, no victims were reported from this type of ammunition

[1332] In September 2013, the Minister of National Defense signed the certification declaring the Chilean Army free of cluster munitions, in accordance with the commitment made under the Oslo Convention

[1333] This initiative was planned and executed by the "Factories and Workshops of the Agreement between SECNAD and the Undersecretariat of Healthcare Networks, signed on March 1, 2011, for all people with and without the FONASA pension system; between SECNAD and the Army Health Command, signed on September 23, 2013, to cancel the differences in benefits (co-payment), and between SECNAD and CAPREDENA- Salud, signed on July 28, 2014, to cancel the differences in benefits (co-payment

[1334] Army” (FAMAE), in accordance with the procedures established for the demilitarization of this type of ammunition

[1335] In compliance with the Convention, Chile sent an updated report on the national situation in this area to the United Nations in 2017. This report, among other points, states that cluster munitions are not produced in the country, specifies that there have been no victims of this type of munition, and reaffirms its commitment to clean up contaminated military ranges

[1336] Defense's Contribution to New Global Challenges In relation to climate change, science and technology, and cyberspace, important challenges for the international community, the defense sector aims to contribute - through participation in various international cooperation bodies and the establishment of links with other countries - to promoting transparency, building trust and establishing agreements and standards that allow for adequate international governance of these phenomena

[1337] a) Cooperation on climate change There is consensus that this issue requires global treatment and an effort from various international actors to reduce the risks posed by global warming and its associated effects

[1338] Indeed, this has been the path followed, with various countries committing to efforts to reduce their impact on the climate and, at the same time, adapt to changing environmental conditions

[1339] This has been done primarily through a series of Conferences of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP

[1340] This effort has had a counterpart at the national level, where Chile has committed— under the principle of "shared but differentiated responsibilities"—to reducing its greenhouse gas emissions and has voluntarily established policies and plans on the matter that include the various sectors of the State

[1341] XI CHAPTER INTERNATIONAL DEFENSE AND SECURITY National Defense Book of Chile 2017 PRINCIPLE OF COMMON BUT DIFFERENTIATED RESPONSIBILITIES According to Principle 7 of the Rio de Janeiro Declaration on Environment and Development: “States shall cooperate in a spirit of global solidarity to conserve, protect and restore the health and integrity of the Earth’s ecosystem

[1342] Since they have contributed in varying degrees to global environmental degradation, States have common but differentiated responsibilities

[1343] Developed countries recognize their responsibility in the international pursuit of sustainable development, given the pressures their societies exert on the global environment and the technologies and financial resources available to them

[1344] In this context, there is also a constant inclusion of the issue of climate change in the various multilateral organizations and forums related to international security and defense; in addition to a tendency to share experiences and generate cooperation mechanisms on climate change among the defense sectors of various countries

[1345] In the case of National Defense in Chile, the inclusion of this issue in the international sectoral agenda has been encouraged, both in the content of bilateral cooperation mechanisms and in multilateral bodies in which the country participates, for example, in the Conference of Defense Ministers of the Americas

[1346] CLIMATE CHANGE AT THE CONFERENCE OF DEFENSE MINISTERS OF THE AMERICAS The XII Conference of Defense Ministers of the Americas included among its four axes a specific one to address climate change, which was called “Environmental Protection and Resilience” and in which Chile acted as Co-rapporteur

[1347] Furthermore, climate change was incorporated into several points of the Final Declaration of the same 2016 Port of Spain CMDA, among which the following stand out: The role of the Defense sector in supporting civil authorities in matters of environmental protection and climate resilience. The commitment to adopt energy and technological innovations to help mitigate and adapt to the effects of climate change. The establishment of an ad-hoc Working Group on environmental protection and climate resilience

[1348] b) Cooperation in science and technology New technological developments and their strategic consequences have a wide range of impacts and challenges for Defense

[1349] The efforts required to address these challenges generally exceed the internal capabilities of each state, hence the need to maintain and strengthen international cooperation agreements and exchanges in the scientific and technological fields of the defense sector, both bilateral and multilateral

[1350] An example of these efforts are the various bilateral cooperation initiatives in science, technology, and defense industry promoted by the Ministry of Defense, such as those listed in international cooperation agreements

[1351] On the other hand, international cooperation is important to confront and regulate complex technological developments, such as lethal autonomous weapons systems

[1352] Although development in these areas is still in its infancy, Chile's international stance has been to address this issue under the umbrella of international humanitarian law, proposing the need to introduce a moratorium or preventive ban on the development of this type of weaponry

[1353] CHILE AND LETHAL AUTONOMOUS WEAPONS SYSTEMS In the field of the development of lethal autonomous weapons, the United Nations has held several conferences, the last of which took place in Geneva in

[1354] These bodies have included panels of experts and have analyzed the current levels of autonomy, the ethical implications, and their consequences for international security

[1355] Chile's position regarding the possible use of weapons systems without human control is one of preventive prohibition, as upheld at the Informal Meeting of Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems, held in Geneva in

[1356] This argument is based on the following reasons: • Although fully autonomous weapons systems do not yet exist, the absence of a regulatory framework could lead to deliberate violations of International Humanitarian Law that could lead to impunity for certain attacks due to the impossibility of attributing their authorship

[1357] • Chile (along with other countries) has raised the need to develop measures of mutual trust and transparency, as well as emphasizing the need to introduce a moratorium or preventive prohibition on the development of LAWS

[1358] It should be noted that many countries have already committed to not developing this type of weapon

[1359] However, the area of scientific and technological cooperation is of particular interest to the defense sector, and efforts will continue to be made to deepen bilateral and multilateral exchanges and developments, while taking into account current international regulations, particularly international humanitarian law

[1372] Establishing and ensuring standards of good conduct in cyberspace that are shared by states, achieving transparency commitments, and generating confidence-building measures to address cybersecurity are complex challenges

[1373] Solutions require coordinated responses that involve both states and international organizations

[1374] An important step forward in this area is the Convention on Cybercrime, adopted by the Council of Europe and known as the Budapest Convention, which has been in force since

[1375] Although its purpose is to combat crimes committed through the Internet and other computer networks—particularly computer fraud, child pornography, hate crimes, and network security breaches—it is the first international instrument to address the need for cooperation among states against the illicit use of cyberspace

[1376] In April 2017, the President of the Republic signed the Decree promulgating the Budapest Convention, which entered into force in August of the same year

[1377] Adherence to this international instrument is one of the measures committed to in the National Cybersecurity Policy, developed within the Interministerial Committee on Cybersecurity, whose Executive Secretariat is headed by the Undersecretariat of Defense of the Ministry of National Defense

[1378] Chile's accession to the Budapest Convention will allow the country to participate in a rapid and effective system of international cooperation, in addition to receiving assistance for developing national capabilities to better combat cybercrime

[1379] To date, the Convention has been ratified by 54 states, including Chile, the first South American country to accede to this instrument

[1380] Defense cooperation with the various regions of the world Chile understands that a preferential view towards Latin America and the inter-American system in general does not mean ignoring the importance of maintaining a cooperation effort with other countries and regions, as long as the country's interests are not limited to its territoriality or its immediate surroundings

[1381] The country is globally embedded in the world through Latin America, and its security is interdependent with global security

[1382] For this reason, the Defense seeks to promote cooperation with various regions, strengthening existing relationships and promoting new cooperative links, in accordance with the evolution of the international scenario and the State's policies

[1403] Cooperation with Europe is part of a political commitment to promoting and protecting international peace and security, the full observance of democracy, human rights, and the promotion of sustainable development and equity in all its aspects

[1404] Chile maintains historic bilateral ties with European states and formal relations with European institutions

[1405] In 2002, Chile signed an Association Agreement with the European Union, many of whose members are also suppliers of investment, technology, and equipment for our country's military capabilities

[1406] In addition to trade and political consultation aspects, Article 14 of this agreement includes cooperation in foreign and security policy

[1407] This instrument states: “To the greatest extent possible, the Parties shall coordinate their positions and take joint initiatives in appropriate international forums, and shall cooperate in matters of foreign and security policy.”

[1408] Chile closely monitors the European Union's Common Security Policy, which reflects and expresses the practices developed by the region to address various problems and threats

[1409] In 2014, Chile and the European Union agreed to institutionalize bilateral dialogue on security and defense and signed the Framework Agreement for participation in the European Union Crisis Management Operations System

[1410] Both instruments reflect the mutual interest in developing active cooperation in matters within the scope of international security and defense

[1411] XI CHAPTER INTERNATIONAL DEFENSE AND SECURITY Chilean National Defence Book 2017 AGREEMENT ON CRISIS MANAGEMENT OPERATIONS BETWEEN CHILE AND THE EUROPEAN UNION In November 2010, the High Representative of the European Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy invited the Chilean Minister of Foreign Affairs to open negotiations to develop an agreement between the EU and Chile establishing a framework for participation in EU crisis management operations. This was then authorised by the Council of the European Union

[1412] Negotiations took place between 2011 and

[1413] The agreement was signed in Brussels on January

[1414] The Agreement has been in force since October 1, 2015, following the completion of its parliamentary approval process

[1415] Through this instrument, Chile became the first Latin American country to join the European Union's crisis management operations system as an associate

[1416] Considerations of the agreement: The agreement significantly reduces negotiations and legal procedures for joining a transaction, limiting it to the exchange of diplomatic notes

[1417] Its most notable aspects are: The Crisis Management System not only involves the deployment of military personnel, but also considers the deployment of police and civilian government personnel

[1418] Chile becomes part of the portfolio of potential contributors in the eyes of European planners

[1419] • The agreement is not mandatory; that is, Chile will always have the sovereign power to decide when, where, and with what means to participate, in accordance with its interests and national legislation

[1420] It also maintains its sovereign powers in the event of a decision to withdraw from an ongoing operation

[1421] • The agreement ensures that criminal jurisdiction over personnel on mission remains in the hands of Chile

[1422] • The agreement leaves open the possibility that Chile may be exempt from contributing to the common costs of the operation, although it does not establish this a priori, so this situation must be evaluated on a case-by-case basis

[1441] Contribution of defense to cooperation in the American continent and the construction of a Zone of Peace in South America Defense cooperation seeks to promote the deepening of ties with countries in the American continent and strengthen regional organizations, fostering mutual trust and transparency in matters of security and defense

[1442] To this end, Chile promotes security cooperation, which is based on the construction and development of a multi-level network of regimes—both neighboring and subregional, Latin American and inter-American—that together provide security for the region

[1443] At the continental level, Chile considers it important to have an inter-American defense system that is agile, flexible, and robust, with broad representation in the subregions that make up the American continent

[1444] For this reason, it supports its review and updating so that it can adapt to changing times

[1445] Both the OAS and the Conference of Defense Ministers of the Americas (CMDA) have made efforts in this regard

[1446] Additionally, the Chilean defense sector's contribution has focused on areas in which the country has expertise, such as natural disasters and emergencies, in addition to promoting the inclusion of gender issues as a crosscutting axis of sectoral policies

[1447] The countries of the Americas permanently face challenges regarding disasters and catastrophes of natural or anthropic origin

[1448] Addressing these phenomena represents a major challenge for countries with diverse needs and limited resources

[1449] In this context, the Armed and Security Forces in the Americas must regularly play a supporting role—if not a direct intervention—given their available capabilities and resources

[1450] While there are subregional and regional efforts to assist those in need, contributions can be scattered rather than coordinated when the response is in an inorganic manner, without a regulatory framework and without a coordinating system

[1451] In this context, during the XII CMDA, the Chilean delegation presented a proposal regarding the creation of an inter-American coordination system for defense against disasters and catastrophes and the creation of an Ad Hoc Working Group to study this issue

[1494] a) Argentina Chile and the Republic of Argentina have developed a relationship of defense cooperation, which constitutes a paradigmatic example of the change experienced in strategic relations in the South American region

[1495] Both countries were able to transform a relationship of conflict into one of high-intensity defense cooperation

[1496] This has been possible thanks to a shared desire to peacefully resolve the border disputes that characterized the bilateral relationship, as well as to pursue a process of bilateral integration within the framework of the Southern Common Market (MERCOSUR), as well as in the Latin American region

[1497] In the field of defense, both countries share a common commitment to increased transparency between states and a growing contribution to international security, especially in United Nations peacekeeping operations

[1498] This shared will has enabled the development of institutionalized cooperation through the establishment of various defense mechanisms and agreements

[1499] MILESTONES IN THE CHILEAN-ARGENTINE RELATIONSHIP Two major milestones have marked the last 30 years of bilateral relations between Chile and Argentina: the 1984 Treaty of Peace and Friendship and the Maipú Treaty of Integration and Cooperation signed in

[1500] Both milestones have laid the foundation for developing increasingly cooperative bilateral relations in multiple areas, with the defense sector being particularly important

[1501] The bilateral architecture for defense cooperation includes the following bodies, mechanisms, and military exercises: Meeting of the Political and Strategic Dialogue between Defense Ministers (DPE) Meeting of Vice-Ministers of Defense Consultation Meetings between the Ministers of Foreign Affairs and Defense (2+2) and Binational Meeting of Ministers of Chile and Argentina Permanent Committee on Security (COMPERSEG) Consultation Meetings between the Defense Staffs of Chile and Argentina Solidarity Exercise Viekaren Exercise Cruz del Sur Air-Ground Exercises Combined Antarctic Naval Patrol (PANC) Combined Argentine-Chilean Antarctic Aid and Rescue Patrol (PARACACH) The efforts put into overcoming historical differences and building a cooperative defense perspective enabled both countries to explicitly address the elimination of their potential for conflict

[1529] Peru Chile and Peru share a close relationship, a history, and an important tradition of cooperation

[1531] Both countries converge in international multilateral institutions, such as the Pacific Alliance, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC), the Organization of American States, the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States, and the Union of South American Nations (UNASUR

[1555] SPECIFIC POLICIES IN PROCESS These are policies that respond to challenges that have acquired a relevant entity in the country, including the Defense sector

[1556] For this reason, the Ministry of National Defense has decided to formulate policies to address these challenges within the context of the guidelines the State has adopted in this regard

[1557] These challenges fundamentally relate to climate change, cyberspace, and technological innovation and development

[1558] Climate Change Policy for Defense According to the 2014 Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) report, the impacts of climate change on the essential infrastructure and territorial integrity of many states are expected to influence countries' security policies (IPCC

[1559] Chile is a member of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

[1560] According to the 2014 National Climate Change Adaptation Plan, the country is considered especially vulnerable: “it has low-lying coastal areas; arid and semi-arid zones; areas with forest cover and areas exposed to forest degradation; it is a country prone to natural disasters; it has areas prone to drought and desertification; it has urban areas with air pollution problems; and areas with fragile ecosystems, including mountain ranges.”

[1561] The Chilean government has made various efforts at the international level, signing agreements based on the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities; and at the national level, establishing institutional frameworks and action plans to address climate change

[1562] These voluntary actions have sought to contribute, on the one hand, to reducing harmful effects on the environment (mitigation measures) and, on the other, to adapting to the effects associated with climate change (adaptation measures

[1563] In the areas of security and defense, the IPCC reports suggest that climate change could have a stronger impact on the most vulnerable countries, reduce available resources, alter territorial and maritime borders, and affect military installations and the modus operandi of the armed forces

[1564] These and other effects of climate change on defense have generated the need to establish sectoral policies to address the phenomenon

[1565] Additionally, it is necessary to take into consideration that the Armed Forces are The initiatives relating to the environment and biodiversity, complementary to this matter, are mentioned in Chapter XIV

[1566] National Climate Change Adaptation Plan 2014, Ministry of the Environment

[1567] XII CHAPTER NATIONAL DEFENSE POLICY Book of National Defense of Chile 2017 important users of fossil fuels, which is why there is a challenge to establish mitigation measures that reduce their greenhouse gas emissions, with the use of new technologies and clean energy being the main alternative to contribute to stopping global warming

[1568] Based on these considerations, in 2015 the Minister of National Defense signed a Directive for the development of a Climate Change Policy for the defense sector, instructing the implementation of work that began with a strategic analysis of how the climate change phenomenon is impacting National Defense and its institutions

[1569] The Defense Sector's Climate Change Policy will be structured around three axes: climate change as a strategic variable, adaptation (of Defense and its institutions to the implications of climate change), and mitigation (measurement of greenhouse gases and measures to reduce them

[1570] In addition, international cooperation issues will be incorporated (to establish mechanisms that contribute, for example, to developing or adapting clean energy in the sector), as well as sectoral requirements (hiring and training of human resources, organizational structure, technology, and financial resources

[1571] Although the Ministry of Defense is part of the national environmental or climate change institutional framework, until now this State Secretariat had not initiated a process leading to the formulation of a specific climate change policy for the defense sector, but only initiatives on environmental protection had been carried out by the institutions of the Armed Forces, which were not organically linked to the national policy on this matter

[1572] Cyber Defense Policy Cyberspace has become a new global reality in a relatively short period of time

[1573] Thanks to the widespread use of the Internet since the 1990s, around half of the world's population now has some level of access to the Internet

[1574] In 2017, just over 70% of the population had some type of internet connection, allowing people to communicate better, conduct more transactions online, and take advantage of e-commerce

[1575] Various industries and services essential to the country, such as electricity, drinking water, and communications, are managed with a high level of dependence on network technologies, and their operation is dependent on the existence of a secure cyberspace

[1576] This dependency creates new risks and threats; National Defense must generate new capabilities to protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information, in order to protect people and their interests, both in national territory and abroad

[1577] Considering the above, in April 2017 the President of the Republic approved the first National Cybersecurity Policy

[1578] This is a state policy that, through five priority areas, describes a series of measures the country will implement over the coming years to protect our population, their information, identity, and economic and social well-being

[1579] This policy identified a series of risks to national cyberspace: internal incidents, natural disasters or force majeure events, hostile activities carried out by international actors, denial of service attacks, criminal activity in and through cyberspace, and finally, attacks on critical infrastructure (physical and information

[1580] Most risks are not confined to a specific institution; rather, their realization (and, therefore, protection) depends on various actors, generating a high level of interdependence that must be taken into account when analyzing these problems

[1581] This involves developing institutional and technological solutions that adequately implement the capacity for interoperation among various national public agencies, including civil society and the private sector, and with international organizations

[1582] Similarly, it is necessary to protect the State's information systems, but also those of other actors, with special emphasis on critical infrastructure such as strategic industries, transportation systems, and public utility services, among others

[1583] The private sector plays a key role in both the provision and use of these technologies; its participation in cybersecurity is essential to any initiative

[1584] From an international security perspective, conflicts between countries can also manifest themselves in cyberspace, both in times of peace and conflict

[1585] This reality has led some countries to develop specific defense policies for their cyberspace operations, outlining the principles the country will uphold regarding the development and conduct of its capabilities and, subsequently, the policies that National Defense will develop to ensure the maintenance of those principles and capabilities

[1586] Chile is currently developing the first version of its Cyber Defense Policy, which is scheduled to be presented in the last quarter of

[1587] Within this context, new challenges arise for the international community, among which are the global and crossborder nature of cyberspace, the growing number and type of cyberattacks, the difficulty of attributing their origin and the increasing ubiquity with which they occur (due to the exponential growth of devices connected to the network

[1588] The Chilean Government believes that cyberspace is not a natural environment, but rather must be subject to the same principles and norms of international law that govern relations between states. In areas where regulatory gaps exist, new international and national regimes and regulations must be created

[1589] For the aforementioned reasons, Chile and a growing group of states in the international community are promoting the development of new international norms, standards of good conduct in cyberspace, transparency commitments, and confidence-building measures that contribute to preventing the escalation of conflicts within cyberspace, as well as in other areas of defense resource use

[1590] A major challenge is to analyze and evaluate what interactions occur between the various forms of conflict and the technological phenomena described, and what solutions are or will be available to the problems these interactions pose

[1591] These solutions are not limited to the acquisition and operation of specific technologies, but rather require a coordinated response involving all those operating in cyberspace, with special consideration given to the training and awareness of these types of risks for the personnel involved and the general public

[1592] The Cyber Defense Policy is subordinate to the Defense Policy and, therefore, upholds the same basic principles mentioned in the previous sections of this Book: among others, respect for the sovereign equality of states; for Public International Law, which includes abstention from the use of force and the threat of force; and the right to self-defense

[1593] This, along with the promotion of democracy and respect for human rights, as well as the protection of the population, national interests, and territorial integrity

[1594] All these principles find full expression in cyberspace

[1595] The Cyber Defense Policy will also contain a series of provisions and areas of work that will allow for progress in compliance with the above principles, and a series of measures to promote the development of a set of capabilities to be developed in the National Defense sector

[1596] These capabilities involve not only the acquisition of material, but also the development of a doctrine for the use of digital capabilities; the training and development of personnel in digital security; the exchange of information and knowledge with national and international, public and private, response centers; and the development of software and tools to address local realities and needs, among other things

[1597] Towards a National Defense Policy on Science, Technology, Innovation and Industry Although concern for technological development has been present in Defense Policy for several years, with initiatives limited to military institutions and the incorporation of the issue in bilateral defense agreements (such as the Maipú Treaty between Chile and Argentina in 2009), it was not until the enactment of Law No. 20,424 in 2010 that the Ministry of National Defense had a Division dedicated to technological development and industry

[1598] Having such an organization has allowed the Ministry to focus its efforts on formulating its first public policy on science, technology, innovation, and the National Defense industry

[1599] Laying the foundations for such a policy requires a comprehensive understanding of the current situation and technological development trends at the national level, and how they relate to global trends

[1600] This vision would allow us to identify, organize, and prioritize the scientific and technological aspects of National Defense

[1601] From a preliminary perspective, the following general objectives appear plausible: the promotion of scientific and technological research, the development of the industrial base linked to National Defense, public-private collaboration, and the training of competent professionals in this technological field

[1602] CHAPTER XII NATIONAL DEFENSE POLICY Book of National Defense of Chile 2017 FOURTH PART MILITARY DEFENSE POLICY CHAPTER XIII

[1603] MILITARY POLICY

[1604] SECTORAL POLICIES IN THE FIELD OF MILITARY POLICY Military Policy is a public policy subsidiary to Defense Policy and embodies the objectives and guidelines that the Government of the Republic, through the Ministry of National Defense, directs to the Armed Forces in relation to the development of capabilities and the development of military institutions

[1605] In terms of capacity development, it sets standards for materials and equipment commonly used by the three institutions, criteria related to technology, logistics procedures, defense investments, and the control and modernization of financial resource management

[1606] Regarding the institutional development of the branches of the Armed Forces, it provides guidelines for their application in areas such as personnel (military career, human rights, education, recruitment and inclusion, among others

[1607] In short, Military Policy consists of a set of specific policies on various subjects, relevant both to the development of capabilities and to the fulfillment of the functions of defense institutions, which must be consistent with each other

[1608] XIII CHAPTER 186 MILITARY POLICY Book of National Defense of Chile 2017 MILITARY POLICY Military Policy is a public policy understood as the set of guidelines that the Ministry of Defense, within the framework of the Defense Policy, directs to the Armed Forces, including the Joint Chiefs of Staff, in the areas of force development and development of military institutions

[1609] It guides the work of the Armed Forces in specific, common and joint tasks, as a harmonious and coordinated whole

[1610] Specifically, it establishes criteria, standards and procedures, and lays the foundation for institutional policies in the areas it addresses

[1611] Approach Military Policy is configured as a set of sectoral policies aimed at responding to the challenges and needs of the Armed Forces in the two areas indicated above: the development of the force and the development of military institutions

[1612] In the formulation of Military Policy, inputs from other public policies are taken into account

[1613] These provide guidelines for moving forward in a coordinated manner toward achieving national objectives, particularly those related to security and development

[1614] This approach allows for the integration of Military Policy with all the areas of public policy that inform it

[1615] On the other hand, defense sector policies are public policies that respond to the frameworks established for them by the State

[1616] Sectoral policies must incorporate the guidelines that the State has defined across the board for its actions as a whole

[1617] In this regard, subjects such as human rights, gender policies, people with disabilities, indigenous peoples, sexual diversity, education, social responsibility, and the environment and biodiversity are of particular relevance

[1618] Organic-functional dimension of the Military Policy From the organic-functional perspective, by provision of Law No. 20,424, the Ministry of Defense is responsible for developing, evaluating and proposing the Defense Policy and the Military Policy

[1619] For its formulation, the Ministry relies on the Undersecretariat of Defense, which prepares them with the support of the Undersecretariat for the Armed Forces and with the advice of the State Joint Chiefs of Staff in matters within its jurisdiction

[1620] According to the law, the Undersecretariat of Defense is responsible for suggesting Military Policy to the Minister and ensuring its periodic updating and explanation

[1621] The basis for this lies in the impact that this policy, as such, can have on the matters that are the subject of the Undersecretariat's other functions: Defense Policy, political and strategic analysis aimed at developing and proposing an assessment of risks and threats to the country in the area of its external security, and primary planning for National Defense

[1622] In turn, the Undersecretariat for the Armed Forces is responsible for proposing to the Minister and coordinating specific policies specifically related to National Defense personnel in matters within its jurisdiction; proposing to the Minister and evaluating sectoral recruitment policy; performing all administrative functions related to territorial, environmental, social responsibility, or development collaboration matters within the jurisdiction of the Ministry or its dependent agencies; and proposing government guidelines for institutional policies on these issues

[1623] By considering government objectives and guidelines directed at the Armed Forces in relation to the development of capabilities and the fulfillment of the functions that are the responsibility of the Ministry of Defense itself and the military institutions, the specific policies in charge of this Undersecretariat are part of the Military Policy

[1624] The coordination of both ministerial bodies is essential to ensuring coherence between all sectoral policies within the framework of Defense Policy

[1625] Finally, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, in its capacity as an advisory body on matters of a joint nature, may contribute its analysis and opinions to the formulation of specific policies that impact such matters and inform Military Policy

[1626] XIV CHAPTER 188 SECTORAL POLICIES IN THE FIELD OF MILITARY POLICY Book of National Defense of Chile 2017 SECTORAL POLICIES

[1627] The policies considered in this Chapter are part of Military Policy

[1628] Most of them correspond to current policies, but are being updated in the context of the modernization of the Ministry of National Defense

[1629] Along with these policies, initiatives are included that address topics recently added to the sector's agenda: sexual diversity, indigenous peoples, and people with disabilities

[1630] Personnel Policy Refers to a set of matters related to the incorporation of personnel into the military institutions of the National Defense, their development while they remain in them and their graduation from them

[1631] Some of these matters have been traditionally addressed from the perspective of their operational impact

[1632] However, they can also be understood from a personnel policy perspective, which includes aspects such as training, capacity building, health, social security, and human rights, among others

[1633] An updated look at these issues suggests the need to advance comprehensive personnel management, in line with the sector's modernization process and the realities of Chilean society

[1634] Human Rights Policy One of the essential principles of coexistence in a democratic society is the recognition of the dignity of the human person

[1635] This translates into respect, promotion, and defense of human rights, and is materialized through the formulation and implementation of a State policy on the matter

[1636] The above is in line with the provisions of Article 5, paragraph 2, of the Political Constitution of the Republic, which provides that the exercise of sovereignty recognizes as a limitation respect for essential rights that emanate from human nature

[1637] He adds that it is the duty of state bodies to respect and promote these rights, guaranteed by the Constitution, as well as by international treaties ratified by Chile and currently in force

[1638] This constitutional provision incorporates the norms of International Human Rights Law into the national legal system, which implies its application in all actions carried out by State bodies

[1639] XIV CHAPTER SECTORAL POLICIES IN THE FIELD OF MILITARY POLICY Book of National Defense of Chile 2017 Respect for and protection of human rights is a matter of special concern to the international community, which has built systems to protect individuals through international regulatory instruments and mechanisms to promote these rights

[1640] Compliance with international treaties related to human rights engages the State's responsibility, and its obligations are enforceable domestically

[1641] To comply with the mandates emanating from International Human Rights Law and the norms contained in the Political Constitution of the Republic, the State of Chile has established a new institutional framework in this area: on January 5, 2016, Law No. 20,885 was published, which creates the Undersecretariat of Human Rights and adapts the organic law of the Ministry of Justice

[1642] This law assigns to the Undersecretariat the responsibility of providing advice and direct collaboration to the relevant Minister in the design and development of policies, plans, and programs related to the promotion and protection of human rights

[1643] The Ministry of National Defense, through the Minister of Defense, participates in this new institutional framework, joining the Interministerial Committee on Human Rights

[1644] The Committee's function is to advise the President of the Republic in determining the guidelines for the Government's intersectoral policy in this area

[1645] This Committee is specifically responsible for developing the National Human Rights Plan

[1646] • Human Rights in National Defense Sectoral policies relating to human rights are framed within the context of the obligations that all State bodies have in their capacity as guarantors and promoters of these rights

[1647] Their respect and promotion in the defense sector also applies to the members of the Armed Forces themselves, since, like everyone else, they are entitled to these rights

[1648] Its exercise, however, is carried out in accordance with special rules directed at the armed forces

[1649] This is explained by the very characteristics of military institutions, which require their members to respect the principles of obedience, professionalism, hierarchy, non-deliberation, and discipline

[1650] Likewise, respect and promotion of human rights extends to members of society - the civil population - during the exercise of the professional tasks that the military branches execute

[1651] In carrying out their duties, the Armed Forces play a fundamental role in ensuring security conditions that allow people to exercise their rights

[1652] This applies whether in actions related to humanitarian aid, in public security activities required by the Constitution and the law, or in situations of armed conflict involving combatant forces and the civilian population; the latter, in accordance with the norms of international humanitarian law

[1653] Advances in human rights in the defense sector Human rights have taken on a strong and necessary role in the public sphere

[1654] This increased prominence has generated significant changes in legislation and public policymaking, with direct impacts on state bodies and the conduct required of public officials, both civilian and military

[1655] This reality is applicable to the Ministry of National Defense and all its dependent bodies, including the Armed Forces

[1656] Under the powers and responsibilities granted to it by Law No. 20,424, the Ministry of National Defense has implemented various initiatives to incorporate relevant changes in the sector related to respect for and promotion of human rights

[1657] In a first area of action, on July 2, 2014, the Advisory Working Group on Inclusion and Non-Discrimination Policies was created by Ministerial Resolution, focusing specifically on matters of gender, sexual diversity, indigenous peoples, and persons with disabilities

[1658] Its purpose is to develop recommendations for policy development, advise on the implementation of an Action Plan, and engage with civil society organizations involved in this area

[1659] The establishment of the Advisory Working Group on Inclusion and Non-Discrimination Policies and the treatment given to the issues on its agenda have contributed to strengthening respect for the principle of non-arbitrary discrimination, which facilitates the incorporation of all Chileans into the Armed Forces

[1660] A second area of action relates to the work carried out by the Ministry of National Defense, including the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and the Armed Forces to review joint, common, and institutional regulatory standards and, as a result, introduce regulatory amendments to eliminate any provision that violates the principle of inclusion and non-arbitrary discrimination in the processes and actions carried out by military defense institutions

[1661] This review action has had in view, primarily, the adaptation of the regulatory regulations to the following legal texts and international treaties: 191 XIV CHAPTER SECTORAL POLICIES IN THE FIELD OF MILITARY POLICY Book of National Defense of Chile 2017 - Law No. 20,609, which establishes measures against discrimination

[1662] Law No. 20,422, establishing standards on equal opportunities and social inclusion for persons with disabilities; - Law No. 20,830, creating the civil union agreement; - Law No. 19,253, establishing standards on the protection, promotion, and development of indigenous peoples and creating the National Corporation for Indigenous Development (CONADI); - Convention No. 169, concerning indigenous and tribal peoples in independent countries, of the International Labour Organization (Supreme Decree No. 236, of October

[1663] A third area of action relates to human rights education

[1664] Policies for education and promoting a culture in this area focus on a continuous and comprehensive educational process, providing fundamental, specialized, and cross-cutting knowledge to civilian and military members of the defense sector

[1665] The Ministry of National Defense has coordinated initiatives to identify, systematize, and make visible the human rights content that should be part of the teaching programs at the Armed Forces' educational institutions

[1666] In a fourth area of action, relating to memory and human rights policies, the Ministry of National Defense has created the Human Rights Unit

[1667] Based within the Cabinet, this Unit aims to facilitate the flow of information between the judges who hear cases involving human rights violations and each branch of the Armed Forces, helping to provide timely and effective responses to the courts that require them

[1668] Finally, a fifth area of ministerial action concerns the decision to develop a sectoral policy on human rights

[1669] In accordance with the guidelines established in the National Human Rights Plan, developed in 2017 by the Interministerial Committee on Human Rights, the sectoral policy will contain a set of principles and objectives that will guide the preparation of plans, programs, and actions aimed at respecting and promoting the exercise of human rights within the Ministry, its Undersecretariats, dependent and related companies and services, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and the Armed Forces

[1670] XIV CHAPTER SECTORAL POLICIES IN THE FIELD OF MILITARY POLICY Chilean National Defense Book 2017 • Human rights challenges in the Defense sector The process aimed at strengthening respect for and promotion of human rights in the Defense sector considers the following challenges: - Implement the human rights policy of the sector, through the generation of a work plan that takes into account all the areas that this policy considers

[1671] Strengthen human rights education, seeking to develop attitudes based on respect for the approach to this subject in National Defense

[1672] Advance, in the Defense sector, in the development of a management capacity to monitor ongoing initiatives and implement new measures within this framework. Code of Military Justice The Ministry of Defense is promoting a reform of the Code of Military Justice with the aim of updating its provisions and bringing them into line with the most advanced standards in the field, particularly those imposed by the advancement of International Humanitarian Law in relation to armed conflicts

[1673] To this end, in 2016, a draft bill was submitted for pre-legislative processing. This bill introduces amendments to substantive military criminal law, the organization of military courts, the Military Public Prosecutor's Office, and the Military Criminal Defense Office, in order to improve standards of impartiality and independence

[1674] It also aims to rationalize the use of resources allocated to Military Justice and to improve procedural rules

[1675] The initiative also includes the idea of implementing, in the military jurisdiction, the criteria imposed by International Human Rights Law and the criminal procedural reform for the entire Chilean legal system, in terms of respect for due process standards

[1676] b) Gender policy

[1677] The Ministry of National Defense has made a commitment to gender equality

[1678] The document “Participation of Women in the Armed Forces,” published in 2005, set out the principles for the policy of integrating women into the Armed Forces

[1679] These principles remain in force and are as follows

[1680] XIV CHAPTER SECTORAL POLICIES

[1681] Equal opportunities between men and women • Integration in the professional career • Professional competence • Equity in treatment • Leadership responsibility towards female subordinates • Reconciliation of family and professional life in institutional planning

[1682] The ministerial policy aims to promote women's participation in various areas of National Defense, as well as to apply a gender perspective across the board in its strategic definitions and policy implementation, by opening, without discrimination, areas within military institutions that were previously restricted to their work

[1683] In 2017, women represented 14.4% of the Armed Forces personnel, including officers, permanent staff, seafarers, permanent civilian employees, and conscript soldiers

[1684] The distribution of women by branch is as follows: Army, 14.9%; Navy, 11%; and Air Force, 18.2%

[1685] Likewise, the ministerial policy seeks to prevent all forms of violence against women and to create appropriate channels for reporting, guidance, and protection, thus avoiding re-victimization

[1686] The Ministry of National Defense and the Armed Forces must act with due diligence to prevent, investigate, and punish violence against women within their jurisdictions

[1687] In peacekeeping operations, they must observe standards of conduct that prohibit sexual exploitation and abuse, promoting exemplary behavior among their peers and the civilian population

[1688] Human rights and gender education and training for members of the three branches of the Armed Forces should be considered a key tool for preventing arbitrary discrimination and violence against women

[1689] Of particular importance is the implementation by the State of Chile of Resolution 1325 "Women, Peace and Security" of the United Nations Security Council

[1690] Chile presented its first Action Plan on this matter in 2009, and its Second Action Plan in 2015, making it the tenth country in the world to generate a second-generation document on "Women, Security, and Peace

[1691] XIV CHAPTER SECTORAL POLICIES

[1692] IN THE AREA OF MILITARY POLICY The Action Plan is based on new Security Council resolutions and, above all, on new guidelines aimed at incorporating indicators for evaluating its compliance

[1693] It is structured around four thematic areas: • Prevention • Participation • Protection • Relief and recovery The execution of the Plan was handed over to an Interministerial Board made up of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Women and Gender Equality, and the Ministry of National Defense, which is in charge of coordination, with the Ministry of the Interior and Public Security joining as a participating institution

[1694] In the Defense sector, and following the guidelines of Resolution 1325, at the national level there has been progress in expanding the participation of women in the Armed Forces ⁴², promoting the participation of uniformed women in peacekeeping operations ⁴³, including the gender perspective in the training of the Matrix Schools, in specializations and post-graduate courses, as well as in the pre-deployment training of the contingent that participates in peacekeeping missions

[1695] In 2017, women represented 13% of the Armed Forces, including officers, permanent staff or seamen, professional enlisted soldiers, permanent civilian employees, and conscript soldiers, with a progressive increase in all branches

[1696] Since 2015, an official has been designated as the Gender Focal Point in peacekeeping missions in which Chile participates (to date, one has been appointed in Haiti and the Central African Republic), responsible for implementing a work program specifically designed to collaborate in the implementation of the 2nd NAP. At the ministerial level, the institutional framework for the inclusion of gender policies in the defense sector has been strengthened through the creation of Gender Units in the Undersecretariats and the Joint Chiefs of Staff

[1697] Progress has been made in eliminating discrimination through legal provisions, such as the publication in March 2017 of Law No. 21,001, which eliminated the Women's Military Service Scale of the Army and replaced it with a new Army Personnel Service Scale. This scale is henceforth composed of mixed personnel

[1698] Furthermore, this echelon currently includes hierarchical ranks from second lieutenant to colonel, which implies a lower maximum rank to achieve than in other line officer echelons

[1699] The new law, once in force, will allow those who serve in the force to eventually reach the rank of Brigadier General and will expand the pool of colonels for the ranks

[1700] Finally, at the international level, the inclusion of the “Women, Peace and Security Agenda” stands out in the international activity of the sector at a global, hemispheric and bilateral level. This topic is developed in Chapter X. c) Sexual diversity The objectives of inclusion and respect for sexual diversity, supported by the entry into force of Law No. 20,609, which establishes measures against discrimination, have made evident the need to review the institutional regulations of the Armed Forces

[1701] to comply with its standards and administrative regulations and prevent cases of discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity

[1702] Thus, the Human Rights Policy of the Ministry of Defense will provide, in accordance with DFL No. 3 of 2017, which establishes the consolidated text of the Organic Law of the Ministry of Justice and Human Rights, a specific line of action focused on: [Page 195] XIV CHAPTER SECTORAL POLICIES IN THE FIELD OF MILITARY POLICY Book of National Defense of Chile 2017 • Preparation of an action protocol against all forms of arbitrary discrimination, considering channels of guidance and protection of the complainants

[1703] Awareness campaigns for the various civilian and military sectors of the Defense sector

[1704] • Ongoing review of regulatory and doctrinal texts regarding the standards of Law No. 20,609, which establishes anti-discrimination measures. • Continued implementation of Law No. 20,830, which creates the Civil Union Agreement. d) Persons with Disabilities In this regard, the Ministry of National Defense's inclusion and non-discrimination agenda aims to integrate persons with disabilities into the defense sector

[1705] It includes the following initiatives: Implementation of Law No. 21,015, of June 2017, on the inclusion of people with disabilities in the workforce

[1706] • Maintain statistical information on persons with disabilities working in the Ministry and the three branches of the Armed Forces

[1707] • Continue compliance with and implementation of Law No. 20,422 of February 2010, which establishes standards for equal opportunities and social inclusion for people with disabilities, with special emphasis on measures to ensure the accessibility of buildings and information websites

[1708] e) Indigenous peoples Without prejudice to the activities previously carried out by the institutions of the Armed Forces in this area, since 2014 the Ministry of National Defense has launched a series of initiatives regarding the inclusion of indigenous peoples, which have been carried out in the Defense sector, among others: [Page 196] XIV CHAPTER SECTORAL POLICIES IN THE FIELD OF MILITARY POLICY Book of National Defense of Chile 2017 • The creation of the Indigenous Unit in the Ministry of National Defense to channel policies and actions in this area

[1709] • The creation of policies that allow descendants of indigenous peoples to learn about military work and motivate them to pursue a career in defense

[1710] • Compliance with the main obligations arising from Convention 169 of the International Labour Organization (ILO), especially that established in its Article 6 regarding indigenous consultation in cases of laws or public policies that affect them

[1711] Military Service Recruitment Policy The Directorate General of National Mobilization (DGMN), which is related to the Ministry of National Defense through the Undersecretariat for the Armed Forces, is the body responsible for directing and monitoring compliance with the legal regulations on mobilization and recruitment

[1712] In addition, it collaborates with public safety through weapons and explosives control, martial arts control, and citizen shooting control

[1713] Finally, it is established as the national authority for the application of the Chemical and Biological Weapons Convention, with the purpose of responding to the requirements of the military institutions of National Defense, public and private organizations, and the general public

[1714] Regarding recruitment, the law establishes that a contingent of young people must be incorporated into the Armed Forces annually and, in accordance with current constitutional and legal provisions, must perform military service

[1715] The current conscription system was implemented in 2006 and is based on the adoption of a military service model whose main characteristic is that, by constitutional provision, it remains a mandatory public duty for men

[1716] However, at the selection stage, it prioritizes the admission of those who voluntarily express their desire to fulfill this public duty

[1717] Thus, the quotas determined by the Armed Forces institutions are filled, first, with young male volunteers

[1718] If these are not sufficient, the needs are met by young, non-voluntary males

[1729] Young citizens who perform or carry out their military service in the Armed Forces make a personal commitment to serve their country. Therefore, in return and for their direct benefit, in addition to providing them with the appropriate military training, they are also provided with values and educational training that fosters their personal growth and their preparation for later entry into the workforce

[1732] Finally, it should be noted that military service allows young citizens who undertake it to identify or strengthen, as appropriate, their interest or vocation for a military career. This paves the way for them to subsequently enter their respective institutions as soldiers in the Professional Troop or as students at their parent schools, provided they meet the relevant requirements

[1733] Education policy in Defense Education in the Defense sector is inserted within the national higher education system, regulated by DFL No. 2, which establishes the consolidated, coordinated and systematized text of Law No. 20,370, with the non-repealed regulations of Decree with Force of Law No. 1, of

[1734] As established in the aforementioned regulation, the educational institutions listed therein, dependent on the Ministry of National Defense and belonging to the Armed Forces, are recognized by the State in the category of Higher Education

[1735] The integration of the National Defense teaching institutes into this category constitutes a relevant element of this public policy, as it allows education in the sector to align its criteria and quality standards with the levels required for all higher education institutions in the country

[1736] The above, without prejudice to maintaining the teaching characteristics of Defense, especially in the Armed Forces

[1737] In this context, education in the defense sector is primarily aimed at military students, although it also includes civilian students

[1738] In the case of civilians, the goal is to enable them to join the advisory and decision-making bodies of the Ministry of National Defense and the Armed Forces, helping to strengthen the processes of studying and analyzing issues from other perspectives and approaches relevant to defense

[1739] It is also a point of interest that there are educational institutes and study centers outside the defense sector, whether private or state-owned, that dedicate part of their work to generating research, outreach, and teaching projects useful to the defense sector

[1740] Page 200] XIV CHAPTER SECTORAL POLICIES IN THE FIELD OF MILITARY POLICY Book of National Defense of Chile 2017 • Direction of defense education and associated functions The directive work in the field of education is carried out by the Ministry of National Defense, by special mandate of the law

[1741] The aforementioned regulations stipulate that, among other things, higher education institutions of the Ministry of National Defense and the Armed Forces will communicate with the State through the Ministry of National Defense

[1742] To this end, the Ministry has the corresponding powers and the bodies created by Law No

[1743] As the body responsible for formulating military policy, the Undersecretariat of Defense participates in the field of defense education through the guidelines and emphasis it provides for the teaching, research, and outreach activities carried out by the National Academy of Political and Strategic Studies (ANEPE), in accordance with the needs of the Ministry of National Defense

[1744] Military education, as directed at the Armed Forces, concurs with the training, coaching and instruction processes for the preparation of the force and is carried out through the following functions and bodies: - Institutional Military Education: This includes content and competencies of specific application for each institution of the Armed Forces

[1745] The responsibility for guiding, planning, and programming this function rests with each branch of the Armed Forces

[1746] Common Military Education: This includes content and skills commonly applied in the Armed Forces

[1747] The responsibility for guiding this area lies with the Undersecretariat for the Armed Forces

[1748] Joint Military Education: This includes content and skills that enable the preparation of military forces for joint employment

[1749] The responsibility for guiding this area lies with the Joint Chiefs of Staff

[1750] • Challenges for education The field of education in Defense poses permanent and ongoing challenges for the sector, especially for the Ministry of National Defense in its leadership role, and for the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Armed Forces in terms of planning, programming and execution

[1751] Among these challenges, the following stand out: [Page 201] XIV CHAPTER SECTORAL POLICIES IN THE FIELD OF MILITARY POLICY Book of National Defense of Chile 2017 - Generate ministerial management capacity for the direction and guidance of sectoral education processes

[1752] Promote a teaching career statute in the Armed Forces with incentives and quality standards

[1753] Encourage the incorporation of methods and techniques, including educational technologies, that strengthen learning outcomes

[1754] Generate areas of applied research for the defense sector, in search of solutions to real and specific problems in the sector

[1755] Seek measures that tend towards efficient use of human and material resources for education

[1756] Incorporate learning objectives that, in addition to those specific to the field of defense and military topics, allow students to develop a holistic understanding of the society they are called to serve as members of the Armed Forces

[1757] Finally, in order to adapt education in the sector to the new human rights requirements established by the government, the Minister of National Defense ordered, in July 2017, the implementation of the human rights curriculum—known as the "Basic Core"—and its implementation in the Armed Forces' education and training programs on the subject

[1758] XIV CHAPTER SECTORAL POLICIES

[1759] IN THE FIELD OF MILITARY POLICY 14.2 Social Responsibility Policy⁵⁰ ⁵⁰ The topic is developed in more detail in Chapter XXVI

[1760] In 2008, the Ministry of National Defense enacted the National Defense Social Responsibility Policy (PRSD) as a way to enhance, systematize, and coordinate the activities of defense institutions other than their primary role, for the benefit of the country

[1761] The central objective of this policy, which is developed by the Undersecretariat for the Armed Forces, is to guide and frame all institutional actions that contribute to the country's sustainable development

[1762] NATIONAL ACADEMY OF POLITICAL AND STRATEGIC STUDIES (ANEPE) The Academy is a Higher Education Institution dependent on the Ministry of National Defense and recognized by the General Education Law (LEGE), whose purpose is to train a critical mass of specialists in matters related to Security and Defense for the country

[1763] In this context, ANEPE develops various activities in the areas of teaching, research, and outreach, aimed at increasing knowledge in this field for personnel from the Armed Forces, Law Enforcement and Public Security Forces, the State Administration, the private sector, and society as a whole, making it a privileged meeting point for these topics

[1764] In the teaching field, its Master's degree in International Relations, Security, and Defense is accredited for four years, a postgraduate program that joins a broad academic offering comprised of another Master's degree, a bachelor's degree, and several diplomas

[1765] The Center for Strategic Research and Studies conducts research and creates knowledge in the sector's fields from a multidimensional, complex, and strategic perspective. It is one of ANEPE's tools for fulfilling its educational, advisory, and integrative role with related organizations, both national and international

[1766] Finally, through its Outreach and Community Engagement activities, it disseminates and projects the Institute's National Defense thinking and academic knowledge in matters at the political and strategic levels of Defense, with an emphasis on areas of political, military, economic, administrative, and international relations sciences that relate to the country's security, defense, and development

[1767] Currently, ANEPE is undergoing a comprehensive modernization process, addressing the following priorities: Updating the Education Project by 2028, Strategic Development Plan with a horizon of 2022, Infrastructure Development Plan, Drafting of the ANEPE Staff Law, which will be submitted to the Executive Branch along with other supporting documents

[1768] XIV CHAPTER SECTORAL POLICIES

[1769] IN THE FIELD OF MILITARY POLICY

[1770] Initiatives related to disaster response According to the current legal framework, emergencies caused by natural disasters (such as earthquakes or volcanic eruptions) or man-made disasters (such as most forest fires) must be addressed by all the instruments available to the State, including the Armed Forces, to obtain results in the most efficient manner possible

[1771] State institutions, in a broad sense, have the essential capacity to establish coordination mechanisms that allow them to deploy and generate efficient responses after a higher-level order or resolution has been issued, but there must be sufficient legal support—establishing tasks, functions, and responsibilities—in the context of emergency response

[1772] Specifically, the institutions and organizations that make up the Defense sector have multiple capabilities to deal with natural disasters

[1773] In the case of the Armed Forces, their characteristics—level of readiness, discipline, development of specific plans, and dual institutional capabilities—allow them to be available whenever necessary

[1774] However, the capabilities of the Armed Forces can be applied in a limited or restricted manner in disaster or emergency situations

[1775] Their participation is limited to the actions established by the National Civil Protection System for disaster prevention, mitigation, and response

[1776] Above all, it must be understood in light of the eventual provisions of the future Civil Protection Law, which aims to create an agency to address emergency needs, establish a National Civil Protection Council, and implement a National Civil Protection Strategy to coordinate interinstitutional efforts during the prevention and response phases

[1777] The Ministry of National Defense is currently collaborating with the Ministry of the Interior to refine a bill establishing a National Emergency and Civil Protection System and creating the National Civil Protection Agency to coordinate inter-institutional efforts in the prevention and response phases

[1778] This initiative contains the following main ideas: • Contribute to the creation of a national system capable of providing an effective and timely response to emergencies that regularly affect the country, particularly by defining the role of the Minister of National Defense and the Armed Forces in these emergencies and their relationships with other State bodies

[1779] XIV CHAPTER SECTORAL POLICIES

[1780] IN THE FIELD OF MILITARY POLICY

[1781] the participation of the Armed Forces and the Ministry of Defense in emergency situations without a declaration of a Constitutional State of Exception

[1782] • Introduce greater development of the whole, granting greater powers to JEMCO in the event of a catastrophe

[1783] • Harmonize defense sector legislation, particularly Law No. 20,424, with disaster-related legislation, especially with regard to policy formulation and the role that the various ministerial bodies should play in this regard

[1784] Initiatives relating to the environment and biodiversity The environmental situation is a permanent concern of the State of Chile and, as such, constitutes an important aspect for the Ministry of National Defense

[1785] This is expressed both in the concern for preserving an environment suitable for the country's development and in the management of the sector's institutions, which make their capacities and skills available to collaborate in the preservation and care of the country's environment in accordance with the policies established by the State for this purpose

[1786] From the perspective of the Defense sector, Law No. 20,424 establishes the importance of environmental issues for the Ministry

[1787] The military institutions of the National Defense and other dependent agencies have progressively oriented their activities toward incorporating environmental considerations into their operations, mirroring the work of other armed forces in this area and enabling the development of international cooperation actions

[1788] This area can be considered from the general perspective of the environment, a subject in which the specific aspects of climate change and biodiversity stand out due to the relevance they have acquired recently

[1789] XIV CHAPTER SECTORAL POLICIES IN THE FIELD OF MILITARY POLICY Book of National Defense of Chile 2017 In 2014, the Council of Ministers for Sustainability and Climate Change updated the previous document under the title of “National Plan for Adaptation to Climate Change”

[1790] Since the publication of this document, plans have been developed for various sectors, as well as specific measures for some ministries, including the Ministry of National Defense

[1791] For the period 2017-2022, the Ministry of the Environment promulgated the new National Climate Change Action Plan, updated in its second version

[1792] Regarding biodiversity, since 2010, Chile has promoted one of the most decisive actions worldwide, creating protected areas in marine environments for their conservation and effective and equitable use

[1793] At the same time, in the Strategic Plan for Biological Diversity (2011-2020), Chile committed to the “Aichi Targets.”

[1794] This commitment establishes that, by 2020, at least 17% of the country's terrestrial and inland water areas and 10% of its marine and coastal areas will be under a conservation regime

[1795] For its part, the Ministry of National Defense is part of the Council of Ministers for the Development of an Ocean Policy, an entity that aims to address the challenges related to the protection of our oceans, which is closely linked to a general security issue and related to sustainable development, where the creation of conservation areas is an important part of said policy

[1796] The Climate Change Policy for Defense is detailed in Chapter XII

[1797] The National Ocean Policy is addressed in Chapter XXX and Chapter XL details initiatives to create conservation zones in our seas
